shelves.title: Home blood-pressure self-monitoring, with self-titration or telemonitoring
shelves.question: Does home self-monitoring of blood pressure, used to titrate treatment, lower blood pressure more than clinic-based usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/administration & dosage · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Antihypertensive Agents/administration & dosage · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory · Calcium Channel Blockers/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Self-monitoring used to titrate treatment lowered systolic blood pressure by about 3.5-5.4 mm Hg more than clinic-based usual care at 12 months in the TASMINH trials, and an individual-patient meta-analysis found the effect depends on co-interventions: self-monitoring alone had no effect (-1.0 mm Hg), while monitoring with systematic titration or support lowered systolic pressure by up to 6.1 mm Hg. All outcomes are blood pressure, a surrogate — no trial here reports cardiovascular events.

cards.headline: TASMINH2: self-monitoring with self-titration and telemonitoring lowered systolic pressure 5.4 mm Hg more than usual care at 12 months
cards.summary: TASMINH2: systolic pressure fell 17.6 vs 12.2 mm Hg at 12 months — a between-group difference of 5.4 mm Hg [2.4 to 8.5] for self-monitoring with self-titration and telemonitoring.
cards.people: 527 participants aged 35-85 years with blood pressure above 140/90 mm Hg despite treatment, in 24 UK general practices (263 self-management, 264 usual care; 480 in the primary analysis); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: From baseline to 12 months, systolic blood pressure fell by 17.6 mm Hg (95% CI 14.9 to 20.3) in the self-management group and by 12.2 mm Hg (9.5 to 14.9) in the control group — a between-group difference of 5.4 mm Hg (2.4 to 8.5; p=0.0004). At 6 months the difference was 3.7 mm Hg (0.8 to 6.6; p=0.013). Side-effects did not differ except leg swelling (32% self-management vs 22% control; p=0.022).
cards.watchOut: Unmasked trial; the intervention bundles self-monitoring, self-titration and telemonitoring, so the effect cannot be credited to monitoring alone. Outcome is blood pressure, not events.
cards.source: McManus RJ et al. Telemonitoring and self-management in the control of hypertension (TASMINH2): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2010 Jul 17;376(9736):163-72. PMID: 20619448. Registry ID: ISRCTN17585681 (record's databank).

cards.headline: TASMINH4: GP titration guided by self-monitoring, with or without telemonitoring, lowered systolic pressure 3.5-4.7 mm Hg more than clinic readings
cards.summary: TASMINH4: clinic systolic pressure 137.0 (self-monitoring) and 136.0 (telemonitoring) vs 140.4 mm Hg usual care — adjusted differences −3.5 and −4.7 mm Hg ; telemonitoring added nothing significant over self-monitoring alone.
cards.people: 1182 hypertensive patients older than 35 years with blood pressure above 140/90 mm Hg, in 142 UK general practices (395 self-monitoring, 393 self-monitoring plus telemonitoring, 394 usual care; 1003 in the primary analysis); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 12 months, clinic systolic blood pressure was 137.0 mm Hg (SD 16.7) with self-monitoring and 136.0 mm Hg (16.1) with telemonitoring versus 140.4 mm Hg (16.5) with usual care — adjusted mean differences versus usual care of -3.5 mm Hg (95% CI -5.8 to -1.2) for self-monitoring alone and -4.7 mm Hg (-7.0 to -2.4) for telemonitoring. Telemonitoring added nothing significant over self-monitoring alone (-1.2 mm Hg, -3.5 to 1.2). Adverse events were similar in all three groups.
cards.watchOut: Unmasked trial in poorly controlled hypertension; here clinicians titrated using the home readings — the active ingredient is titration guided by better data, not the monitor itself. No event outcomes.
cards.source: McManus RJ et al. Efficacy of self-monitored blood pressure, with or without telemonitoring, for titration of antihypertensive medication (TASMINH4): an unmasked randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2018 Mar 10;391(10124):949-959. PMID: 29499873. Registry ID: ISRCTN83571366 (record's databank, printed as 'ISRCTN 83571366').

cards.headline: Individual-patient meta-analysis: self-monitoring alone did nothing; with co-interventions it lowered systolic pressure by up to 6.1 mm Hg
cards.summary: The individual-patient meta-analysis: self-monitoring alone had no effect (−1.0 mm Hg) ; combined with systematic titration or intensive support the reduction reached 6.1 mm Hg .
cards.type: Systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: Individual data from 25 randomised trials; primary-outcome data at 12 months from 15 studies (7,138 of 8,292 randomised participants); the abstract does not state a pooled mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Self-monitoring was associated with lower clinic systolic blood pressure at 12 months than usual care (-3.2 mm Hg, 95% CI -4.9 to -1.6), but the effect ranged from no effect with self-monitoring alone (-1.0 mm Hg, -3.3 to 1.2) to a 6.1 mm Hg reduction (-9.0 to -3.2) when monitoring was combined with intensive support including systematic medication titration. Ambulatory blood pressure showed no association in the four trials (1,478 patients) testing monitoring with little or no co-intervention.
cards.watchOut: Substantial heterogeneity remained, partly from differing targets and monitoring regimes; the gradient by co-intervention intensity is a between-trial comparison, not a randomised dose comparison.
cards.source: Tucker KL et al. Self-monitoring of blood pressure in hypertension: a systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis. PLoS Med. 2017 Sep 19;14(9):e1002389. PMID: 28926573. Registry ID: none in the record's databank — systematic review/meta-analysis, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: home monitoring lowers blood pressure when it drives titration — not by itself
cards.summary: Home monitoring lowers blood pressure when it drives titration — not by itself; every outcome here is blood pressure, a surrogate, with no event data.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: two UK primary-care randomised trials (527 and 1,182 participants) and an individual-patient meta-analysis of 25 trials.
cards.result: Used to titrate treatment, home self-monitoring lowered systolic blood pressure by 3.5-5.4 mm Hg more than clinic-based usual care at 12 months (TASMINH2, TASMINH4); telemonitoring added nothing significant over self-monitoring alone in TASMINH4, and the meta-analysis shows monitoring without titration or support has no effect (-1.0 mm Hg). This shelf is stamped LIKELY: consistent randomised evidence on a surrogate outcome (blood pressure), with no event outcomes in any card.
cards.watchOut: Do not credit the monitor alone: every positive card pairs readings with titration or structured support. Effects were shown in poorly controlled hypertension and may not transfer to already-controlled patients.
cards.source: Synthesis of McManus RJ et al. Lancet. 2010;376(9736):163-72. PMID: 20619448; McManus RJ et al. Lancet. 2018;391(10124):949-959. PMID: 29499873; Tucker KL et al. PLoS Med. 2017;14(9):e1002389. PMID: 28926573. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm in older men
shelves.question: Does one-time ultrasound screening of older men reduce aneurysm-related death enough to justify a screening programme?
shelves.mesh: Aortic Aneurysm, Abdominal/diagnostic imaging/mortality/surgery · Elective Surgical Procedures · Mass Screening/methods · Ultrasonography · Aortic Aneurysm, Abdominal/mortality/surgery · Aortic Rupture/mortality/surgery · Denmark/epidemiology
shelves.balance: Proposed LIKELY, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — aneurysm-mortality claim): In MASS, inviting men aged 65-74 to one ultrasound scan reduced aneurysm-related death from 0.33% to 0.19% over about 4 years (42% relative reduction, 95% CI 22 to 58), and the smaller Viborg trial found a 67% relative reduction (29 to 84) in aneurysm-specific mortality. The Cochrane synthesis of the four screening trials found reduced aneurysm mortality in men (OR 0.60, 0.47 to 0.78) but no significant difference in all-cause mortality at 3-5 years (OR 0.95, 0.85 to 1.07), and no demonstrated benefit in women. Screening roughly doubled aneurysm surgery in men. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: MASS: inviting 65-74-year-old men to one ultrasound scan cut aneurysm-related death from 0.33% to 0.19%
cards.summary: MASS: aneurysm-related deaths 0.19% vs 0.33% — a 42% relative reduction [22 to 58] from one invited ultrasound scan; 53% relative among men who attended.
cards.people: 67,800 men aged 65-74 years (33,839 invited to screening, 33,961 controls); 27,147 (80%) of the invited group attended and 1,333 aneurysms were detected. Men only, by design.
cards.result: There were 65 aneurysm-related deaths (absolute risk 0.19%) in the invited group and 113 (0.33%) in the control group — a 42% relative reduction (95% CI 22 to 58; p=0.0002), with a 53% relative reduction (30 to 64) among men who attended screening, over a mean follow-up of 4.1 years for detected aneurysms. Thirty-day mortality was 6% (24 of 414) after elective aneurysm surgery and 37% (30 of 81) after emergency surgery.
cards.watchOut: The headline outcome is cause-specific mortality; the trial's abstract does not report an all-cause mortality difference. Benefit is stated for men aged 65-74 — the Cochrane card below finds insufficient evidence in women.
cards.source: Ashton HA et al. The Multicentre Aneurysm Screening Study (MASS) into the effect of abdominal aortic aneurysm screening on mortality in men: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2002 Nov 16;360(9345):1531-9. PMID: 12443589. Registry ID: none in the record's databank (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: Viborg trial: screening Danish men aged 65 or more reduced aneurysm-specific mortality by 67% (relative)
cards.summary: Viborg: 9 vs 27 aneurysm deaths — a 67% relative reduction [29 to 84]; number needed to screen 352 ; 75% fewer emergency operations.
cards.people: 12,639 men born 1921-33 living in Viborg County, Denmark; 4,860 of 6,333 men randomised to screening were scanned (attendance 76.6%) and 191 (4.0% of those screened) had an aneurysm. Men only.
cards.result: Over a mean follow-up of 52 months, deaths due to abdominal aortic aneurysm occurred in 9 patients in the screened group and 27 in the control group — specific mortality was reduced by 67% relative (95% CI 29 to 84); the number needed to screen to save one life was 352. The screened group underwent 75% fewer emergency operations (51 to 91). Mortality from other causes was non-significantly reduced by 8%.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre trial with only 36 aneurysm deaths in total, so the relative estimate is imprecise; absolute event counts (9 vs 27) are printed above alongside the relative figure.
cards.source: Lindholt JS et al. Screening for abdominal aortic aneurysms: single centre randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2005 Apr 2;330(7494):750. PMID: 15757960. Registry ID: none in the record's databank (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: Cochrane synthesis of the four screening trials: aneurysm mortality down in men, all-cause mortality not significantly different
cards.summary: Cochrane (four trials): aneurysm mortality in men OR 0.60 [0.47 to 0.78], but all-cause mortality not significantly different (OR 0.95) and no demonstrated benefit in women.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: Four randomised trials involving 127,891 men and 9,342 women; only one trial included women. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age.
cards.result: At 3-5 years there was a significant decrease in mortality from abdominal aortic aneurysm in men (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.78) but not in women (OR 1.99, 0.36 to 10.88), and a decreased incidence of ruptured aneurysm in men (OR 0.45, 0.21 to 0.99). There was no significant difference in all-cause mortality for men (OR 0.95, 0.85 to 1.07) or women (OR 1.06, 0.93 to 1.21). Surgery for aneurysm increased significantly in men (OR 2.03, 1.59 to 2.59).
cards.watchOut: The all-cause mortality odds ratio of 0.95 sits inside the 0.5-2.0 band and is not significant — it is printed here, as required, beside the cause-specific benefit claim, and is not itself evidence of a total-mortality benefit. Evidence in women is a single trial with very wide intervals.
cards.source: Cosford PA, Leng GC. Screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2007 Apr 18;(2):CD002945. PMID: 17443519. Registry ID: none in the record's databank — systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one scan in older men prevents aneurysm death; total mortality and women remain unproven
cards.summary: One scan in older men prevents aneurysm death at the cost of roughly twice as much aneurysm surgery; total mortality and women remain unproven — Tier C, proposed LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: MASS (67,800 men), the Viborg trial (12,639 men), and the Cochrane synthesis of four trials (127,891 men, 9,342 women).
cards.result: One-time ultrasound screening of men aged about 65-74 reduced aneurysm-related death in both large trials (MASS: 0.19% vs 0.33% absolute, 42% relative reduction; Viborg: 9 vs 27 deaths, 67% relative reduction; Cochrane OR 0.60) at the cost of roughly twice as much aneurysm surgery. All-cause mortality was not significantly different in the synthesis (men OR 0.95, 0.85 to 1.07). Proposed stamp LIKELY, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Fence: no demonstrated benefit in women; the claim is prevention of aneurysm death, not of death overall. The later VIVA trial (PMID 28859943) tested combined screening for aneurysm, peripheral arterial disease and hypertension — a different question — and is not carded here.

shelves.title: E-cigarettes for smoking cessation
shelves.question: Do nicotine e-cigarettes help smokers quit more than nicotine replacement therapy or non-nicotine e-cigarettes?
shelves.mesh: Electronic Nicotine Delivery Systems · Nicotine/administration & dosage · Smoking Cessation/methods · Tobacco Use Cessation Devices/adverse effects · Tobacco Use Disorder/therapy · Vaping/adverse effects · Breath Tests
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Nicotine e-cigarettes produced higher quit rates than nicotine replacement therapy in the largest head-to-head trial (1-year abstinence 18.0% vs 9.9%; relative risk 1.83, 95% CI 1.30 to 2.58) and in the Cochrane living review (relative risk 1.63, 1.30 to 2.04; an additional four quitters per 100), and higher quit rates than non-nicotine e-cigarettes (relative risk 1.94, 1.21 to 3.13). The earliest trial (Bullen 2013) was underpowered and inconclusive on its own. Most abstinent e-cigarette users were still vaping at one year (80%), and long-term safety data remain limited (longest follow-up two years in the review).

cards.headline: Hajek 2019: e-cigarettes nearly doubled 1-year abstinence versus nicotine replacement (18.0% vs 9.9%)
cards.summary: Hajek 2019: 1-year abstinence 18.0% vs 9.9% on nicotine replacement (relative risk 1.83 ) — but 80% of e-cigarette abstainers were still vaping at 52 weeks, vs 9% still using replacement products.
cards.people: 886 adults attending UK National Health Service stop-smoking services, randomised to an e-cigarette starter pack or nicotine-replacement products of their choice for up to 3 months, both with at least 4 weeks of weekly behavioural support; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Sustained, biochemically validated abstinence at 1 year was 18.0% in the e-cigarette group versus 9.9% in the nicotine-replacement group (relative risk 1.83, 95% CI 1.30 to 2.58; P<0.001) — an absolute difference of 8.1 percentage points. Among 1-year abstainers, 80% (63 of 79) of the e-cigarette group were still using their assigned product at 52 weeks, versus 9% (4 of 44) for nicotine replacement. Throat or mouth irritation was more frequent with e-cigarettes (65.3% vs 51.2%) and nausea more frequent with nicotine replacement (37.9% vs 31.3%); there were no significant differences in wheezing or shortness of breath.
cards.watchOut: Continued vaping among quitters means the trial tests switching nicotine delivery as much as quitting nicotine; follow-up is 1 year and the trial was not designed to assess long-term vaping safety.
cards.source: Hajek P et al. A Randomized Trial of E-Cigarettes versus Nicotine-Replacement Therapy. N Engl J Med. 2019 Feb 14;380(7):629-637. PMID: 30699054. Registry ID: ISRCTN60477608 (record's databank).

cards.headline: Bullen 2013: the first e-cigarette trial was underpowered — abstinence 7.3% vs 5.8% on patches, differences not significant
cards.summary: Bullen 2013, the first trial: abstinence 7.3% (nicotine e-cigarette) vs 5.8% (patches) vs 4.1% (placebo e-cigarette) — underpowered, no significant difference.
cards.people: 657 adult smokers wanting to quit, in Auckland, New Zealand, randomised 4:4:1 to 16 mg nicotine e-cigarettes (n=289), 21 mg nicotine patches (n=295), or placebo (non-nicotine) e-cigarettes (n=73), with low-intensity telephone support; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Biochemically verified continuous abstinence at 6 months was 7.3% (21 of 289) with nicotine e-cigarettes, 5.8% (17 of 295) with patches, and 4.1% (3 of 73) with placebo e-cigarettes — risk differences of 1.51 percentage points (95% CI -2.49 to 5.51) versus patches and 3.16 (-2.29 to 8.61) versus placebo, neither significant. Adverse-event counts did not differ significantly between groups (137, 119 and 36 events respectively).
cards.watchOut: Abstinence was far lower than the power calculation assumed, so this trial alone could not establish superiority — it is carded as the field's starting point, with the decisive evidence on the Hajek and Cochrane cards.
cards.source: Bullen C et al. Electronic cigarettes for smoking cessation: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2013 Nov 16;382(9905):1629-37. PMID: 24029165. Registry ID: ACTRN12610000866000, stated in the record's abstract (no databank SI field on the record).

cards.headline: Walker 2020: adding a nicotine e-cigarette to patches raised 6-month abstinence to 7% versus 4% with a nicotine-free e-cigarette and 2% with patches alone
cards.summary: Walker 2020: patches plus a nicotine e-cigarette reached 7% abstinence vs 4% with a nicotine-free e-cigarette and 2% with patches alone.
cards.people: 1,124 adult smokers in New Zealand who were e-cigarette-naive and motivated to quit (patches alone n=125; patches plus nicotine e-cigarette n=500; patches plus nicotine-free e-cigarette n=499), with 6 weeks of telephone behavioural support; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Carbon-monoxide-verified continuous abstinence at 6 months was 7% (35 of 500) with patches plus a nicotine e-cigarette, versus 4% (20 of 499) with patches plus a nicotine-free e-cigarette (risk difference 2.99 percentage points, 95% CI 0.17 to 5.81) and 2% (3 of 125) with patches alone (risk difference 4.60, 1.11 to 8.09). Serious adverse events did not differ significantly between groups and none were judged treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: Absolute quit rates were low in all arms, and loss to follow-up was much higher in the patches-only group (50%) than in the e-cigarette groups (32-33%), which can bias the patches-alone comparison.
cards.source: Walker N et al. Nicotine patches used in combination with e-cigarettes (with and without nicotine) for smoking cessation: a pragmatic, randomised trial. Lancet Respir Med. 2020 Jan;8(1):54-64. PMID: 31515173. Registry ID: NCT02521662 (record's databank).

cards.headline: Cochrane living review: high-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes beat nicotine replacement for quitting
cards.summary: Cochrane living review: high-certainty evidence nicotine e-cigarettes beat nicotine replacement (relative risk 1.63 ) — about four extra quitters per 100 .
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane, living review)
cards.people: 78 completed studies representing 22,052 participants, of which 40 were randomised trials (search to 1 July 2022); the main nicotine-replacement comparison pooled 6 studies with 2,378 participants.
cards.result: Quit rates were higher with nicotine e-cigarettes than with nicotine replacement therapy (relative risk 1.63, 95% CI 1.30 to 2.04; high certainty) — in absolute terms about an additional four quitters per 100 (2 to 6) — and higher than with non-nicotine e-cigarettes (relative risk 1.94, 1.21 to 3.13; moderate certainty; about seven additional quitters per 100, 2 to 16). Adverse-event rates were similar between nicotine e-cigarettes and nicotine replacement (relative risk 1.02, 0.88 to 1.19); serious adverse events were rare and the comparison was imprecise (relative risk 1.12, 0.82 to 1.52). The commonest adverse effects were throat/mouth irritation, headache, cough and nausea, tending to dissipate with continued use.
cards.watchOut: The review is a living review (2022 version carded here); the main limitation it names is imprecision from few trials with low event rates, and the longest follow-up was two years, so long-term safety is not established by this evidence.

shelves.title: General health checks in primary care
shelves.question: Do routine general health checks reduce illness or death, or mainly find risk factors?
shelves.mesh: Diagnosis · Disease · Health Promotion/methods · Morbidity · Primary Prevention · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Directive Counseling
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Across 17 randomised trials (251,891 participants), general health checks had little or no effect on total mortality (risk ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.03; high-certainty evidence), cancer mortality (1.01, 0.92 to 1.12) or ischaemic heart disease events (0.98, 0.94 to 1.03). The largest single trial, Inter99, likewise found no effect on ischaemic heart disease, stroke or total mortality at 10 years (hazard ratio 1.00, 0.91 to 1.09). Health checks do find risk factors and diagnoses — the trials say that finding them this way does not translate into fewer deaths or events.

cards.headline: Cochrane synthesis of 17 trials: health checks had no effect on total mortality (risk ratio 1.00)
cards.summary: Cochrane (17 trials): general health checks had no effect on total mortality (risk ratio 1.00 [0.97 to 1.03]; 233,298 participants) or cancer mortality (1.01).
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: 17 randomised trials, 15 reporting outcome data (251,891 participants), in adults unselected for disease or risk factors; geriatric trials were excluded. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Health checks had little or no effect on total mortality (risk ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.03; 11 trials, 233,298 participants, 21,535 deaths; high-certainty evidence), cancer mortality (risk ratio 1.01, 0.92 to 1.12; 8 trials), fatal and non-fatal ischaemic heart disease (risk ratio 0.98, 0.94 to 1.03; 4 trials; high-certainty), and probably little or no effect on cardiovascular mortality (risk ratio 1.05, 0.94 to 1.16; moderate-certainty) or stroke (risk ratio 1.05, 0.95 to 1.17; moderate-certainty). The authors conclude general health checks are unlikely to be beneficial.
cards.watchOut: The component screening tests inside a health check were, in the review's words, incompletely studied individually — this shelf grades the bundled general health check, not single-disease screening programmes (which have their own shelves). Risk ratios near 1.0 here are precise nulls from high-certainty evidence, not weak signals.

cards.headline: Inter99: population screening plus repeated lifestyle counselling changed nothing at 10 years — not even mortality
cards.summary: Inter99: at 10 years, hazard ratios 1.03 (ischaemic heart disease), 0.98 (stroke) and 1.00 (total mortality) — screening plus repeated lifestyle counselling changed nothing.
cards.people: 59,616 people aged 30-60 years in Copenhagen suburbs randomised to invitation for screening and lifestyle counselling (n=11,629; 52.4% participated at baseline) or no invitation (n=47,987); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 10 years there was no significant difference in the primary endpoint of ischaemic heart disease incidence (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.13) or in stroke (0.98, 0.87 to 1.11), the combined endpoint (1.01, 0.93 to 1.09), or total mortality (1.00, 0.91 to 1.09); 3,163 people died during follow-up. The authors conclude the programme had no effect on ischaemic heart disease, stroke, or mortality at population level.
cards.watchOut: Only about half of those invited participated, so the trial tests offering the programme to a population (the policy question), not the effect in attenders; apparent lower mortality among attenders in observational analyses of this trial is substantially explained by self-selection.
cards.source: Jorgensen T et al. Effect of screening and lifestyle counselling on incidence of ischaemic heart disease in general population: Inter99 randomised trial. BMJ. 2014 Jun 9;348:g3617. PMID: 24912589. Registry ID: NCT00289237 (record's databank).

cards.summary: A precise null across the randomised evidence: health checks find risk factors but do not reduce deaths or events — LIKELY, for the null.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: a Cochrane synthesis of 17 randomised trials (251,891 participants) and the Inter99 population trial (59,616 people).
cards.result: The randomised evidence is a precise null: total mortality risk ratio 1.00 (0.97 to 1.03) across the pooled trials and hazard ratio 1.00 (0.91 to 1.09) in Inter99, with no effect on cancer mortality, ischaemic heart disease or stroke. This shelf is stamped LIKELY — LIKELY the null: high-certainty pooled evidence plus a concordant large population trial.

shelves.title: Collaborative care for depression and anxiety in primary care
shelves.question: Does collaborative (care-manager + specialist-supervised) care improve depression outcomes versus usual primary care?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Case Management · Cooperative Behavior · Depressive Disorder/economics/therapy · Family Practice/economics/organization & administration/standards · Health Services Accessibility · Health Services Research
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Collaborative care improved depression outcomes across 79 randomised trials (24,308 participants) in the Cochrane synthesis — short-term standardised mean difference -0.34 (95% CI -0.41 to -0.27) with response risk ratio 1.32 (1.22 to 1.43), sustained at long-term follow-up — and in the IMPACT trial 45% of older adults achieved at least a 50% symptom reduction at 12 months versus 19% on usual care. Anxiety outcomes improved similarly. Benefits were not demonstrated at very long-term follow-up in the synthesis.

cards.headline: IMPACT: collaborative care more than doubled treatment response in depressed older adults (45% vs 19%)
cards.summary: IMPACT: 45% vs 19% of depressed older adults achieved at least a halving of symptoms at 12 months (odds ratio 3.45 , printed beside its absolute rates).
cards.people: 1,801 patients aged 60 years or older with major depression (17%), dysthymic disorder (30%), or both (53%), in 18 primary care clinics in 5 US states (906 IMPACT intervention, 895 usual care); the abstract does not state mean age beyond the 60-plus eligibility or the sex mix.
cards.result: At 12 months, 45% of intervention patients had a 50% or greater reduction in depressive symptoms versus 19% of usual-care participants (odds ratio 3.45, 95% CI 2.71 to 4.38; P<.001). Intervention patients also had greater rates of depression treatment (odds ratio 2.98, 2.34 to 3.79), lower depression severity (between-group difference -0.4 on a 0-4 range), less functional impairment (-0.91 on a 0-10 range) and greater quality of life (0.56 on a 0-10 range), all P<.001.
cards.watchOut: Population is older adults (60+) in US primary care; the intervention is a package (care manager, psychiatric supervision, supported antidepressant management, brief psychotherapy) and the trial cannot separate its components. Odds ratios overstate the relative effect compared with the printed absolute rates (45% vs 19%), which are given alongside.
cards.source: Unutzer J et al. Collaborative care management of late-life depression in the primary care setting: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2002 Dec 11;288(22):2836-45. PMID: 12472325. Registry ID: none in the record's databank (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: Cochrane synthesis of 79 trials: collaborative care improved depression and anxiety outcomes at short, medium and long term
cards.summary: Cochrane (79 trials): collaborative care improved depression outcomes at every horizon — short-term standardised difference −0.34 , response risk ratio 1.32 .
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: 79 randomised trials (90 relevant comparisons) involving 24,308 participants of all ages with depression or anxiety; the abstract does not state a pooled mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Depression outcomes improved more with collaborative care than usual care in the short term (standardised mean difference -0.34, 95% CI -0.41 to -0.27; response risk ratio 1.32, 1.22 to 1.43), medium term (standardised mean difference -0.28, -0.41 to -0.15; risk ratio 1.31, 1.17 to 1.48) and long term (standardised mean difference -0.35, -0.46 to -0.24; risk ratio 1.29, 1.18 to 1.41), but not at very long term (risk ratio 1.12, 0.98 to 1.27). Anxiety outcomes improved similarly (short-term standardised mean difference -0.30, -0.44 to -0.17; risk ratio 1.50, 1.21 to 1.87). Secondary benefits included medication use, mental-health quality of life and patient satisfaction, with less evidence for physical quality of life.
cards.watchOut: Included studies varied in risk of bias, and effect sizes are modest (standardised mean differences around 0.3); the very-long-term depression comparison is null, so durability beyond the long-term window is unproven.
cards.source: Archer J et al. Collaborative care for depression and anxiety problems. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012 Oct 17;10(10):CD006525. PMID: 23076925. Registry ID: none in the record's databank — systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: TEAMcare: collaborative care for depression with diabetes or heart disease improved depression and all three medical targets together
cards.summary: TEAMcare: in depression with diabetes or heart disease, collaborative care improved all three medical targets together — glycated hemoglobin −0.58%, LDL −6.9 mg/dL, systolic pressure −5.1 mm Hg.
cards.people: 214 participants with poorly controlled diabetes, coronary heart disease, or both, plus coexisting depression, in 14 primary care clinics in Washington State; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 12 months the intervention group had greater overall improvement across glycated hemoglobin (difference 0.58%), LDL cholesterol (difference 6.9 mg per deciliter), systolic blood pressure (difference 5.1 mm Hg) and depression scores (difference 0.40 points on the Symptom Checklist-20) than controls (P<0.001 for the combined model), with more frequent adjustment of insulin, antihypertensive and antidepressant medicines and better quality of life and satisfaction with care.
cards.watchOut: Small single-system trial (214 participants) whose primary outcome is a modelled combination of four measures; it extends collaborative care to multimorbid patients but is not powered for clinical events.

cards.headline: Synthesis: organising depression care around a supervised care manager works — modestly, and not forever by default
cards.summary: Organising depression care around a supervised care manager works — modestly, across many trials, and for anxiety too.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: IMPACT (1,801 older adults), the Cochrane synthesis (79 trials, 24,308 participants), and TEAMcare (214 patients with depression plus chronic disease).
cards.result: Collaborative care consistently improved depression response (IMPACT 45% vs 19% achieving at least halved symptoms; pooled response risk ratio 1.32 short term, 1.29 long term) and anxiety outcomes, and in multimorbid patients improved medical control alongside depression. This shelf is stamped LIKELY: many randomised trials pointing the same way, with modest average effect sizes.
cards.watchOut: Do not promise permanence: the synthesis found no demonstrated benefit at very long-term follow-up, and effects depend on the full package — a care manager without specialist supervision and treat-to-target follow-up is not the tested intervention.
cards.source: Synthesis of Unutzer J et al. JAMA. 2002;288(22):2836-45. PMID: 12472325; Archer J et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012;10(10):CD006525. PMID: 23076925; Katon WJ et al. N Engl J Med. 2010;363(27):2611-20. PMID: 21190455. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: HIV self-testing
shelves.question: Does making HIV self-tests available increase testing uptake and linkage versus facility-based testing alone?
shelves.mesh: Cluster Analysis · Counseling/methods/statistics & numerical data · HIV Infections/drug therapy/psychology · Malawi · Mass Screening/methods/statistics & numerical data · Outpatients/psychology/statistics & numerical data · HIV Infections/diagnosis/epidemiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for uptake; linkage less certain): Facility-based self-testing in Malawi raised same-day testing among outpatients from 13% to 51% (adjusted odds ratio 8.52, 95% CI 3.98 to 18.24 versus standard provider-initiated testing), and the earlier randomised-trial synthesis found self-testing doubled testing uptake among men (risk ratio 2.12, 1.51 to 2.98). STAR-programme community distribution in Zimbabwe delivered tens of thousands of kits with about a quarter of surveyed participants linking to post-test services, and no social harms were reported in the Malawi or Zimbabwe trials. Evidence that self-testing increases linkage to treatment, rather than testing itself, is thinner — the synthesis explicitly calls for more research on supporting linkage.

cards.headline: Malawi facility trial: offering self-tests in outpatient departments raised same-day HIV testing from 13% to 51%
cards.summary: Malawi facility trial: same-day HIV testing 51% with self-tests offered in outpatients vs 13% standard provider testing (adjusted odds ratio 8.52 ); no coercion reported in the self-test group.
cards.people: 15 outpatient departments at high-burden facilities in central and southern Malawi; 5,885 outpatients aged 15 years or older completed exit surveys (2,097 self-testing, 1,951 standard provider-initiated testing, 1,837 optimised provider-initiated testing); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Same-day HIV testing occurred in 1,063 (51%) of 2,097 patients in the self-testing group, versus 248 (13%) of 1,951 with standard provider-initiated testing and 261 (14%) of 1,837 with optimised provider-initiated testing — adjusted odds ratio 8.52 (95% CI 3.98 to 18.24) versus standard and 6.29 (2.96 to 13.38) versus optimised provider testing. About 4% of patients in the provider-testing groups felt coerced to test and about 1% felt coerced to share results; no coercion was reported in the self-testing group.
cards.watchOut: The outcome is testing on the day of the visit, not new diagnoses, linkage to care, or treatment initiation; odds ratios from a cluster trial overstate the relative effect next to the printed absolute rates (51% vs 13%).
cards.source: Dovel K et al. Effect of facility-based HIV self-testing on uptake of testing among outpatients in Malawi: a cluster-randomised trial. Lancet Glob Health. 2020 Feb;8(2):e276-e287. PMID: 31981557. Registry ID: NCT03271307 (record's databank); the abstract also lists Pan African Clinical Trials registration PACTR201711002697316.

cards.headline: STAR Zimbabwe: community-led self-test distribution matched paid distribution on new diagnoses and linkage, at lower cost per kit
cards.summary: STAR Zimbabwe: community-led distribution matched paid distribution on new diagnoses ( 3.7% vs 3.6% ) and linkage, at lower cost per kit.
cards.people: 40 village groups in rural Zimbabwe randomised to community-led self-test distribution or paid door-to-door distribution over 4 weeks; 27,812 kits distributed in community-led and 36,699 in paid-distribution communities; 11,150 participants surveyed 4 months later (5,683 community-led). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: New HIV diagnosis was reported by 211 (3.7%) of community-led versus 197 (3.6%) of paid-distribution participants (adjusted odds ratio 1.1, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.56), and linkage to confirmatory testing, pre-exposure prophylaxis or voluntary medical male circumcision by 318 (25.9%) versus 361 (23.9%) (adjusted odds ratio 1.1, 0.75 to 1.49). Cost per kit distributed was US$6.29 for community-led and US$10.25 for paid distribution. No social harms were reported.
cards.watchOut: This STAR trial compares two self-test distribution models with each other, not self-testing against facility testing — it shows community distribution is deliverable at scale, while the uptake-versus-facility comparison rests on the Malawi card and the synthesis card. Only about a quarter of surveyed participants linked to post-test services in either arm.

cards.headline: Randomised-trial synthesis: self-testing doubled uptake and testing frequency among men
cards.summary: Pooled randomised evidence: self-testing doubled uptake among men (risk ratio 2.12) ; the pooled diagnosis estimate (2.02 [0.37 to 10.76]) is imprecise and printed as such.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: Five randomised trials (4,145 participants, four countries) comparing self-testing with standard testing services, all offering free oral-fluid tests and all conducted among men (search to 1 June 2016); no pooled mean age is stated.
cards.result: Self-testing doubled uptake of testing among men (risk ratio 2.12, 95% CI 1.51 to 2.98; three trials) and nearly doubled testing frequency among men who have sex with men (rate ratio 1.88, 1.17 to 3.01; about two more tests over 12-15 months). The pooled estimate for HIV-positive diagnosis was imprecise (risk ratio 2.02, 0.37 to 10.76 as printed in the record). Across the trials there was no indication of harm attributable to self-testing and minimal increase in risk-taking behaviour.
cards.watchOut: All five trials were in men and offered free tests, so the estimate does not directly cover women or paid distribution; the diagnosis estimate's interval is very wide and sits across the 0.5-2.0 band — it is not solid evidence of more diagnoses. The authors state more research is needed on supporting linkage to confirmatory testing and care.
cards.source: Johnson CC et al. Examining the effects of HIV self-testing compared to standard HIV testing services: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Int AIDS Soc. 2017 May 15;20(1):21594. PMID: 28530049. Registry ID: none in the record's databank — systematic review/meta-analysis, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: self-tests clearly get more people tested; linkage after a self-test is the weak link
cards.summary: Self-tests clearly get more people tested; linkage to care after a positive self-test is the weak link — LIKELY for uptake only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: a Malawi facility cluster trial (5,885 outpatients), a STAR Zimbabwe distribution cluster trial (11,150 surveyed), and a synthesis of five randomised trials (4,145 participants).
cards.result: Making self-tests available increased testing in every design: same-day testing 51% versus 13% in Malawi (adjusted odds ratio 8.52), doubled uptake in the pooled trials (risk ratio 2.12), and community distribution in Zimbabwe reached scale with no reported social harms. This shelf is stamped LIKELY for the uptake claim. Linkage is graded more cautiously on the cards: only about a quarter of Zimbabwe survey participants linked to post-test services, and the synthesis calls linkage support an open research question.
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade testing uptake into proven treatment benefit: no card here shows self-testing increasing antiretroviral initiation or viral suppression, and demand is highly price-sensitive in related randomised work — free distribution is part of the tested model.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dovel K et al. Lancet Glob Health. 2020;8(2):e276-e287. PMID: 31981557; Sibanda EL et al. BMJ Glob Health. 2021;6(Suppl 4):e005000. PMID: 34275872; Johnson CC et al. J Int AIDS Soc. 2017;20(1):21594. PMID: 28530049. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Brief alcohol interventions in primary care
shelves.question: Do brief alcohol interventions in primary care reduce drinking in hazardous and harmful drinkers?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Alcohol Drinking/therapy · Alcoholism/therapy · Emergencies/epidemiology · Family Practice/statistics & numerical data · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Alcoholism/prevention & control/rehabilitation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The Cochrane synthesis of 69 trials (33,642 participants) found moderate-quality evidence that brief intervention reduced drinking by 20 g of alcohol per week (95% CI -28 to -12) at one year versus minimal or no intervention — a small average effect with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 73%). The large pragmatic SIPS trial, however, found no additional benefit from brief advice or lifestyle counselling beyond simple screening feedback and a leaflet. Longer (extended) interventions added nothing over brief ones.

cards.headline: Cochrane synthesis of 69 trials: brief intervention cut drinking by 20 g per week at one year — a small average effect
cards.summary: Cochrane (69 trials): brief intervention cut drinking by 20 g/week at one year [−28 to −12] against a ~244 g/week baseline — a small average effect, moderate-quality evidence, I² = 73%.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: 69 studies randomising 33,642 hazardous or harmful drinkers in general practice (55%), emergency care (39%) or other primary care; mean baseline consumption among reporting studies was 244 g/week. The primary meta-analysis pooled 34 studies (15,197 participants). Sex mix is not pooled in the abstract, which reports subgroup analyses showing reductions in both men and women.
cards.result: Participants receiving brief intervention consumed less alcohol than minimal/no-intervention participants after one year (mean difference -20 g/week, 95% CI -28 to -12; moderate-quality evidence; I2 = 73%). Effects on binges per week (-0.08, -0.14 to -0.02), drinking days per week (-0.13, -0.23 to -0.04) and drinking intensity (-0.2 g/drinking day, -3.1 to 2.7) were little or none. Extended intervention was no better than brief intervention (mean difference 2 g/week, -42 to 45; low-quality evidence). Only five studies reported adverse effects (very low-quality evidence), with none clearly attributable to the intervention.
cards.watchOut: 20 g/week is about two UK units against a baseline of 244 g/week (30.5 units) — a small relative change, from unblinded trials with attrition bias and substantial heterogeneity. The population is hazardous/harmful drinkers not seeking treatment, not people with alcohol dependence (medicines for dependence are a different shelf, #404).
cards.source: Kaner EFS et al. Effectiveness of brief alcohol interventions in primary care populations. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018 Feb 24;2(2):CD004148. PMID: 29476653. Registry ID: none in the record's databank — systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: SIPS trial: brief advice and lifestyle counselling added nothing beyond screening feedback and a leaflet
cards.summary: SIPS: brief advice (odds ratio 0.85 ) and lifestyle counselling ( 0.78 ) added nothing beyond screening feedback plus a leaflet.
cards.people: 3,562 patients aged 18 or more presenting in English primary care, of whom 900 screened positive for hazardous or harmful drinking and 756 received an intervention; the sample was predominantly male (62%) and white (92%), and 34% were current smokers. Mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: At 6 and 12 months there were no significant differences between the three strategies in the proportion with a negative AUDIT result (score below 8): versus the leaflet group, the odds ratio was 0.85 (95% CI 0.52 to 1.39) for five minutes of structured brief advice and 0.78 (0.48 to 1.25) for 20 minutes of brief lifestyle counselling. A per-protocol analysis confirmed the findings. All groups received simple feedback on their screening result.
cards.watchOut: Every SIPS participant — including controls — was screened and told their result, so the trial tests the added value of advice over feedback, not brief intervention versus nothing; its null does not erase the Cochrane comparison against minimal intervention, and the two are fenced apart on the synthesis card.
cards.source: Kaner E et al. Effectiveness of screening and brief alcohol intervention in primary care (SIPS trial): pragmatic cluster randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2013 Jan 9;346:e8501. PMID: 23303891. Registry ID: ISRCTN06145674 (record's databank).

cards.headline: Synthesis: a small average reduction in the pooled trials, none beyond feedback in the biggest pragmatic trial
cards.summary: A small average reduction in the pooled trials, none beyond feedback in the biggest pragmatic trial — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: a Cochrane synthesis of 69 trials (33,642 participants; primary analysis 15,197) and the SIPS cluster trial (900 screen-positive patients).
cards.result: Brief interventions reduced drinking by about 20 g/week at one year versus minimal or no intervention in the pooled evidence (moderate quality, I2 = 73%), while SIPS found brief advice (odds ratio 0.85) and counselling (0.78) added nothing to screening feedback plus a leaflet. Extended counselling added nothing over brief intervention. This shelf is stamped POSSIBLE: a real but small and heterogeneous average effect, sensitive to what the control group received.
cards.watchOut: Fence: hazardous and harmful drinkers in primary care only — not alcohol dependence, and not digital interventions (excluded from the Cochrane review). Present the effect as ~20 g/week, not as a relative percentage.

shelves.title: Expedited partner therapy for sexually transmitted infections
shelves.question: Does giving patients antibiotics (or prescriptions) for their partners reduce reinfection and partner infection versus partner referral alone?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Azithromycin/therapeutic use · Cefixime/therapeutic use · Chlamydia Infections/drug therapy/transmission · Contact Tracing/methods · Drug Therapy, Combination/therapeutic use · Gonorrhea/drug therapy/transmission
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the largest trial (Golden 2005), expedited partner treatment reduced persistent or recurrent gonorrhoea or chlamydial infection from 13% to 10% (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.98), driven by gonorrhoea (3% vs 11%) rather than chlamydia (11% vs 13%). The Cochrane synthesis found expedited therapy better than simple patient referral for reinfection (risk ratio 0.71, 0.56 to 0.89), but the effect attenuated when high-attrition trials were excluded (0.80, 0.62 to 1.04) and in chlamydia-only trials (0.90, 0.60 to 1.35), and it was not superior to enhanced patient referral. A trichomonas trial found patient-delivered treatment no better than referral for partner treatment or reinfection, though cheaper. All relative effects sit inside the 0.5-2.0 band and are graded accordingly.

cards.headline: Golden 2005: expedited partner treatment cut recurrent or persistent infection from 13% to 10%, driven by gonorrhoea
cards.summary: Golden 2005: recurrent or persistent infection 10% vs 13% (relative risk 0.76 ), driven by gonorrhoea ( 3% vs 11% ).
cards.people: Women and heterosexual men with gonorrhoea or chlamydial infection (929 analysed in the expedited-treatment group and 931 in the standard-referral group at follow-up); the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Persistent or recurrent gonorrhoea or chlamydial infection at 3-19 weeks occurred in 92 of 929 patients (10%) assigned to expedited partner treatment versus 121 of 931 (13%) assigned to standard referral (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.98). The effect was larger for gonorrhoea (3% vs 11%; P=0.01) than for chlamydial infection (11% vs 13%; P=0.17). Patients in the expedited group were significantly more likely to report that all partners were treated and less likely to report sex with an untreated partner.
cards.watchOut: The relative risk of 0.76 lies inside the 0.5-2.0 band — supportive, not solid on its own; the absolute difference is 3 percentage points, and the chlamydia subgroup (the commoner infection) was not significant on its own.
cards.source: Golden MR et al. Effect of expedited treatment of sex partners on recurrent or persistent gonorrhea or chlamydial infection. N Engl J Med. 2005 Feb 17;352(7):676-85. PMID: 15716561. Registry ID: none in the record's databank (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: Kissinger 2006: for trichomonas, patient-delivered partner treatment was no better than referral — but cost less
cards.summary: Kissinger 2006 (trichomonas): patient-delivered partner treatment was no better than referral on reinfection — but cost less.
cards.people: 463 women attending a family planning clinic who were culture-positive for Trichomonas vaginalis, randomised to standard partner referral, booklet-enhanced referral, or patient-delivered partner treatment; most were under 24 years old and most had one partner, per the abstract (no mean age stated).
cards.result: The percentage of women reporting their partners were treated was similar for patient-delivered treatment and standard referral (and significantly lower for booklet-enhanced referral), and follow-up infection rates were similar across groups. Patient-delivered treatment cost less than referral and was cost-saving compared with both referral strategies.
cards.watchOut: Outcomes rest substantially on women's reports of partner treatment, and the trial's own conclusion is a null on effectiveness — it supports expedited therapy as cheaper, not as more effective, for trichomonas.
cards.source: Kissinger P et al. Patient-delivered partner treatment for Trichomonas vaginalis infection: a randomized controlled trial. Sex Transm Dis. 2006 Jul;33(7):445-50. PMID: 16531939. Registry ID: none in the record's databank (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: Cochrane synthesis: expedited therapy beat simple referral on reinfection, but the effect shrank in the cleanest analyses
cards.summary: Cochrane: reinfection risk ratio 0.71 vs simple referral, attenuating to 0.80 in the cleanest analyses — every ratio here sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band , and the cards say so.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: 26 trials (17,578 participants; 9,015 women and 8,563 men) of partner-notification strategies for sexually transmitted infections, including HIV (search to 31 August 2012); no pooled mean age is stated.
cards.result: Expedited partner therapy was better than simple patient referral for preventing reinfection in trials of infections causing urethritis or cervicitis (6 trials; risk ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.89; moderate-quality evidence), but the effect attenuated when trials with attrition above 20% were excluded (2 trials; risk ratio 0.80, 0.62 to 1.04) and in chlamydia-only trials (2 trials; risk ratio 0.90, 0.60 to 1.35). Expedited therapy was not superior to enhanced patient referral (3 trials; risk ratio 0.96, 0.60 to 1.53; low-quality evidence). It increased the number of partners treated per index patient (mean difference about 0.43-0.51 across infection groups). No consistent differences in adverse effects between strategies were found where measured.
cards.watchOut: Every reinfection risk ratio here sits inside the 0.5-2.0 band and several intervals cross 1.0 in sensitivity analyses — the synthesis supports a probable small benefit over simple referral only, which is why this shelf is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
cards.source: Ferreira A et al. Strategies for partner notification for sexually transmitted infections, including HIV. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2013 Oct 3;2013(10):CD002843. PMID: 24092529. Registry ID: none in the record's databank — systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: expedited partner therapy probably reduces reinfection a little versus bare referral — and gets more partners treated
cards.summary: Expedited partner therapy probably reduces reinfection a little versus bare referral and gets more partners treated — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Golden 2005 (about 1,860 patients analysed), Kissinger 2006 (463 women), and the Cochrane synthesis (26 trials, 17,578 participants).
cards.result: Against simple partner referral, handing patients treatment for their partners reduced reinfection modestly (Golden: 10% vs 13%, relative risk 0.76; pooled risk ratio 0.71) and increased partners treated per index patient by roughly half a partner; against enhanced referral there was no advantage, and for trichomonas the advantage was cost, not cure. This shelf is stamped POSSIBLE: consistent direction, small effects inside the 0.5-2.0 band, fragile in sensitivity analyses.
cards.watchOut: Fence: the evidence covers gonorrhoea, chlamydia and trichomonas partner management; the Cochrane review found too few trials to conclude for HIV and syphilis partner strategies. Legality of expedited therapy varies by jurisdiction and is outside this evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Golden MR et al. N Engl J Med. 2005;352(7):676-85. PMID: 15716561; Kissinger P et al. Sex Transm Dis. 2006;33(7):445-50. PMID: 16531939; Ferreira A et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2013;2013(10):CD002843. PMID: 24092529. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Workplace wellness programmes
shelves.question: Do employer wellness programmes improve employee health, health-care use, or costs?
shelves.mesh: Commerce · Health Behavior · Health Expenditures · Health Promotion/economics · Health Status · Occupational Health · Occupational Health Services/economics
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference on health and economic outcomes): Two large randomised trials agree. In the BJ's Wholesale Club trial (32,974 employees), a wellness programme improved two self-reported behaviours (regular exercise and actively managing weight) but had no significant effect on 10 clinical measures, 38 spending and utilisation measures, or employment outcomes at 18 months. In the Illinois Workplace Wellness Study (4,834 employees), the programme had no significant effects on biometrics, medical diagnoses or medical use at 12 or 24 months, though more treated employees reported having a primary care physician (92.2% vs 86.1% at 24 months) and health beliefs improved slightly. Neither trial found the cost savings employers typically expect, within its follow-up window.

cards.headline: Song & Baicker 2019: wellness programme changed self-reported exercise and weight management, but not clinical measures, spending, or jobs outcomes
cards.summary: Song & Baicker 2019: self-reported exercise +8.3 points and weight management +13.6 points — and no significant effects on clinical measures, spending or employment outcomes.
cards.people: 160 worksites of a large US warehouse retailer; 32,974 employees (mean age 38.6 years, SD 15.2; 45.9% women) — 20 treatment worksites (4,037 employees) and 140 control worksites for administrative outcomes, with 20 primary control worksites (4,106 employees) for surveys and screenings. Mean participation was 1.3 programme modules.
cards.result: After 18 months, two self-reported outcomes were higher at treatment sites: engaging in regular exercise (69.8% vs 61.9%; adjusted difference 8.3 percentage points, 95% CI 3.9 to 12.8) and actively managing weight (69.2% vs 54.7%; adjusted difference 13.6 points, 7.1 to 20.2). There were no significant effects on the other 27 self-reported outcomes, any of 10 clinical markers (including cholesterol, blood pressure and body mass index), any of 38 medical and pharmaceutical spending and utilisation measures, or 3 employment outcomes (absenteeism, tenure, job performance).
cards.watchOut: Survey and screening participation was incomplete (about 36-45%), and follow-up was 18 months — the trial cannot exclude benefits or savings emerging over longer horizons, and its programme was one employer's design.
cards.source: Song Z, Baicker K. Effect of a Workplace Wellness Program on Employee Health and Economic Outcomes: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2019 Apr 16;321(15):1491-1501. PMID: 30990549. Registry ID: NCT03167658 (record's databank).

cards.headline: Illinois Workplace Wellness Study: no effects on biometrics, diagnoses, or medical use at 12 or 24 months
cards.summary: Illinois Workplace Wellness Study: no effects on biometrics, diagnoses or medical use at 12 or 24 months.
cards.people: 4,834 employees of the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (3,300 treatment, 1,534 control; 2,770 women; mean age 43.9 years, SD 11.3), randomised individually, with incentives and paid time off for screenings, health risk assessments and wellness activities in the treatment group.
cards.result: No significant effects of the programme on clinician-collected biometrics (16 outcomes), medical diagnoses (diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia), or medical use (office, inpatient and emergency visits) were seen after 12 or 24 months. At 24 months more treatment-group employees reported having a primary care physician (92.2% [1,106 of 1,200] vs 86.1% [477 of 554]; adjusted P=.002), and employee health beliefs improved on average — beliefs about their own chance of having a body mass index above 30, high cholesterol, high blood pressure and impaired glucose jointly decreased by 0.07 SDs (95% CI -0.12 to -0.01; P=.02) — though individual belief measures were not significant.
cards.watchOut: A university workforce is not a general employee population, and the trial's incentives were for participation rather than outcomes. This PubMed record is the study's health-outcomes report; the study's economics-journal report is not PubMed-indexed and no figures from it are used here.
cards.source: Reif J et al. Effects of a Workplace Wellness Program on Employee Health, Health Beliefs, and Medical Use: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2020 Jul 1;180(7):952-960. PMID: 32453346. Registry ID: AEARCTR-0001368 (American Economic Association RCT Registry number stated in the record's abstract; no databank SI field on the record).

cards.headline: Synthesis: two large randomised trials, one verdict — wellness programmes move self-reported behaviour, not health or costs, in 1-2 years
cards.summary: Two large randomised trials, one verdict: wellness programmes move self-reported behaviour, not health or costs, within 1–2 years — LIKELY, for the null.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: 32,974 retail employees in 160 worksites and 4,834 university employees, both randomised.
cards.result: Across both trials there were no significant effects on clinical measures, diagnoses, health-care spending or use, or employment outcomes within 18-24 months; the only consistent positives were self-reported behaviours (exercise, weight management), having a primary care physician, and health beliefs. This shelf is stamped LIKELY — LIKELY the null on health and economic outcomes in the short term: two large, concordant randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: Fence: follow-up of 18-24 months cannot judge long-run returns, and results come from two US employers' multicomponent programmes — targeted programmes (for example smoking cessation alone) are graded on their own shelves.

shelves.title: Financial incentives for smoking cessation in pregnancy
shelves.question: Do financial incentives increase quit rates in pregnant smokers, during pregnancy and after delivery?
shelves.mesh: Birth Weight · Breath Tests · Carbon Monoxide/analysis · Cotinine/analysis · Health Promotion/economics/methods · Motivation · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials in different health systems agree. In the Scottish CPIT trial, offering up to £400 of vouchers on top of routine cessation services raised cotinine-verified cessation in late pregnancy from 8.6% to 22.5% (relative risk 2.63, 95% CI 1.73 to 4.01; absolute difference 14.0 percentage points; number needed to treat 7.2). In the French FISCP trial, abstinence-contingent vouchers raised continuous abstinence before delivery from 7% to 16% (odds ratio 2.45, 1.34 to 4.49). Birth weight did not differ significantly in CPIT (3,140 g vs 3,120 g); the French trial's neonatal findings were secondary and partly post hoc, and are fenced as such on its card.

cards.headline: CPIT: up to £400 in vouchers raised verified late-pregnancy quitting from 8.6% to 22.5%
cards.summary: CPIT: cotinine-verified late-pregnancy quitting 22.5% vs 8.6% (relative risk 2.63 , absolute difference 14.0 points, NNT 7.2 ) with up to £400 in vouchers.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (phase II, single centre)
cards.people: 612 self-reported pregnant smokers (306 incentives, 306 control; 303 controls in the intention-to-treat analysis) in NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde, a materially deprived inner-city population; women were at least 16 years old, under 24 weeks pregnant, and English-speaking. Mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Cotinine-verified cessation at 34-38 weeks was achieved by 69 women (22.5%) in the incentives group versus 26 (8.6%) in the control group — relative risk of not smoking 2.63 (95% CI 1.73 to 4.01; P<0.001), absolute risk difference 14.0 percentage points (8.2 to 19.7), number needed to treat 7.2 (5.1 to 12.2). Mean birth weight was 3,140 g (SD 600) in the incentives group versus 3,120 g (SD 590) in controls (P=0.67). No harms of financial incentives were documented.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre phase II trial: incentives were added to an already-structured specialist service (face-to-face appointment, free nicotine replacement, support calls), so the effect is for incentives as an add-on, in a deprived population with low baseline quit rates. The relative risk of 2.63 clears the 2.0 fence and is printed with its absolute rates alongside.
cards.source: Tappin D et al. Financial incentives for smoking cessation in pregnancy: randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2015 Jan 27;350:h134. PMID: 25627664. Registry ID: ISRCTN87508788 (record's databank).

shelves.title: Blood-pressure control in Black barbershops
shelves.question: Does pharmacist-led blood-pressure care delivered through Black-owned barbershops, with barber encouragement, lower systolic pressure far more than barber health promotion alone — and what did the programme's earlier barber-monitoring trial find?
shelves.mesh: Black or African American · Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Barbering · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Cohort Studies · Drug Therapy, Combination · Health Promotion/methods,statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two cluster-randomised trials from the same research programme, a decade apart, show venue-based barbershop care works — and that what the barber hands the patron to matters enormously. BARBER-1 (17 Dallas barbershops): barbers checking blood pressure and promoting physician follow-up raised hypertension control rates by 8.8 percentage points versus pamphlets, with only a marginal systolic effect (−2.5 mm Hg, non-significant). The 2018 Los Angeles trial (52 barbershops, 319 men): barber encouragement coupled with pharmacists prescribing in the shop under collaborative agreements cut systolic pressure 21.6 mm Hg more than health promotion alone, and 63.6% versus 11.7% reached below 130/80 mm Hg. Blood-pressure endpoints only — no event outcomes — so the stamp rests on trial count and effect size, not on outcomes beyond pressure.

cards.headline: Victor 2018: pharmacist-led care in Black barbershops cut systolic pressure 21.6 mm Hg more than barber health promotion alone
cards.summary: Barbershop pharmacist trial (2018): pharmacist-led care in Black barbershops cut systolic pressure 21.6 mm Hg more than barber health promotion alone.
cards.people: 319 Black male patrons with systolic blood pressure of 140 mm Hg or more, enrolled from 52 Black-owned barbershops in a cluster-randomised trial; barbershops were assigned to a pharmacist-led intervention (barbers encouraged meetings in barbershops with specialty-trained pharmacists who prescribed drug therapy under collaborative practice agreements with participants' doctors) or an active control (barbers encouraged lifestyle modification and doctor appointments). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At baseline, mean systolic blood pressure was 152.8 mm Hg in the intervention group and 154.6 mm Hg in the control group. At 6 months, mean systolic pressure fell by 27.0 mm Hg (to 125.8) in the intervention group and by 9.3 mm Hg (to 145.4) in the control group — a mean reduction 21.6 mm Hg greater with the intervention (95% confidence interval, 14.7 to 28.4; P<0.001). Blood pressure below 130/80 mm Hg was achieved by 63.6% of the intervention group versus 11.7% of controls (P<0.001). Cohort retention in the intervention group was 95%, with few adverse events (three cases of acute kidney injury).
cards.watchOut: The intervention is intensive — specialty pharmacists prescribing on site under collaborative agreements — and follow-up was 6 months: the trial proves the model works where it is staffed and funded, not that effect sizes this large survive routine scale-up or years of follow-up.
cards.source: Victor RG et al. A Cluster-Randomized Trial of Blood-Pressure Reduction in Black Barbershops. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(14):1291-1301. PMID: 29527973. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02321618, from the record's databank fields.

cards.people: Black male patrons with elevated blood pressure at 17 Black-owned barbershops in Dallas County, Texas (intervention: 9 shops, about 75 hypertensive patrons per shop; comparison: 8 shops, about 77 per shop), after a 10-week baseline screening period, followed for 10 months; the abstract does not state mean age or the total number of hypertensive patrons.
cards.result: The hypertension control rate increased more in intervention barbershops than in comparison barbershops (absolute group difference 8.8% [95% confidence interval, 0.8% to 16.9%]; P = .04), and the effect persisted after adjustment for covariates (P = .03). cards.watchOut: Pinned at build as the topic file's 'earlier barbershop intervention trial'. cards.summary: Barbershops work as a venue; putting a prescribing pharmacist in them is what moves pressure — LIKELY.

shelves.title: Pedometers and exercise referral in primary care: PACE-UP and e-coachER
shelves.question: Do primary-care activity interventions work at scale — a pedometer programme with and without nurse support (PACE-UP), and an exercise-referral scheme augmented with web-based support (e-coachER) — on objectively measured activity a year later?
shelves.mesh: Actigraphy/statistics & numerical data · Health Promotion/methods · London · Nurses · Primary Health Care · Walking · Behavior Therapy
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — pedometer programmes raise activity · POSSIBLE — web support added to exercise referral does not (the treatment made no difference). PACE-UP (1023 inactive adults aged 45–75 in London primary care) found a pedometer programme added about 650 steps a day and about 34 extra minutes a week of moderate-to-vigorous activity at 12 months — and posting the kit worked as well as nurse consultations. e-coachER (450 inactive adults with chronic conditions already referred to an exercise scheme) found adding web-based behavioural support produced a weak, non-significant activity difference at 12 months. One positive trial carries the pedometer claim to LIKELY under this library's behavioural-trial convention (unblindable by nature, judged on trial count and rigour); the web-augmentation null rests on one trial and is POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: PACE-UP 2017: a primary-care pedometer programme added ~650 steps a day at 12 months — posted kits matched nurse support
cards.summary: PACE-UP (2017): a primary-care pedometer programme added about 650 steps a day at 12 months — posted kits matched nurse support.
cards.type: Parallel three-arm cluster randomised trial (randomised by household) with 12-month follow-up
cards.people: 1023 predominantly inactive adults aged 45–75 years from 922 households, cluster-randomised across seven London primary care practices to usual care (338), a postal pedometer intervention (339), or a nurse-supported pedometer intervention (346); 956 (93%) provided 12-month outcome data. Average baseline step count was 7479 (SD 2671) per day and moderate-to-vigorous activity in bouts was 94 (SD 102) min/week.
cards.result: At 12 months, mean steps/day were 7246 (SD 2671) on usual care, 8010 (2922) postal, and 8131 (3228) nurse-supported. Versus control, additional steps/day were 642 (95% CI 329–955) for postal and 677 (365–989) for nurse support; additional moderate-to-vigorous activity in bouts was 33 min/week (17–49) postal and 35 (19–51) nurse-supported. There were no significant differences between the two interventions at 12 months. The recruitment rate was 10% (1023 of 10,467 invited) — a stated study limitation.
cards.watchOut: Only 10% of invited patients took part — volunteers for a walking trial are not a practice population — and the gain (about a tenth more steps) is real but modest against guideline activity targets.
cards.source: Harris T et al. Effect of a Primary Care Walking Intervention with and without Nurse Support on Physical Activity Levels in 45- to 75-Year-Olds: The Pedometer And Consultation Evaluation (PACE-UP) Cluster Randomised Clinical Trial. PLoS Med. 2017;14(1):e1002210. PMID: 28045890. Registry ID: ISRCTN98538934, stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: e-coachER 2021: adding web-based support to an exercise referral scheme had no significant effect on activity at 12 months
cards.summary: e-coachER (2021): adding web-based support to an exercise referral scheme had no significant effect on activity at 12 months.
cards.type: Multicentre individually randomised controlled trial, 12 months
cards.people: 450 inactive adults with chronic health conditions referred to exercise referral schemes at three UK sites, randomised to usual exercise referral alone or referral plus the e-coachER web-based behavioural support (with pedometer, activity sheets and user guide); primary analysis included 232 participants with usable accelerometer data at 12 months; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the pedometer kit works; the web add-on to referral did not — split stamp
cards.summary: The pedometer kit works; the web add-on to referral did not — Split: LIKELY · POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PACE-UP (1023 inactive adults, primary care) and e-coachER (450 referred inactive adults with chronic conditions).
cards.result: The two trials test different rungs of the same ladder. Handing inactive primary-care patients a pedometer, a 12-week walking programme and a diary — by post or with nurse consultations — raised objectively measured activity a year later by ~650 steps/day and ~34 min/week of bouted moderate-to-vigorous activity (LIKELY). Adding interactive web support on top of an existing exercise referral scheme did not significantly change activity (POSSIBLE, the null, one trial with substantial missing outcome data). The exercise-as-treatment shelves (#452–#461) test exercise for disease endpoints and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Both trials measure activity, not events: no card on this shelf shows a pedometer or referral scheme preventing a heart attack, a fall, or a death.

shelves.title: The J-curve is an artefact: when abstainer bias is removed and genes do the randomising, moderate drinking shows no protection — risk rises with dose for stroke, heart failure and blood pressure, and total mortality is lowest at or below about 100 g a week
shelves.question: Is moderate alcohol drinking actually protective against death and cardiovascular disease, as the J-shaped curve from observational studies suggests?
shelves.mesh: Alcohol Drinking/*adverse effects/mortality · Cardiovascular Diseases/etiology · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: For decades the observational J-curve — moderate drinkers outliving abstainers — was quoted as settled. Four analyses dismantle it from four directions. Wood 2018 (PMID: 29676281) pooled individual data on 599,912 current drinkers: all-cause mortality was lowest at or below about 100 g of alcohol per week (roughly five to six standard drinks), and above that, life expectancy at age 40 fell by about 6 months at 100–200 g/week, 1–2 years at 200–350 g/week and 4–5 years above 350 g/week; per additional 100 g/week, risk rose for stroke (HR 1.14), heart failure (1.09), fatal hypertensive disease (1.24) and coronary disease excluding myocardial infarction (1.06) — only myocardial infarction itself ran the other way (HR 0.94, all hazard ratios relative measures). Millwood 2019 (PMID: 30955975) used alcohol-metabolism genotypes in 512,715 Chinese adults as nature's randomisation: the conventional analysis reproduced the U-shape, but genotype-predicted intake showed a continuous, positive association with stroke (relative risk per 280 g/week 1.27 for ischaemic stroke, 1.58 for intracerebral haemorrhage) and no association with myocardial infarction (0.96) — the 'protection' did not survive the genetic test. Zhao 2023 (PMID: 37000449) re-ran the mortality meta-analysis across 107 cohorts (4.8 million participants) while modelling former-drinker and other abstainer biases: occasional drinkers (RR 0.96, P=.41) and low-volume drinkers (RR 0.93, P=.07) had no significant mortality advantage over lifetime nondrinkers, while risk became significant at 45–64 g/day (RR 1.19) and ≥65 g/day (RR 1.35), and appeared at lower intakes in women (RR 1.22). The Global Burden of Disease 2020 analysis (PMID: 35843246) lands in between: the theoretical minimum-risk exposure was effectively zero for ages 15–39, with a shallow J only in older adults. Nobody has randomised alcohol, and nobody will; this is as close to causal as the question gets. PROPOSED LIKELY (no protective effect) (Tier C: entirely observational and genetic-epidemiological evidence).

cards.headline: Wood 2018: in 599,912 current drinkers, mortality was lowest at or below ~100 g of alcohol per week; stroke, heart failure and hypertensive death rose linearly with dose, and only myocardial infarction fell
cards.summary: Wood 2018: in 599,912 current drinkers, mortality was lowest at or below ~100 g of alcohol per week; stroke, heart failure and hypertensive death rose linearly with dose, and only myocardial infarction fell
cards.people: Combined individual-participant analysis of 83 prospective studies in 19 high-income countries (Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, EPIC-CVD, UK Biobank): 599,912 current drinkers without previous cardiovascular disease, followed for 5.4 million person-years, with 40,310 deaths and 39,018 incident cardiovascular events. Hazard ratios are adjusted relative measures, corrected for long-term variability in consumption using 152,640 repeat assessments.
cards.result: All-cause mortality showed a positive curvilinear association with consumption, with minimum risk around or below 100 g per week. Per 100 g/week higher consumption, hazard ratios were 1.14 for stroke (95% CI 1.10 to 1.17), 1.06 for coronary disease excluding myocardial infarction (1.00 to 1.11), 1.09 for heart failure (1.03 to 1.15), 1.24 for fatal hypertensive disease (1.15 to 1.33) and 1.15 for fatal aortic aneurysm (1.03 to 1.28); myocardial infarction ran inversely (0.94; 0.91 to 0.97). Compared with drinking >0–≤100 g/week, drinking >100–≤200, >200–≤350 or >350 g/week was associated with lower life expectancy at age 40 of approximately 6 months, 1–2 years, or 4–5 years respectively.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is among current drinkers — the abstainer group, with its sick-quitter contamination, is excluded by design, which is the study's strength for dose-response and its limit for the 'should a nondrinker start?' question (it cannot speak to it). The single inverse association, myocardial infarction, sits alongside positive associations for every other cardiovascular endpoint including total coronary disease measures — quoting the MI figure alone reverses the paper's message.
