cards.headline: Millwood 2019: in 512,715 Chinese adults, self-reported drinking showed the usual U-shape — but genotype-predicted drinking showed stroke risk rising continuously with dose and no protection for myocardial infarction
cards.summary: Millwood 2019: in 512,715 Chinese adults, self-reported drinking showed the usual U-shape — but genotype-predicted drinking showed stroke risk rising continuously with dose and no protection for myocardial infarction
cards.type: Prospective cohort with Mendelian randomisation (Millwood 2019, China Kadoorie Biobank)
cards.people: China Kadoorie Biobank prospective study: 512,715 adults followed about 10 years; 161,498 participants genotyped for two variants (ALDH2-rs671 and ADH1B-rs1229984) that strongly alter alcohol intake, used as Mendelian-randomisation instruments. Conventional analyses related self-reported intake to disease; genetic analyses related genotype-predicted mean male intake (4 to 256 g/week across genotype groups) to the same outcomes; few women drank, providing a negative-control population.
cards.result: Conventional epidemiology reproduced U-shaped associations of self-reported intake with ischaemic stroke (14,930 events), intracerebral haemorrhage (3,496) and acute myocardial infarction (2,958), with the lowest risks at about 100 g/week. The genetic analysis showed no U-shape: genotype-predicted intake was continuously, log-linearly associated with stroke — relative risk per 280 g/week 1.58 for intracerebral haemorrhage (95% CI 1.36 to 1.84) and 1.27 for ischaemic stroke (1.13 to 1.43) — and was not significantly associated with myocardial infarction (0.96; 0.78 to 1.18). Both self-reported and genotype-predicted intake were strongly positively associated with systolic blood pressure. The authors conclude the apparently protective effects of moderate intake against stroke are largely non-causal.
cards.watchOut: Mendelian randomisation assumes the variants act only through alcohol intake; ALDH2 also produces acetaldehyde toxicity symptoms, which is part of the mechanism but complicates a pure 'dose' reading. Drinking in this cohort was mainly spirits, in men, in China — the genetic logic travels better than the exact dose-response numbers. The myocardial-infarction result is 'no association', which refutes protection less completely than the stroke results refute it there.

cards.headline: Zhao 2023: across 107 cohorts and 4.8 million participants, correcting for former-drinker and abstainer biases erased the mortality advantage of low-volume drinking (RR 0.93, P=.07); risk was significant from 45 g/day
cards.summary: Zhao 2023: across 107 cohorts and 4.8 million participants, correcting for former-drinker and abstainer biases erased the mortality advantage of low-volume drinking (RR 0.93, P=.07); risk was significant from 45 g/day
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies (Zhao 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analyses of 107 cohort studies of alcohol use and all-cause mortality published 1980–2021, contributing 724 risk estimates from 4,838,825 participants and 425,564 deaths. Mixed linear regression modelled relative risks, with prespecified adjustment for sampling variation, former-drinker bias and other study-quality criteria, stratified by cohort median age and sex.
cards.result: In the fully adjusted model there was no significantly reduced mortality risk among occasional drinkers (>0 to <1.3 g/day; relative risk 0.96; 95% CI 0.86 to 1.06; P=.41) or low-volume drinkers (1.3–24.0 g/day; RR 0.93; P=.07) compared with lifetime nondrinkers. Risk was nonsignificantly increased at 25–44 g/day (RR 1.05; P=.28) and significantly increased at 45–64 g/day (RR 1.19) and ≥65 g/day (RR 1.35; both P<.001). Mortality risks were significantly larger for female drinkers versus female lifetime nondrinkers (RR 1.22; P=.03), appearing at lower consumption levels than in men.
cards.watchOut: The correction is model-based: the conclusion is that the J-curve shrinks to non-significance when studies with biased abstainer reference groups are handled properly — a statement about the literature's artefacts as much as about alcohol. A relative risk of 0.93 with P=.07 in low-volume drinkers leaves a sliver of room for a tiny benefit; the paper's claim, and this shelf's, is that no protection is established, not that a minuscule one is disproven to zero.
cards.source: Zhao J et al. Association Between Daily Alcohol Intake and Risk of All-Cause Mortality: A Systematic Review and Meta-analyses. JAMA Network Open. 2023. PMID: 37000449. cards.headline: GBD 2020: the minimum-risk drinking level was effectively zero under age 40; a shallow J-curve appeared only in older adults, varying by region
cards.summary: GBD 2020: the minimum-risk drinking level was effectively zero under age 40; a shallow J-curve appeared only in older adults, varying by region
cards.type: Systematic analysis / burden modelling (GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators 2022)
cards.people: Global Burden of Disease 2020 systematic analysis: burden-weighted dose-response relative-risk curves across 22 health outcomes, used to estimate the theoretical minimum risk exposure level (TMREL) and the non-drinker equivalence level for 21 regions, by 5-year age group, sex and year, 1990–2020.
cards.result: Among people aged 15–39 years in 2020, the TMREL ranged from 0 to 0.603 standard drinks per day across regions. Among those aged 40 and older, the burden-weighted curve was J-shaped in all regions, with a TMREL from 0.114 to 1.87 standard drinks per day and non-drinker equivalence from 0.193 to 6.94 drinks per day. Of the population consuming harmful amounts of alcohol in 2020, 59.1% were aged 15–39 years and 76.9% were male. The authors conclude recommendations should vary by age and location, with stronger intervention aimed at younger drinkers.
cards.watchOut: A modelled synthesis, not a measurement: its older-adult J-curve is inherited from the same observational relative risks that Zhao and Millwood challenge, weighted by regional disease patterns — where ischaemic heart disease dominates the burden, a small apparent cardioprotection moves the minimum. Read it as 'the case for any benefit is confined to older adults in some regions', not as a prescription of a drink a day after 40.
cards.source: GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators. Population-level risks of alcohol consumption by amount, geography, age, sex, and year: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2020. The Lancet. 2022. PMID: 35843246. cards.headline: Synthesis: no causal protection at any dose is established; the lowest-risk intake is at or near zero for the young and no more than ~100 g/week for older drinkers — LIKELY (no protective effect)
cards.summary: Synthesis: no causal protection at any dose is established; the lowest-risk intake is at or near zero for the young and no more than ~100 g/week for older drinkers — LIKELY (no protective effect)
cards.people: Four complementary analyses: an individual-participant dose-response pooling (599,912 drinkers), a Mendelian-randomisation cohort (512,715 adults), a bias-adjusted mortality meta-analysis (107 cohorts, 4.8 million participants), and the GBD 2020 global modelling.
cards.result: Dose-response: mortality minimum around ≤100 g/week, life expectancy falling steeply above 200 g/week; stroke, heart failure and hypertensive death rising linearly per 100 g/week. Genetics: stroke risk rises continuously with genotype-predicted intake (RR 1.27–1.58 per 280 g/week) with no U-shape and no MI association. Bias correction: low-volume drinking confers no significant mortality advantage over lifetime abstention (RR 0.93–0.96, both non-significant). Global modelling: minimum-risk exposure ≈0 below age 40. The protective J-curve is best explained by abstainer bias and confounding.
cards.watchOut: There is no randomised trial of alcohol and there never will be; Mendelian randomisation and bias modelling are the strongest available instruments, and each carries assumptions. The shelf refutes cardioprotection as a reason to drink; it does not quantify every harm (cancer, injury, dependence sit largely outside these four records), and it does not turn 'no benefit' into 'any drink is dangerous' — the absolute risks at genuinely low intake are small, which is precisely why the bias artefacts could masquerade as benefit for so long.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wood AM et al. The Lancet. 2018 (PMID: 29676281); Millwood IY et al. The Lancet. 2019 (PMID: 30955975); Zhao J et al. JAMA Network Open. 2023 (PMID: 37000449); GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators. The Lancet. 2022 (PMID: 35843246).

shelves.title: Tai chi and falls: fall rates fell by roughly two-fifths in the first year in pooled trials — the protection fades with time, and the evidence on injuries is thin
shelves.question: In community-dwelling older adults, does tai chi reduce falls and fall injuries?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/prevention & control · Exercise · Humans · Incidence · Postural Balance/physiology · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk Factors · Tai Ji/methods
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two meta-analyses of randomised trials and the best single trial agree that tai chi reduces falls in older adults, with the effect strongest in the first year. Lomas-Vega 2017 (PMID: 28736853) pooled 10 RCTs: fall incidence IRR 0.57 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.70) short term — a 43% relative reduction — attenuating to 0.87 (0.77 to 0.98) beyond 12 months; injurious falls IRR 0.50 short term on very low-quality evidence; time to first fall unchanged (HR 0.98). Del-Pino-Casado 2016 (PMID: 27430918), pooling 13 controlled trials as absolute risk reduction, found the same direction with low heterogeneity. In the landmark single trial, Li 2005 (PMID: 15814861), 256 inactive adults aged 70–92 randomised to thrice-weekly tai chi for 6 months had 38 falls versus 73 on stretching, with injurious falls in 7% versus 18%. The general falls-prevention shelf (#161) homes the later Li 2018 trial of Tai Ji Quan against multimodal exercise; this shelf answers the tai-chi-specific question and does not re-card it. What the evidence does not show: fewer fractures, a delay in the first fall, or protection that survives stopping practice.

cards.headline: Lomas-Vega 2017: 10 RCTs — tai chi cut the fall rate by 43% relative in the first year (IRR 0.57) and injurious falls by half, but the effect shrank to 13% relative beyond a year and time to first fall did not move
cards.summary: Lomas-Vega 2017: 10 RCTs — tai chi cut the fall rate by 43% relative in the first year (IRR 0.57) and injurious falls by half, but the effect shrank to 13% relative beyond a year and time to first fall did not move
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 randomised controlled trials of tai chi versus other treatments for falls prevention in older adults and at-risk adults, searched to May 2016. Outcomes: fall incidence rate ratio (IRR) and hazard ratio for time to first fall.
cards.result: There was high-quality evidence of a medium protective effect on fall incidence over the short term (IRR 0.57, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.70 — a 43% relative reduction) and a small protective effect over the long term (IRR 0.87, 0.77 to 0.98 — 13% relative). For injurious falls, very low-quality evidence suggested a medium protective effect short term (IRR 0.50, 0.33 to 0.74) and a small effect long term (IRR 0.72, 0.54 to 0.95). There was no effect on time to first fall (HR 0.98, 0.69 to 1.37), on moderate-quality evidence.
cards.watchOut: The pooled benefit is a rate effect — fewer falls per person-year — not a delay in the first fall, which did not change. The injurious-falls estimate rests on very low-quality evidence, and protection attenuates sharply after 12 months: the trials support tai chi as continuing practice, not as a course that inoculates.
cards.source: Lomas-Vega R et al. Tai Chi for Risk of Falls. A Meta-analysis. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2017. PMID: 28736853. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Li 2005: in 256 inactive adults aged 70–92, six months of thrice-weekly tai chi halved the fall count (38 vs 73) and cut injurious falls from 18% to 7%
cards.summary: Li 2005: in 256 inactive adults aged 70–92, six months of thrice-weekly tai chi halved the fall count (38 vs 73) and cut injurious falls from 18% to 7%
cards.people: 256 physically inactive, community-dwelling adults aged 70 to 92 (mean 77.5 years) in Portland, Oregon, randomised to a three-times-weekly Tai Chi group or a stretching control group for 6 months, with a further 6-month post-intervention follow-up. Primary outcome: number of falls.
cards.result: At the end of the 6-month intervention there were significantly fewer falls in the Tai Chi group (38 vs 73 falls, P = .007), fewer fallers (28% vs 46%, P = .01) and fewer injurious falls (7% vs 18%, P = .03). After adjustment for baseline covariates, the risk of multiple falls was 55% lower relative (risk ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.70). Functional balance, physical performance and fear of falling all improved significantly (P < .001), and the gains were maintained at the 6-month post-intervention follow-up.
cards.watchOut: The control was stretching, not usual care, and participants were volunteers able to attend classes three times a week — the trial shows what tai chi does in people who actually practise it, which is also the population the meta-analyses pool.
cards.source: Li F et al. Tai Chi and fall reductions in older adults: a randomized controlled trial. The Journals of Gerontology. Series A, Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences. 2005. cards.headline: Del-Pino-Casado 2016: a second synthesis of 13 controlled trials found a significant absolute reduction in fall risk, with low heterogeneity and no sign the effect depended on the comparator
cards.summary: Del-Pino-Casado 2016: a second synthesis of 13 controlled trials found a significant absolute reduction in fall risk, with low heterogeneity and no sign the effect depended on the comparator
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 13 controlled trials (Del-Pino-Casado 2016)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 controlled trials published before June 2015 testing tai chi for fall prevention in frail and at-risk adults, with absolute risk reduction (ARR) as the effect measure.
cards.result: Tai chi significantly prevented the risk of falling on the pooled absolute risk reduction. Heterogeneity across trials was low, the assessed risk of publication bias was reduced, and no significant effect differences were observed between studies comparing tai chi with other interventions and studies comparing it with no treatment.
cards.watchOut: This synthesis pools absolute risk reductions rather than rate ratios, so its numbers cannot be averaged with Lomas-Vega's; and the PubMed record typesets its pooled ARR figure as a formula, so this card reports the finding's direction and significance rather than a number that cannot be verified from the record.
cards.source: Del-Pino-Casado R et al. The Effect of Tai Chi on Reducing the Risk of Falling: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. The American Journal of Chinese Medicine. 2016. PMID: 27430918. cards.headline: Synthesis: fewer falls while practice continues — LIKELY (benefit), with injuries and durability the weak points
cards.summary: Synthesis: fewer falls while practice continues — LIKELY (benefit), with injuries and durability the weak points
cards.people: Two meta-analyses (10 RCTs and 13 controlled trials) and the landmark 256-participant RCT of thrice-weekly tai chi versus stretching in inactive adults aged 70–92.
cards.result: Fall incidence falls by about 43% relative in the first year (IRR 0.57, 0.46 to 0.70), attenuating to about 13% relative beyond a year (IRR 0.87); the single best trial counted 38 falls versus 73 and injurious falls in 7% versus 18% of participants. Injurious falls overall rest on very low-quality evidence, time to first fall is unchanged, and no trial reports fractures.
cards.watchOut: Tai chi is one option inside the broader falls-prevention evidence homed on shelf #161 (which cards Li 2018's Tai Ji Quan trial against multimodal exercise); this shelf does not show tai chi is superior to other exercise — Lomas-Vega's comparisons were against mixed controls, and the head-to-head question belongs to #161.

shelves.title: Yoga for blood pressure: pooled trials suggest about 5–10 mm Hg systolic — but the trials are small, unblinded and wildly inconsistent, and yoga did not beat ordinary exercise
shelves.question: In adults with hypertension, does yoga lower blood pressure?
shelves.mesh: Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Chi-Square Distribution · Combined Modality Therapy · Humans · Hypertension/physiopathology/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Yoga
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the direction is consistent across three syntheses and the size is clinically meaningful if real, but the underlying trials are small, unblindable and extremely heterogeneous. In hypertension-specific trials, Cramer 2014 (PMID: 24795403) found −9.65 mm Hg systolic versus usual care on very low-quality evidence (I² = 90%), and no effect versus exercise. Wu 2019 (PMID: 30792067), pooling 49 controlled trials and 3,517 participants, found average reductions of 5.0/3.9 mm Hg, with the largest modelled effects (11/6 mm Hg) when breathing and meditation were included and practice was three times a week in hypertensive samples. Cramer 2014 (PMID: 24636547), across 44 RCTs in broader populations, found −5.85/−4.12 mm Hg versus usual care. Read together: yoga probably lowers blood pressure by roughly 4–6 mm Hg on average against doing nothing — comparable to other lifestyle measures — but no trial shows it lowers pressure more than ordinary exercise, and none measures cardiovascular events. It is an adjunct, not a substitute for drug treatment.

cards.headline: Cramer 2014: 7 RCTs, 452 patients — yoga lowered systolic pressure by 9.7 mm Hg against usual care, on evidence graded very low quality with heterogeneity above 90%
cards.summary: Cramer 2014: 7 RCTs, 452 patients — yoga lowered systolic pressure by 9.7 mm Hg against usual care, on evidence graded very low quality with heterogeneity above 90%
cards.people: Seven randomised controlled trials (total 452 patients) of yoga interventions of at least 8 weeks versus usual care or an active control, in people with prehypertension (120–139/80–89 mm Hg) or hypertension (≥140/≥90 mm Hg), searched to February 2014.
cards.result: Compared with usual care, very low-quality evidence showed systolic blood pressure lower by a mean of 9.65 mm Hg (95% CI −17.23 to −2.06, P = 0.01; 6 RCTs, n = 278) and diastolic lower by 7.22 mm Hg (−12.83 to −1.62), with heterogeneity I² = 90% and 92%. Subgroup effects appeared in trials of hypertensive patients and in trials allowing antihypertensive co-medication, but not in mixed prehypertension trials or no-medication trials. Compared with exercise, no evidence of an effect on systolic or diastolic pressure was found. More adverse events occurred during yoga than during usual care.
cards.watchOut: A 9.7 mm Hg average built from 278 patients with I² = 90% is not a stable estimate — the confidence interval runs from −17 to −2 mm Hg — and the comparison that matters clinically, yoga versus other exercise, was null.
cards.source: Cramer H et al. A systematic review and meta-analysis of yoga for hypertension. American Journal of Hypertension. 2014. PMID: 24795403. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wu 2019: 49 controlled trials, 3,517 participants — average reductions of 5.0/3.9 mm Hg, rising to a modelled 11/6 mm Hg when practice included breathing and meditation three times a week in hypertensive samples
cards.summary: Wu 2019: 49 controlled trials, 3,517 participants — average reductions of 5.0/3.9 mm Hg, rising to a modelled 11/6 mm Hg when practice included breathing and meditation three times a week in hypertensive samples
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 49 controlled trials (Wu 2019)
cards.people: 49 controlled trials (56 interventions) of yoga in adults reporting pre- and post-intervention blood pressure against a nonexercise/nondiet control, searched to June 2018. Participants averaged 49 years, were overweight, and had mean baseline pressure 129.3/80.7 mm Hg; yoga was practised about 4.8 sessions a week for about 13 weeks.
cards.result: On average, yoga reduced systolic BP by 5.0 mm Hg and diastolic BP by 3.9 mm Hg versus controls (weighted mean effect size −0.47 for both; P < .001). In additive models controlling for publication bias and study quality, among samples with hypertension practising 3 sessions per week, interventions that included breathing techniques and meditation/mental relaxation elicited reductions of 11/6 mm Hg, compared with 6/3 mm Hg for interventions without those components.
cards.watchOut: The set includes non-randomised controlled trials, and the 11/6 mm Hg figure is a modelled best-case combination of features, not the result of any single trial — the average trial delivered about 5/4 mm Hg against controls that did nothing.
cards.source: Wu Y et al. Yoga as Antihypertensive Lifestyle Therapy: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Mayo Clinic Proceedings. 2019. PMID: 30792067. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Blood Pressure/physiology · Female · Humans · Hypertension/prevention & control/therapy · Male · Meditation · Middle Aged · Primary Prevention/methods · Relaxation Therapy/methods · Stress, Psychological/prevention & control · Yoga

cards.headline: Cramer 2014 (cardiovascular risk factors): 44 RCTs, 3,168 participants — systolic −5.9 and diastolic −4.1 mm Hg versus usual care, alongside small improvements in lipids and HbA1c
cards.summary: Cramer 2014 (cardiovascular risk factors): 44 RCTs, 3,168 participants — systolic −5.9 and diastolic −4.1 mm Hg versus usual care, alongside small improvements in lipids and HbA1c
cards.people: 44 randomised controlled trials (3,168 participants) of yoga for predefined cardiovascular risk factors in healthy participants, non-diabetic participants at high cardiovascular risk, or participants with type 2 diabetes, searched to August 2013.
cards.result: Relative to usual care or no intervention, yoga improved systolic blood pressure (mean difference −5.85 mm Hg, 95% CI −8.81 to −2.89) and diastolic (−4.12, −6.55 to −1.69), heart rate (−6.59 bpm), waist circumference (−1.95 cm), total cholesterol (−13.09 mg/dl), triglycerides (−20.97 mg/dl), HbA1c (−0.45%) and insulin resistance. Risk of bias was high or unclear for most trials. Relative to exercise, only HDL cholesterol differed (+3.70 mg/dl).
cards.watchOut: Broad-population risk-factor trials, not hypertension treatment trials: the blood-pressure averages mix people with normal pressure into the pool, which dilutes — and in a treatment-seeking hypertensive patient may understate — the effect.
cards.source: Cramer H et al. Effects of yoga on cardiovascular disease risk factors: a systematic review and meta-analysis. International Journal of Cardiology. 2014. PMID: 24636547. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology/prevention & control · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk Factors · Risk Reduction Behavior · Yoga

cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but modest average effect against doing nothing — POSSIBLE (benefit), unproven against exercise
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but modest average effect against doing nothing — POSSIBLE (benefit), unproven against exercise
cards.people: Three meta-analyses: 7 hypertension RCTs (452 patients), 49 controlled trials (3,517 participants) and 44 cardiovascular-risk-factor RCTs (3,168 participants).
cards.result: Versus usual care or no intervention, pooled systolic reductions run from about 6 to 10 mm Hg and diastolic from about 4 to 7 mm Hg, with the most inclusive synthesis averaging 5.0/3.9 mm Hg. Versus exercise, both Cramer syntheses found no blood-pressure advantage. Certainty is low to very low throughout: small trials, no blinding, heterogeneity up to I² = 92%.
cards.watchOut: No trial measures stroke, myocardial infarction or death, and none tests yoga as a replacement for antihypertensive drugs; the honest clinical statement is 'an adjunct roughly comparable to other lifestyle measures', not a treatment.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cramer H et al. American Journal of Hypertension. 2014 (PMID: 24795403); Wu Y et al. Mayo Clinic Proceedings. 2019 (PMID: 30792067); Cramer H et al. International Journal of Cardiology. 2014 (PMID: 24636547).

shelves.title: Wearable trackers and weight: pooled short trials say devices help a little; the one large two-year trial found the tracker group lost LESS weight
shelves.question: In adults with overweight, does adding a wearable activity tracker to a weight-loss programme help weight loss, or hinder it?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Body Mass Index · Caloric Restriction · Female · Healthy Lifestyle · Humans · Male · Obesity/therapy · Wearable Electronic Devices · Weight Loss · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on the time horizon. In pooled short-term trials in overweight adults with chronic conditions, wearable-based strategies ranked best for weight reduction (McDonough 2021, PMID: 33731385), and trackers reliably raise physical activity. But the only large long-term randomised test, IDEA (Jakicic 2016, PMID: 27654602), found the opposite of the marketing claim: over 24 months, adding a wearable to a behavioural programme produced 3.5 kg of weight loss versus 5.9 kg without it. The long-term systematic review (Fawcett 2020, PMID: 32154788) found five studies of a year or more and no advantage over comparators in any of them. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE small benefit in short pooled trials / LIKELY (no advantage over standard programmes long term — in the largest trial, less weight loss). A tracker is a reasonable activity prompt; as a weight-loss intervention in its own right it has failed its biggest test.

cards.headline: IDEA (Jakicic 2016): 471 young adults over 24 months — the group given a wearable lost 3.5 kg; the group self-monitoring on a website lost 5.9 kg
cards.summary: IDEA (Jakicic 2016): 471 young adults over 24 months — the group given a wearable lost 3.5 kg; the group self-monitoring on a website lost 5.9 kg
cards.people: 471 adults aged 18–35 with BMI 25 to <40 at the University of Pittsburgh. All received a low-calorie diet, prescribed increases in physical activity and group counselling; from month 6, telephone counselling, text prompts and web materials were added, the standard group began website self-monitoring of diet and activity, and the enhanced group was given a wearable device with a web interface instead. 74.5% completed the study.
cards.result: Weight change at 24 months differed significantly between groups: estimated mean weight loss was 3.5 kg (95% CI 2.6 to 4.5) in the wearable-enhanced group and 5.9 kg (5.0 to 6.8) in the standard group — a difference of 2.4 kg (1.0 to 3.7; P = .002) in favour of the group without the device. Body composition, fitness, physical activity and dietary intake improved significantly in both groups with no significant between-group differences.
cards.watchOut: One trial, in young adults, with a specific armband device and interface of its era — it does not prove modern trackers harm weight loss. But it is the only large long-term randomised test of the actual consumer proposition, and it points the wrong way.
cards.source: Jakicic JM et al. Effect of Wearable Technology Combined With a Lifestyle Intervention on Long-term Weight Loss: The IDEA Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27654602. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01131871. cards.headline: McDonough 2021: network meta-analysis of 31 RCTs in overweight adults with chronic comorbidities — wearable-only strategies ranked best for weight, on standardised effects from mostly short trials
cards.summary: McDonough 2021: network meta-analysis of 31 RCTs in overweight adults with chronic comorbidities — wearable-only strategies ranked best for weight, on standardised effects from mostly short trials
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis, 31 RCTs (McDonough 2021)
cards.people: 31 randomised controlled trials of wearable-based physical-activity interventions in individuals with overweight/obesity and chronic comorbidities, comparing six strategies (control; traditional non-wearable interventions; commercial wearable only; research-grade accelerometer/pedometer only; and multicomponent versions of each) in a Bayesian network meta-analysis.
cards.result: For body-weight reduction, accelerometer/pedometer-only (SMD −4.44, 95% CrI −8.94 to 0.07) and commercial wearable-only (SMD −2.76, −4.80 to −0.81) strategies were the most effective compared with the other treatments and control. For BMI reduction, multicomponent accelerometer/pedometer (SMD −3.43, −4.94 to −2.09) and commercial wearable-only (SMD −1.99, −4.95 to 0.96) ranked most effective.
cards.watchOut: Standardised mean differences from mostly short trials in patients with chronic conditions — a different question from adding a tracker to a full behavioural programme for two years, which is where IDEA found less weight loss. Ranking statistics flatter strategies whose credible intervals cross zero, as the accelerometer-only interval does.
cards.source: McDonough DJ et al. Health wearable devices for weight and BMI reduction in individuals with overweight/obesity and chronic comorbidities: systematic review and network meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021. PMID: 33731385. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42020158191. cards.headline: Fawcett 2020: of the five studies lasting a year or more, none showed wearable interventions beating their comparators — though participants still lost weight over time
cards.summary: Fawcett 2020: of the five studies lasting a year or more, none showed wearable interventions beating their comparators — though participants still lost weight over time
cards.people: Systematic review of wearable technology for long-term (≥1 year) weight loss in overweight and obese adults: five intervention studies (4 randomised trials, 1 non-randomised study), supplemented by six systematic reviews and four commentaries.
cards.result: The interventions delivered by wearable devices did not show a benefit over comparator interventions, but overweight and obese participants still lost weight over time. The included studies were likely to suffer from bias, and significant variance in objectives, methods and results prevented meta-analysis. The reviewers note the challenge of separating decreasing device use over time from the effect of the devices themselves.
cards.watchOut: A narrative review resting on five heterogeneous studies — its value is showing how thin the long-term evidence base is, not in estimating an effect.
cards.source: Fawcett E et al. Long-Term Weight Management Using Wearable Technology in Overweight and Obese Adults: Systematic Review. JMIR mHealth and uHealth. 2020. PMID: 32154788. cards.headline: Synthesis: short-term pooled benefit, long-term failure — SPLIT (POSSIBLE short term / no long-term advantage)
cards.summary: Synthesis: short-term pooled benefit, long-term failure — SPLIT (POSSIBLE short term / no long-term advantage)
cards.people: One 471-participant 24-month RCT, a 31-trial network meta-analysis in comorbid populations, and a systematic review of the five studies lasting at least a year.
cards.result: Short trials pool in the devices' favour on standardised measures; at a year and beyond, no study shows an advantage over comparators, and the largest trial found 2.4 kg LESS weight loss with the device (3.5 vs 5.9 kg at 24 months). Trackers raise activity; sustained weight loss is a different outcome and has not followed.
cards.watchOut: The diet-composition question these programmes sit inside is homed on shelf #209, and brief vigorous everyday activity (a different, device-measured question) on shelf #2580; this shelf is only about the tracker as a weight-loss tool.

shelves.title: Produce prescriptions: vouchers are redeemed and produce intake rises, and HbA1c fell within groups in small studies — but the one pilot randomised trial found no significant advantage over control
shelves.question: In adults with food insecurity and diet-related disease, do produce prescriptions improve diet, glucose control and food security?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Commerce · Diet, Healthy/economics/methods/statistics & numerical data · Food Supply/economics/methods/statistics & numerical data · Fruit · Health Promotion · Health Surveys · Humans · Hypertension/diet therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Poverty · Program Evaluation · Urban Population/statistics & numerical data · Vegetables
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the programmes do what they mechanically promise: people redeem the vouchers and eat more produce. But the health-outcome evidence is one small pilot trial and uncontrolled before-and-after studies. The pilot RCT (Bryce 2021, PMID: 34150472; n = 112) found no significant between-group difference in HbA1c, blood pressure or BMI, though HbA1c fell within the intervention group (9.64% to 9.14%). The uncontrolled Detroit evaluation (Bryce 2017, PMID: 28702315) reported HbA1c falling from 9.54% to 8.83% in 65 patients — a fall of the size regression to the mean alone could produce in patients recruited for poor control. In food-insecure hypertensive patients, Trapl 2018 (PMID: 30447106) documented voucher redemption by 86% of participants and significantly improved self-reported fruit and vegetable intake, with no health outcomes measured. Food security itself was not an endpoint in any of the three studies. Tier C: a shelf resting on a pilot trial and observational programme evaluations, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: Bryce 2021: pilot RCT, 112 patients — HbA1c fell half a point within the produce-prescription group (9.64% to 9.14%) but the between-group difference was not significant
cards.summary: Bryce 2021: pilot RCT, 112 patients — HbA1c fell half a point within the produce-prescription group (9.64% to 9.14%) but the between-group difference was not significant
cards.people: 112 low-income patients with diabetes at a Detroit federally qualified health centre, randomised to the 15-week Fresh Prescription programme (up to $80 — $10 for up to eight weeks — for produce at the centre's farmers' market) or to standard treatment plus information on community resources. Outcomes: HbA1c, blood pressure and BMI at baseline and within three months of completion.
cards.result: There were no significant between-group differences for any outcome at programme completion (all P > .05); the effect size for HbA1c was small (partial η² = 0.02). Within the Fresh Rx group, HbA1c fell significantly from 9.64% to 9.14% (P = 0.006); the control group did not change (9.38% to 9.41%, P = 0.89). BMI and blood pressure did not change in either group.
cards.watchOut: A pilot, powered for feasibility: the within-group fall in the intervention arm is exactly the pattern regression to the mean produces in patients enrolled for poor control, and the trial's own between-group test — the valid one — was null.
cards.source: Bryce R et al. A pilot randomized controlled trial of a fruit and vegetable prescription program at a federally qualified health center in low income uncontrolled diabetics. Preventive Medicine Reports. 2021. PMID: 34150472. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record.

cards.headline: Bryce 2017: in 65 uncontrolled diabetic patients, HbA1c fell from 9.54% to 8.83% over a 13-week produce-prescription programme — with no control group
cards.summary: Bryce 2017: in 65 uncontrolled diabetic patients, HbA1c fell from 9.54% to 8.83% over a 13-week produce-prescription programme — with no control group
cards.people: 65 low-income adults with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c > 6.5% within three months before the programme) at a Detroit federally qualified health centre who participated in the 13-week Fresh Prescription programme (up to $40 of produce at the centre's farmers' market) and had biometric data before and after.
cards.result: HbA1c fell from 9.54% to 8.83% (P = 0.001) between the three months before and the three months after the programme. Weight (208.3 to 209.0 lb) and blood pressure (135.1/79.3 to 135.8/77.6 mm Hg) did not change (P > .05).
cards.watchOut: Pre-post with no comparator: patients were enrolled because their HbA1c was high, so some fall was expected with no intervention at all. The same clinic's randomised pilot (Bryce 2021, carded on this shelf) is the corrective.

cards.headline: Trapl 2018: 224 food-insecure hypertensive patients — 86% redeemed produce vouchers and fruit-and-vegetable intake rose significantly, in an uncontrolled programme evaluation
cards.summary: Trapl 2018: 224 food-insecure hypertensive patients — 86% redeemed produce vouchers and fruit-and-vegetable intake rose significantly, in an uncontrolled programme evaluation
cards.people: 224 adults with hypertension screening positive for food insecurity at 3 safety-net clinics in Cuyahoga County, Ohio (mean age 62; 72% female; 97% African American), offered the PRxHTN programme: three monthly non-physician visits with blood-pressure measurement, nutrition counselling and four $10 farmers'-market produce vouchers per visit. Dietary measures at visits 1 and 3; voucher use from market redemption logs.
cards.result: 86% of participants visited a farmers' market to use their vouchers (median 2 visits; one-third reported it was their first farmers'-market visit ever) and the median number of vouchers redeemed was 8 of 12. Among the 137 participants with follow-up survey data, fruit and vegetable consumption improved significantly and fast-food consumption declined. Blood-pressure outcomes were not reported.
cards.watchOut: Diet was self-reported by the 61% of participants with follow-up surveys, with no control group — the study shows the model reaches people and changes reported shopping, not that it changes health.
cards.source: Trapl ES et al. Dietary Impact of Produce Prescriptions for Patients With Hypertension. Preventing Chronic Disease. 2018. PMID: 30447106. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: reach and diet change are documented; health benefit is not — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: reach and diet change are documented; health benefit is not — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: One pilot RCT (n = 112), one uncontrolled before-and-after study (n = 65) and one uncontrolled programme evaluation (n = 224), all in US safety-net populations with food insecurity.
cards.result: Voucher redemption is high (86%) and self-reported produce intake rises. HbA1c fell within intervention groups in both Detroit studies (about 0.5–0.7 percentage points), but the single randomised between-group comparison was not significant, and no study measured food security or clinical events as endpoints.
cards.watchOut: Larger US produce-prescription programmes (including Gus Schumacher Nutrition Incentive Program sites) have been evaluated mainly for reach and consumption; an adequately powered trial with glycaemic and food-security endpoints is still the missing study. Medically tailored meals — a heavier intervention for sicker patients — are homed on shelf #2605.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bryce R et al. Preventive Medicine Reports. 2021 (PMID: 34150472); Bryce R et al. Preventive Medicine Reports. 2017 (PMID: 28702315); Trapl ES et al. Preventing Chronic Disease. 2018 (PMID: 30447106).

shelves.title: Medically tailored meals: an instrumental-variable cohort links them to half the admission rate, a small crossover trial shows diet quality transformed — and no trial has yet tested admissions or HbA1c
shelves.question: In patients with diabetes or heart failure, do medically tailored meals reduce admissions and improve control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Case-Control Studies · Cohort Studies · Diet, Healthy/economics · Female · Food Assistance/economics · Food Supply/economics · Health Care Costs/statistics & numerical data · Hospitalization/economics · Humans · Male · Massachusetts · Middle Aged · Nutritive Value · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Retrospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the direction is consistent and the mechanism is proven, but the headline outcome has never been randomised. The admissions claim comes from a single instrumental-variable cohort (Berkowitz 2019, PMID: 31009050): IRR 0.51 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.80) for inpatient admissions — a 49% relative reduction — in recipients far sicker than their matched comparators, a design whose answer depends on an unverifiable instrument. The randomised evidence is a 44-patient crossover trial (Berkowitz 2019, PMID: 30421335) showing diet quality transformed while meals were delivered (Healthy Eating Index 71.3 vs 39.9) with less food insecurity and less hypoglycaemia, but no HbA1c or admissions endpoint. Pooling the wider food-is-medicine literature in diabetes (Gao 2023, PMID: 36470724), five RCTs gave HbA1c 0.47 percentage points lower, with I² = 88% and half the literature at high risk of bias. Tier C: the shelf's main claim is observational-dependent, flagged for the developer's personal verdict. A definitive admissions trial remains the missing study.

cards.headline: Berkowitz 2019: 499 meal recipients matched to 521 non-recipients — instrumental-variable analysis estimated 49% relatively fewer inpatient admissions (IRR 0.51) and lower monthly costs
cards.summary: Berkowitz 2019: 499 meal recipients matched to 521 non-recipients — instrumental-variable analysis estimated 49% relatively fewer inpatient admissions (IRR 0.51) and lower monthly costs
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study with instrumental-variable analysis (Berkowitz 2019)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort linking the Massachusetts All-Payer Claims database (2011–2015) to Community Servings, a non-profit delivering 10 ready-to-consume, dietitian-tailored meals weekly. 499 recipients with at least 360 days of pre-intervention claims were near/far matched to 521 non-recipients (mean age 52.7 years). Before matching, recipients were far sicker: mean prior inpatient admissions 1.6 vs 0.2, mean prior costs $80,617 vs $16,138, HIV 21.9% vs 0.7%, cancer 37.9% vs 11.3%, diabetes 33.7% vs 7.0%.
cards.result: In instrumental-variable analyses, meal receipt was associated with significantly fewer inpatient admissions (incidence rate ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.80 — a 49% relative reduction; risk difference −519 per 1000 person-years) and fewer skilled-nursing-facility admissions (IRR 0.28, 0.01 to 0.60). The models estimated mean monthly costs of $3,838 if everyone in the matched cohort received treatment versus $4,591 if no one did (difference −$753, −$1,225 to −$280), including programme costs.
cards.watchOut: The admissions claim rests on an instrument whose validity cannot be verified from the data: recipients differed enormously from non-recipients before matching, and an instrument correlated with any unmeasured severity would manufacture exactly this result. It is the strongest observational design available for the question — and it is still observational.
cards.source: Berkowitz SA et al. Association Between Receipt of a Medically Tailored Meal Program and Health Care Use. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31009050. Registry ID: none — observational study. cards.headline: Berkowitz 2019 (crossover RCT): 44 food-insecure diabetic patients — Healthy Eating Index 71.3 on meals versus 39.9 off meals, with less food insecurity and less hypoglycaemia
cards.summary: Berkowitz 2019 (crossover RCT): 44 food-insecure diabetic patients — Healthy Eating Index 71.3 on meals versus 39.9 off meals, with less food insecurity and less hypoglycaemia
cards.people: 44 adults with type 2 diabetes, HbA1c > 8.0% and food insecurity, randomised to the order of two 12-week periods: 'on-meals' (home delivery of 10 Community Servings meals per week) and 'off-meals' (usual care plus a healthy-eating brochure). Primary outcome: Healthy Eating Index 2010 score from three 24-hour recalls per period.
cards.result: Mean on-meal HEI score was 71.3 (SD 7.5) versus 39.9 (SD 7.8) off-meal (difference 31.4 points, P < 0.0001), with improvements in almost all sub-categories. Participants reported less food insecurity (42% on-meal vs 62% off-meal, P = 0.047), less hypoglycaemia (47% vs 64%, P = 0.03) and fewer days where mental health interfered with quality of life (5.65 vs 9.59 of 30 days, P = 0.03). HbA1c was not an outcome.
cards.watchOut: It proves the meals change what people eat — unsurprising when the food is provided — over 12 weeks in 44 people. It cannot speak to admissions, costs or glycaemic control, the outcomes the programme is sold on.
cards.source: Berkowitz SA et al. Medically Tailored Meal Delivery for Diabetes Patients with Food Insecurity: a Randomized Cross-over Trial. Journal of General Internal Medicine. 2019. PMID: 30421335. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02426138. cards.headline: Gao 2023: across food-is-medicine interventions in diabetes, five pooled RCTs (n = 843) showed HbA1c lower by 0.47 percentage points — with I² of 88% and half the literature at high risk of bias
cards.summary: Gao 2023: across food-is-medicine interventions in diabetes, five pooled RCTs (n = 843) showed HbA1c lower by 0.47 percentage points — with I² of 88% and half the literature at high risk of bias
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of food-is-medicine interventions (produce prescriptions, medically tailored meals and medically tailored groceries) in low-income or food-insecure people with prediabetes or diabetes, from 16 studies published 2000–2021.
cards.result: Five of 8 studies reported a significant increase in fruit and vegetable intake, and 7 of 14 reported a significant decrease in A1C. Pooling 5 randomised controlled trials (n = 843), A1C was lower by a mean difference of −0.47 percentage points (95% CI −0.66 to −0.29) versus control, with heterogeneity I² = 88%. Half of the included studies were at high risk of bias from missing data, detection bias and confounding.
cards.watchOut: This pools a family of interventions, most of them not medically tailored meals, in small trials with very high heterogeneity — it supports the food-is-medicine direction, not the specific admissions and cost claims made for tailored meal programmes.
cards.source: Gao Y et al. The Effect of Food is Medicine Interventions on Diabetes-related Health Outcomes Among Low-income and Food-insecure Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: mechanism proven, admissions unproven — POSSIBLE (benefit) on observational-dependent evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: mechanism proven, admissions unproven — POSSIBLE (benefit) on observational-dependent evidence
cards.people: One instrumental-variable cohort (499 recipients, 521 matched non-recipients), one 44-patient randomised crossover trial, and a 16-study food-is-medicine meta-analysis in diabetes.
cards.result: Diet quality improves dramatically while meals are delivered (HEI +31.4 points) and food insecurity and hypoglycaemia fall. The pooled RCT effect on HbA1c across food-is-medicine interventions is −0.47 percentage points. The admission and cost effects (IRR 0.51; −$753/month) come from a single observational analysis whose instrument cannot be validated.
cards.watchOut: The cohort's recipients had mixed chronic disease (HIV, cancer and diabetes predominated), not the diabetes-or-heart-failure population of this shelf's question alone; the heart-failure-specific evidence is thinner still. Produce prescriptions — the lighter intervention — are homed on shelf #2604.

shelves.title: Very-low-nicotine cigarettes: smokers given them smoked fewer cigarettes, took in less nicotine and showed no sign of smoking harder to compensate — and immediate reduction beat gradual
shelves.question: In smokers, do very-low-nicotine cigarettes reduce smoking and dependence without compensatory smoking?
shelves.mesh: Biomarkers/urine · Creatinine/urine · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Inhalation Exposure/analysis · Linear Models · Nicotine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/standards · Substance Withdrawal Syndrome · Tars/analysis/standards · Tobacco Products/analysis/standards · Tobacco Use Disorder/prevention & control · United States · United States Food and Drug Administration
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for the question asked, two large double-blind randomised trials agree. Donny 2015 (PMID: 26422724; n = 840) found smokers randomised to cigarettes at or below 2.4 mg nicotine per gram smoked about 5–7 fewer cigarettes a day at 6 weeks than controls (14.9 vs 21.3–22.2 per day at 0.4 mg/g), with lower nicotine exposure and dependence and no significant rise in expired carbon monoxide or total puff volume — minimal compensatory smoking. Hatsukami 2018 (PMID: 30193275; n = 1,250) showed immediate reduction to 0.4 mg/g beat both gradual reduction and continued normal nicotine on all three toxicant-exposure biomarkers over 20 weeks, while gradual reduction was indistinguishable from control — the policy-relevant finding that a standard must bite at once. The boundary of the claim: outcomes are cigarettes smoked and exposure biomarkers over weeks, in smokers not seeking treatment; biomarkers of biological harm did not consistently improve over 20 weeks (Hatsukami 2019, PMID: 31140663), and no trial measures disease outcomes or population-level quitting.

cards.headline: Donny 2015: 840 smokers, 6 weeks — those on 0.4 mg/g cigarettes smoked 14.9 a day versus 21.3–22.2 on normal-nicotine cigarettes, with less dependence and no rise in carbon monoxide
cards.summary: Donny 2015: 840 smokers, 6 weeks — those on 0.4 mg/g cigarettes smoked 14.9 a day versus 21.3–22.2 on normal-nicotine cigarettes, with less dependence and no rise in carbon monoxide
cards.people: 840 adults smoking at least 5 cigarettes per day with no current interest in quitting, at 10 US sites, randomised double-blind to their usual brand or to investigational cigarettes with nicotine content ranging from 15.8 mg per gram of tobacco (commercial level) down to 0.4 mg/g, provided free for 6 weeks; 780 completed. Primary outcome: cigarettes smoked per day during week 6.
cards.result: During week 6, cigarettes per day were lower for participants assigned to 2.4, 1.3 or 0.4 mg/g cigarettes (16.5, 16.3 and 14.9 respectively) than for those assigned to their usual brand (22.2) or to 15.8 mg/g cigarettes (21.3) (P < .001). The 5.2 mg/g group averaged 20.8 per day, not significantly different from controls. Lower-nicotine cigarettes also reduced exposure to and dependence on nicotine and craving during abstinence, without significantly increasing expired carbon monoxide level or total puff volume, suggesting minimal compensation. Adverse events were generally mild and similar among groups.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks, free cigarettes, and smokers not trying to quit: the trial models the early phase of a regulatory nicotine standard, not years of real-world compliance — dropout, illicit normal-nicotine supply and population quitting are outside its frame.

cards.headline: Hatsukami 2018: 1,250 smokers, 20 weeks — immediate reduction to 0.4 mg/g lowered all three toxicant biomarkers versus gradual reduction and versus control; gradual reduction achieved nothing
cards.summary: Hatsukami 2018: 1,250 smokers, 20 weeks — immediate reduction to 0.4 mg/g lowered all three toxicant biomarkers versus gradual reduction and versus control; gradual reduction achieved nothing
cards.people: 1,250 daily smokers with no intention to quit within 30 days at 10 US sites (mean age 45; 77% completed), randomised double-blind to (1) immediate reduction to 0.4 mg nicotine per gram, (2) gradual reduction from 15.5 to 0.4 mg/g in five monthly steps, or (3) continued 15.5 mg/g cigarettes, over 20 weeks. Co-primary outcomes: breath carbon monoxide, urine 3-HPMA (acrolein metabolite) and urine phenanthrene tetraol (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons) as area under the curve.
cards.result: Exposure was significantly lower with immediate versus gradual reduction for carbon monoxide (mean difference −4.06 ppm, 95% CI −4.89 to −3.23), 3-HPMA (ratio of geometric means 0.83, 0.77 to 0.88) and PheT (0.88, 0.83 to 0.93), and likewise for immediate versus control (CO −3.38 ppm; 3-HPMA 0.81; PheT 0.86). No significant differences were observed between gradual reduction and control for any biomarker (CO +0.68 ppm, P = .18; 3-HPMA 0.98; PheT 0.98).
cards.watchOut: Biomarkers of exposure, not of disease — and the gradual arm's complete failure is as important as the immediate arm's success: a phased standard that spends months at intermediate nicotine levels buys no exposure reduction at all.
cards.source: Hatsukami DK et al. Effect of Immediate vs Gradual Reduction in Nicotine Content of Cigarettes on Biomarkers of Smoke Exposure: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 30193275. cards.headline: Hatsukami 2019: in the same 1,250-smoker trial, biomarkers of inflammation and oxidative stress did not consistently improve with nicotine reduction over 20 weeks
cards.summary: Hatsukami 2019: in the same 1,250-smoker trial, biomarkers of inflammation and oxidative stress did not consistently improve with nicotine reduction over 20 weeks
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised trial (Hatsukami 2019)
cards.people: Secondary analysis of the 1,250-participant immediate-versus-gradual reduction trial (503 immediate, 498 gradual, 249 control; mean age 45.1; mean 17.1 cigarettes/day), with biomarkers of inflammation, oxidative stress and haematological parameters assessed at baseline and at 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 weeks.
cards.result: No consistent significant differences were observed across groups (Bayes factors indicated the data were insensitive), with the sole exception of red blood cell size variability, which was lower with immediate versus gradual reduction (mean difference −0.11, 95% CI −0.18 to −0.04) and versus control (−0.15, −0.23 to −0.06). The authors conclude it remains unclear whether switching to very low nicotine cigarettes leads to a short-term reduction in biomarkers of tobacco-related harm.
cards.watchOut: Twenty weeks may be too short for inflammatory markers to move, and insensitive Bayes factors mean absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence — but this analysis blocks any claim that reduced exposure has already been shown to mean reduced biological harm.
cards.source: Hatsukami DK et al. Effects of immediate versus gradual nicotine reduction in cigarettes on biomarkers of biological effects. Addiction. 2019. PMID: 31140663. Registry ID: none in the record (secondary analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02139930). cards.headline: Synthesis: fewer cigarettes, less exposure, no compensation signal — LIKELY (benefit) for behaviour and exposure, harm unmeasured
cards.summary: Synthesis: fewer cigarettes, less exposure, no compensation signal — LIKELY (benefit) for behaviour and exposure, harm unmeasured
cards.people: Two double-blind randomised trials (n = 840 over 6 weeks; n = 1,250 over 20 weeks) of research cigarettes with graded nicotine content in smokers not seeking treatment, plus a biomarker-of-effect analysis of the larger trial.
cards.result: At nicotine contents of 2.4 mg/g and below, smokers smoked roughly 5–7 fewer cigarettes per day and took in less nicotine, with no significant compensatory rise in carbon monoxide or puff volume. Immediate reduction to 0.4 mg/g reduced all measured toxicant exposures versus gradual reduction and control; gradual reduction did not differ from control. Biomarkers of biological harm did not consistently change over 20 weeks.
cards.watchOut: This shelf answers the product-standard question — what happens to smoking behaviour and exposure when nicotine is removed — not the cessation question. Aids for smokers who want to quit are homed on shelves #2607–#2609 and #531.
cards.source: Synthesis of Donny EC et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2015 (PMID: 26422724); Hatsukami DK et al. JAMA. 2018 (PMID: 30193275); Hatsukami DK et al. Addiction. 2019 (PMID: 31140663).

shelves.title: Quitline counselling: multiple proactive calls raise quit rates by about a quarter to two-fifths relative — worth roughly 2–3 extra quitters per 100 callers at a year
shelves.question: In smokers trying to quit, does telephone quitline counselling increase abstinence?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Counseling/methods · Female · Hotlines · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pregnancy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Smoking Cessation/methods/statistics & numerical data · Telephone
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a large, consistent randomised literature with a real-world confirmation. The Cochrane synthesis (Matkin 2019, PMID: 31045250) pooled 104 trials and 111,653 smokers: multiple sessions of proactive counselling for helpline callers raised long-term abstinence with RR 1.38 (95% CI 1.19 to 1.61) relative, and telephone counselling offered to recruited smokers gave RR 1.25 (1.15 to 1.35) — both graded moderate certainty after downgrading for heterogeneity. In absolute terms the effect is modest: in the randomised trial embedded in the operating California Smokers' Helpline (Zhu 2002, PMID: 12362011), 12-month abstinence was 9.1% with the counselling protocol versus 6.9% in controls. Quitlines are cheap, scalable and genuinely effective — and even with them about 9 in 10 callers are smoking at a year, which is why counselling is normally paired with pharmacotherapy (shelves #2608, #225).

cards.headline: Matkin 2019 (Cochrane): 104 trials, 111,653 smokers — proactive telephone counselling raised quit rates, RR 1.38 relative in helpline callers and 1.25 in recruited smokers
cards.summary: Matkin 2019 (Cochrane): 104 trials, 111,653 smokers — proactive telephone counselling raised quit rates, RR 1.38 relative in helpline callers and 1.25 in recruited smokers
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 104 RCTs (Matkin 2019, Cochrane)
cards.people: 104 randomised or quasi-randomised trials (111,653 participants) of proactive or reactive telephone counselling for smokers, searched to May 2018. Participants were mostly general-population adults; some trials included teenagers, pregnant women and people with long-term or mental-health conditions. 100 of 104 trials tested proactive (counsellor-initiated) counselling. Risk of bias: 58.7% of trials high, 30.8% unclear, 11.5% low.
cards.result: Among trials of smokers who contacted helplines (14 trials, 32,484 participants), quit rates were higher with multiple sessions of proactive counselling than with self-help materials or a single brief call (RR 1.38, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.61; I² = 72%). In studies recruiting smokers who had not called a helpline (65 trials, 41,233 participants), telephone counselling increased quit rates (RR 1.25, 1.15 to 1.35; I² = 52%). Both estimates were downgraded to moderate certainty for substantial unexplained heterogeneity. Subgroup analyses found no clear dependence on co-interventions or on whether participants were actively trying to quit.
cards.watchOut: Relative effects on a low base rate: an RR of 1.25–1.38 turns a 7% quit rate into roughly 9–10%, not into a third of smokers quitting. Most of the underlying trials are old and unblindable — moderate certainty is the ceiling for this literature.
cards.source: Matkin W et al. Telephone counselling for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019. PMID: 31045250. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zhu 2002: a randomised trial embedded in the live California quitline (3,282 callers) — 12-month abstinence 9.1% with the counselling protocol versus 6.9% in controls
cards.summary: Zhu 2002: a randomised trial embedded in the live California quitline (3,282 callers) — 12-month abstinence 9.1% with the counselling protocol versus 6.9% in controls
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial embedded in a quitline service (Zhu 2002)
cards.people: 3,282 callers to the California Smokers' Helpline randomised within the operating service: 1,973 to the treatment group (self-help materials plus assignment to up to seven counselling sessions) and 1,309 to control (self-help materials; counselling available if they called back — 31.6% received some). Counselling was actually provided to 72.1% of the treatment group, a mean of 3.0 sessions.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat abstinence at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months was 23.7%, 17.9%, 12.8% and 9.1% in the treatment group versus 16.5%, 12.1%, 8.6% and 6.9% in controls (P < .001). After factoring out controls who received counselling and the corresponding treatment subgroup, counselling approximately doubled abstinence (12-month 7.5% vs 4.1%; absolute difference 3.4 percentage points). Among callers who made at least one quit attempt, 12-month abstinence was 23.3% versus 18.4% (P < .001).
cards.watchOut: The control group's self-help materials plus on-request counselling dilute the contrast: the trial measures the proactive protocol against a real service floor, which is the right policy comparison but understates counselling versus nothing.
cards.source: Zhu SH et al. Evidence of real-world effectiveness of a telephone quitline for smokers. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2002. PMID: 12362011. cards.headline: Synthesis: a modest absolute gain, consistently found — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a modest absolute gain, consistently found — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.people: One Cochrane synthesis of 104 trials (111,653 smokers) and one 3,282-caller randomised trial run inside an operating quitline.
cards.result: Proactive multi-session counselling raises long-term abstinence by RR 1.25–1.38 relative depending on how smokers are reached; in absolute terms the embedded service trial found 9.1% versus 6.9% abstinent at 12 months (about 2 extra quitters per 100 callers), with a decontaminated estimate of counselling roughly doubling abstinence. Certainty is moderate, limited by heterogeneity and the age and bias risk of the underlying trials.
cards.watchOut: Quitline counselling is usually adjunctive to pharmacotherapy in modern services; the effect of counselling alone should not be quoted as the effect of a combined quitline-plus-medication programme. Text-message programmes are a separate question (shelf #2513).
cards.source: Synthesis of Matkin W et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019 (PMID: 31045250); Zhu SH et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2002 (PMID: 12362011).

shelves.title: Combination NRT: patch plus a fast-acting form beats either alone — quit rates about 27% higher relative, the one high-certainty dosing answer in the NRT literature
shelves.question: In smokers, does combination nicotine replacement (patch plus a fast-acting form) beat single-form NRT?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Smoking Cessation/methods · Nicotine · Nicotinic Agonists/adverse effects · Tobacco Use Cessation Devices · Delivery of Health Care
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — unusually for a dosing question, the evidence is high-certainty. The Cochrane review of NRT forms, doses, durations and schedules (Theodoulou 2023, PMID: 37335995) found combination NRT — a patch plus a fast-acting form — beat single-form NRT for abstinence at six months or longer with RR 1.27 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.37) relative, I² = 12%, across 16 studies and 12,169 smokers, while patch and fast-acting forms used alone produced similar quit rates (RR 0.90). The largest head-to-head pharmacotherapy trial (Piper 2009, PMID: 19884613; n = 1,504) fits the same pattern: patch plus lozenge was the only one of five regimens significantly better than placebo at 6 months after correction for multiple comparisons (OR 2.34). In absolute terms the combination advantage is a few additional quitters per 100 smokers treated — real, cheap and safe, and the default way NRT should be prescribed. Starting NRT before quit day (preloading) is covered by the same Cochrane review's comparisons and is homed on shelf #2609 with its dedicated trial.

cards.headline: Theodoulou 2023 (Cochrane): combination NRT beat single-form NRT with high-certainty evidence — RR 1.27 (1.17 to 1.37), 16 studies, 12,169 smokers
cards.summary: Theodoulou 2023 (Cochrane): combination NRT beat single-form NRT with high-certainty evidence — RR 1.27 (1.17 to 1.37), 16 studies, 12,169 smokers
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 68 RCTs (Theodoulou 2023, Cochrane)
cards.people: 68 completed randomised studies (43,327 participants) comparing one form, dose, duration or schedule of NRT with another in smokers motivated to quit, searched to April 2022. Abstinence was measured at at least six months using the most rigorous definition available. 28 of 68 studies were judged at high risk of bias.
cards.result: There is high-certainty evidence that combination NRT (a fast-acting form plus a patch) results in higher long-term quit rates than a single form (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.37; I² = 12%; 16 studies, 12,169 participants); restricting the analysis to studies at low or unclear risk of bias did not alter this result. High-certainty evidence from 8 studies (3,319 participants) suggests fast-acting NRT and patch alone give similar quit rates (RR 0.90, 0.77 to 1.05). Higher-dose 42/44 mg patches were not clearly better than 21/22 mg patches (RR 1.09, 0.93 to 1.29), while 21 mg beat 14 mg patches (RR 1.48, 1.06 to 2.08).
cards.watchOut: The comparison is combination versus single-form NRT, not versus no treatment: the 27% relative advantage sits on top of NRT's own established effect and translates to a few extra quitters per 100 treated.

cards.headline: Piper 2009: 1,504 smokers, five active treatments against placebo — patch plus lozenge was the only regimen still significantly ahead at 6 months after correcting for multiple comparisons (OR 2.34)
cards.summary: Piper 2009: 1,504 smokers, five active treatments against placebo — patch plus lozenge was the only regimen still significantly ahead at 6 months after correcting for multiple comparisons (OR 2.34)
cards.people: 1,504 adults smoking at least 10 cigarettes per day and motivated to quit, randomised double-blind at two US research sites to nicotine lozenge, nicotine patch, sustained-release bupropion, patch plus lozenge, bupropion plus lozenge, or placebo; all participants received six individual counselling sessions. Outcome: biochemically confirmed 7-day point-prevalence abstinence, including at 6 months post-quit.
cards.result: All pharmacotherapies differed from placebo without protection for multiple comparisons (odds ratios 1.63–2.34). With such protection, only the nicotine patch plus nicotine lozenge produced significantly higher abstinence rates at 6 months than placebo (OR 2.34, P < .001).
cards.watchOut: A placebo comparison rather than combination-versus-single directly — but it is the largest head-to-head pharmacotherapy trial of its era, and the combination's survival of multiplicity correction while single forms failed it is the pattern the Cochrane pooling later confirmed.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the default prescription should be two forms at once — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the default prescription should be two forms at once — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.people: One Cochrane synthesis of 68 NRT-comparison trials (43,327 participants) and one 1,504-participant six-arm placebo-controlled trial.
cards.result: Combination NRT beats single-form NRT for long-term abstinence (RR 1.27 relative, high certainty, I² = 12%); neither single form beats the other; and in the head-to-head trial only the combination regimen separated from placebo at 6 months after multiplicity correction (OR 2.34). Absolute gains are a few extra quitters per 100 smokers treated.
cards.watchOut: This shelf compares ways of using NRT with each other; NRT versus no treatment and NRT in pregnancy (shelf #1356) are separate questions, as are varenicline (shelf #225) and cytisine (shelf #410).

shelves.title: Pre-loading and reduce-to-quit: the pooled preloading signal is positive but the largest trial missed its primary endpoint; NRT-assisted gradual reduction roughly doubles eventual quitting in smokers not ready to stop
shelves.question: In smokers, does starting NRT before quit day (pre-loading) or reducing-to-quit with NRT improve success?
shelves.mesh: Biomarkers/blood · Bupropion/therapeutic use · Carbon Monoxide/blood · Cotinine/blood · Electronic Nicotine Delivery Systems · Humans · Nicotine/therapeutic use · Nicotinic Agonists/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Smoking/adverse effects/blood · Smoking Cessation/methods · Smoking Prevention · Tobacco Use Cessation Devices · Tobacco Use Disorder/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two strategies for smokers who cannot or will not stop abruptly, each with a real but insecure signal. For pre-loading, the dedicated pragmatic trial (Preloading Investigators 2018, PMID: 29899061; n = 1,792) missed its primary endpoint unadjusted (17.5% vs 14.4% abstinent at 6 months; OR 1.25, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.62) and reached significance only after adjustment for reduced varenicline use in the preloading arm (OR 1.34, 1.03 to 1.73). The Cochrane NRT review homed on shelf #2608 pooled 9 preloading studies (4,395 participants) at RR 1.25 (1.08 to 1.44) relative, moderate certainty — but the effect did not survive restriction to studies at low or unclear risk of bias. For reduce-to-quit, the harm-reduction Cochrane review (Lindson-Hawley 2016, PMID: 27734465) found NRT-assisted reduction in smokers not ready to quit raised both cutting down by at least half (RR 1.75, 1.44 to 2.13) and eventual quitting (RR 1.87, 1.43 to 2.44) versus placebo, on low-quality evidence, with biomarker falls smaller than the falls in cigarette counts. Neither strategy has evidence on health outcomes; both are reasonable offers to smokers who would otherwise do nothing.

cards.headline: Preloading RCT (2018): 1,792 smokers — four weeks of patch before quit day gave 17.5% versus 14.4% abstinence at 6 months, a difference whose confidence interval crossed zero (P = 0.08)
cards.summary: Preloading RCT (2018): 1,792 smokers — four weeks of patch before quit day gave 17.5% versus 14.4% abstinence at 6 months, a difference whose confidence interval crossed zero (P = 0.08)
cards.people: 1,792 daily smokers in English primary care and smoking cessation clinics (899 preloading, 893 control), randomised open-label to standard smoking-cessation pharmacotherapy and behavioural support, with or without four weeks of 21 mg nicotine patch worn before quit day ('preloading'). Primary outcome: biochemically confirmed prolonged abstinence at six months.
cards.result: Abstinence at six months was 157/899 (17.5%) with preloading versus 129/893 (14.4%) in controls: difference 3.0 percentage points (95% CI −0.4 to 6.4), odds ratio 1.25 (0.97 to 1.62), P = 0.08 in the primary analysis. Because the preloading arm used less varenicline after quit day, the planned adjusted analysis gave OR 1.34 (1.03 to 1.73), P = 0.03 (difference 3.8 points, 0.4 to 7.2); the adjusted 12-month OR was 1.36 (1.02 to 1.80). Gastrointestinal symptoms, chiefly nausea, occurred in 4.0 percentage points more participants with preloading, 5.9% discontinued it for intolerance, and serious adverse events were 8 versus 8.
cards.watchOut: The trialists' own conclusion was that evidence was insufficient to confidently show benefit: the positive reading depends on adjusting for an unintended consequence — preloading made participants less likely to use varenicline afterwards — which may itself be part of preloading's real-world effect.
cards.source: Preloading Investigators. Effects on abstinence of nicotine patch treatment before quitting smoking: parallel, two arm, pragmatic randomised trial. BMJ. 2018. PMID: 29899061. cards.headline: Lindson-Hawley 2016 (Cochrane): in smokers not ready to quit, NRT-assisted reduction raised cutting down by at least half (RR 1.75 relative) and eventual quitting (RR 1.87 relative) versus placebo
cards.summary: Lindson-Hawley 2016 (Cochrane): in smokers not ready to quit, NRT-assisted reduction raised cutting down by at least half (RR 1.75 relative) and eventual quitting (RR 1.87 relative) versus placebo
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 24 trials (Lindson-Hawley 2016, Cochrane)
cards.people: 24 randomised or quasi-randomised trials of interventions to reduce harm from continued tobacco use in smokers with no immediate desire to quit; 14 tested nicotine replacement therapy as an aid to reduction. Outcomes were measured at least six months from the start of the intervention. No trial directly tested whether harm-reduction strategies reduced the harms to health caused by smoking.
cards.result: In a pooled analysis of eight trials (3,081 participants), NRT (gum, inhaler or a choice of product) significantly increased the likelihood of reducing cigarettes per day by at least 50% versus placebo (RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.44 to 2.13) and significantly increased the likelihood of ultimately quitting smoking (RR 1.87, 1.43 to 2.44; quality of evidence graded low). Carbon monoxide and cotinine generally showed smaller reductions than cigarette consumption, indicating partial compensation.
cards.watchOut: A different population from the preloading trial — smokers unwilling to quit now — and the cessation outcome, though roughly doubled in relative terms, starts from a very low base rate. The compensation finding matters: people smoke each remaining cigarette harder, so exposure falls less than consumption.
cards.source: Lindson-Hawley N et al. Interventions to reduce harm from continued tobacco use. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016. PMID: 27734465. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two second-best strategies with genuine but fragile signals — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: two second-best strategies with genuine but fragile signals — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: One 1,792-participant pragmatic preloading trial, one Cochrane harm-reduction review (24 trials; 8 pooled NRT-reduction trials, 3,081 participants), and the preloading comparison inside the Cochrane NRT review homed on shelf #2608 (9 studies, 4,395 participants, RR 1.25 relative).
cards.result: Preloading: pooled estimates favour it (RR about 1.25 relative) but the largest trial's primary analysis was null (OR 1.25, 0.97 to 1.62) and the pooled effect does not survive risk-of-bias restriction. Reduce-to-quit with NRT: ≥50% reduction RR 1.75 and eventual quitting RR 1.87 relative versus placebo, on low-quality evidence, with partial compensation on biomarkers. Neither approach has health-outcome evidence.
cards.watchOut: Preloading and abrupt quitting with standard NRT are not mutually exclusive in practice, but the trial evidence tests them as alternatives; smokers ready to quit today should not delay a quit attempt to preload. Combination NRT — the better-supported optimisation — is shelf #2608.
cards.source: Synthesis of Preloading Investigators. BMJ. 2018 (PMID: 29899061); Lindson-Hawley N et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016 (PMID: 27734465); with the preloading analysis of Theodoulou A et al. shelves.title: Heated tobacco: switching lowers several toxicant biomarkers toward abstinence levels in industry-run trials — and there is no randomised evidence at all that it helps anyone quit
shelves.question: In adults who smoke, do heated tobacco products reduce exposure to toxicants compared with cigarettes — and compared with quitting?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Prevalence · Smoking · Smoking Cessation · Tobacco Products · Tobacco Use Cessation Devices
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the exposure half of the industry claim is supported by randomised data; the cessation half has never been tested. Switching from cigarettes to heated tobacco lowered biomarkers of exposure — in one 180-day trial (Gale 2021, PMID: 34196886) to levels similar to those in smokers who abstained entirely — and improved 5 of 8 pre-specified biomarkers of biological effect over 6 months (Lüdicke 2019, PMID: 31270101). But the Cochrane review (Tattan-Birch 2022, PMID: 34988969) found 13 studies in which not one reported smoking-cessation outcomes; adverse events were no different from continued smoking (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.15); follow-up was a median of 13 weeks; and every randomised trial was funded by a tobacco company. Compared with quitting, there is no comparison to make: no trial measures disease outcomes, and dual use — the common real-world pattern — sits outside the trials' exclusive-use designs. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (lower toxicant exposure than continued smoking) / no evidence of a cessation benefit. Tier C: surrogate-outcome evidence from a single interested source, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: Tattan-Birch 2022 (Cochrane): 13 studies, every RCT tobacco-company funded — no study reported whether heated tobacco helps smokers quit; adverse events did not differ from continued smoking (RR 1.03)
cards.summary: Tattan-Birch 2022 (Cochrane): 13 studies, every RCT tobacco-company funded — no study reported whether heated tobacco helps smokers quit; adverse events did not differ from continued smoking (RR 1.03)
cards.type: Systematic review, 11 RCTs and 2 time-series studies (Tattan-Birch 2022, Cochrane)
cards.people: 13 completed studies: 11 randomised trials assessing safety and biomarkers (2,666 participants) and 2 time-series studies of population impact, searched to January 2021. Eight RCTs were judged at unclear risk of bias and three at high risk; median follow-up was 13 weeks. All RCTs were funded by tobacco companies.
cards.result: No studies reported smoking cessation outcomes. There was insufficient evidence for a difference in adverse events between smokers randomised to switch to heated tobacco and those continuing cigarettes (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.15; I² = 0%; 6 studies, 1,713 participants), and the evidence on serious adverse events was very imprecise (RR 0.79, 0.33 to 1.94; 4 studies, 1,472 participants). There was moderate-certainty evidence for lower NNAL and carboxyhaemoglobin at follow-up in the heated-tobacco groups than in the cigarette groups.
cards.watchOut: The absence of cessation outcomes is itself the finding: the products are sold with an implied switching benefit, yet as of this review not one randomised trial had measured whether smokers actually stop smoking on them.
cards.source: Tattan-Birch H et al. Heated tobacco products for smoking cessation and reducing smoking prevalence. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2022. PMID: 34988969.
