cards.headline: Lüdicke 2019: 984 smokers switched to the Tobacco Heating System 2.2 (IQOS) for 6 months — 5 of 8 biomarkers of biological effect improved versus continued smoking
cards.summary: Lüdicke 2019: 984 smokers switched to the Tobacco Heating System 2.2 (IQOS) for 6 months — 5 of 8 biomarkers of biological effect improved versus continued smoking
cards.people: 984 adult US smokers randomised to continue smoking their preferred cigarette brand (n = 496) or to use the Tobacco Heating System 2.2 (IQOS brand; n = 488) for 6 months, as part of a candidate modified-risk tobacco product assessment. Eight co-primary endpoints indicative of biological and functional effects: HDL-C, white-cell count, FEV1 % predicted, carboxyhaemoglobin, total NNAL, sICAM-1, 11-dehydro-thromboxane B2 and 8-epi-prostaglandin F2α.
cards.result: At 6 months there were statistically significant favourable changes in 5 of the 8 biomarkers of effect (HDL-C, white-cell count, FEV1 % predicted, carboxyhaemoglobin and total NNAL) in smokers who switched to THS compared with those who continued smoking, all in the same direction as with smoking cessation, with similar nicotine levels in both groups. Biomarkers of exposure (including 3-HPMA, total NNN and exhaled carbon monoxide) were markedly reduced.
cards.watchOut: An industry trial of the manufacturer's own product, designed for a regulatory modified-risk application (the Cochrane review records that every RCT in this field was tobacco-company funded). Biomarkers of effect are surrogates, and 3 of the 8 co-primary endpoints did not significantly improve.
cards.source: Lüdicke F et al. Effects of Switching to a Heat-Not-Burn Tobacco Product on Biologically Relevant Biomarkers to Assess a Candidate Modified Risk Tobacco Product: A Randomized Trial. cards.headline: Gale 2021: after 180 days, exclusive tobacco-heating-product users' exposure biomarkers had fallen to levels similar to smokers who had abstained entirely
cards.summary: Gale 2021: after 180 days, exclusive tobacco-heating-product users' exposure biomarkers had fallen to levels similar to smokers who had abstained entirely
cards.people: Healthy volunteer smokers in the UK randomised in an ambulatory setting to continue smoking, switch exclusively to a tobacco heating product, or abstain from smoking, with biomarkers of exposure and of potential harm (oxidative stress, cardiovascular, respiratory and cancer-related) assessed at baseline and up to 180 days.
cards.result: In continuing smokers, biomarkers of exposure and potential harm remained stable between baseline and day 180. In the group that switched to the tobacco heating product, most biomarkers of exposure reduced significantly, becoming similar to those in the abstinence control group; several biomarkers of potential harm — including total NNAL, 8-epi-prostaglandin F2α type III, fractional exhaled nitric oxide and white-cell count — also changed significantly in a direction consistent with lessened health impact.
cards.watchOut: Exposure biomarkers approaching abstinence levels is the strongest result in this literature — but exposure is not disease, follow-up was 180 days, the trial was conducted by the product's manufacturer, and no cessation or clinical endpoint was measured.
cards.source: Gale N et al. Changes in biomarkers after 180 days of tobacco heating product use: a randomised trial. Internal and Emergency Medicine. 2021. PMID: 34196886. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: exposure down, cessation untested, disease unknown — SPLIT (POSSIBLE for exposure / no evidence for quitting)
cards.summary: Synthesis: exposure down, cessation untested, disease unknown — SPLIT (POSSIBLE for exposure / no evidence for quitting)
cards.people: One Cochrane review (11 RCTs, 2,666 participants; 2 time-series studies) and the two largest industry switching trials (984 smokers over 6 months; 180-day three-arm trial with an abstinence control).
cards.result: Toxicant exposure falls substantially on switching, in one trial to near-abstinence levels, and several biomarkers of biological effect move in the direction of cessation. Against that: zero cessation outcomes in any trial, adverse events indistinguishable from continued smoking (RR 1.03), median follow-up 13 weeks across the field, universal industry funding, and no disease endpoints anywhere.
cards.watchOut: For a smoker who wants to stop, the interventions with actual cessation evidence are on shelves #2607–#2609, #225 and #531; heated tobacco should not be quoted to patients as a quit method on current evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tattan-Birch H et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2022 (PMID: 34988969); Lüdicke F et al. Cancer Epidemiology, Biomarkers & Prevention. 2019 (PMID: 31270101); Gale N et al. Internal and Emergency Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 34196886).

shelves.title: Vancomycin versus metronidazole for C. difficile: a tie in mild disease, a clear vancomycin win in severe disease — severity, not habit, should pick the drug
shelves.question: In adults with Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea, is oral vancomycin superior to metronidazole — and does the answer depend on disease severity?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Anti-Infective Agents/therapeutic use* · Clostridioides difficile* · Double-Blind Method · Enterocolitis, Pseudomembranous/drug therapy* · Female · Humans · Male · Metronidazole/administration & dosage/therapeutic use* · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Vancomycin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use*
shelves.balance: SPLIT — severity decides. The only prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled head-to-head trial (Zar FA et al., PMID: 17599306; 172 enrolled, 150 completing) found the two drugs effectively tied in mild disease (clinical cure 90% on metronidazole vs 98% on vancomycin, P=.36) and clearly separated in severe disease (76% vs 97%, P=.02), with recurrence much the same either way (15% vs 14%). The 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of CDI antibiotic therapy (Stabholz Y et al., PMID: 37690610) points the same way at scale: initial treatment failure was higher with metronidazole than with glycopeptides (RR 1.58, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.27; 5 RCTs, 843 patients), while all-cause mortality did not differ significantly between vancomycin and metronidazole (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.32; 4 RCTs, 808 patients; very low certainty). Neither drug is the modern recurrence story — fidaxomicin and recurrence prevention live on shelf #170 — but as a cure question, this trial is why severity, not habit, should pick between these two. PROPOSED SPLIT: metronidazole matches vancomycin in mild disease; vancomycin is superior in severe disease.

cards.headline: Zar 2007: in mild C. difficile diarrhoea the drugs tied (cure 90% vs 98%), in severe disease vancomycin won clearly (97% vs 76%, P=.02)
cards.summary: Zar 2007: in mild C. difficile diarrhoea the drugs tied (cure 90% vs 98%), in severe disease vancomycin won clearly (97% vs 76%, P=.02)
cards.people: 172 patients with Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhoea enrolled between October 1994 and June 2002, stratified before randomisation by clinical criteria into mild or severe disease, and assigned to oral metronidazole 250 mg four times daily or oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days, each with an oral placebo; 150 patients completed the trial and were followed for 21 days for cure, failure, relapse or intolerance.
cards.result: Among patients with mild disease, clinical cure was 90% with metronidazole and 98% with vancomycin (P=.36). Among patients with severe disease, clinical cure was 76% with metronidazole and 97% with vancomycin (P=.02). Clinical symptoms recurred in 15% of patients treated with metronidazole and 14% of those treated with vancomycin. The authors conclude the drugs are equally effective for mild disease, but vancomycin is superior for severe disease.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, enrolled over eight years (1994–2002) in the pre-fidaxomicin era, with 150 completers — the severe-disease subgroup that drives the conclusion is small, and severity was assigned by the trial's own clinical criteria, not a modern score. It answers vancomycin versus metronidazole only; it says nothing about fidaxomicin, which is carded on shelf #170.
cards.source: Zar FA et al. A comparison of vancomycin and metronidazole for the treatment of Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea, stratified by disease severity. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2007. PMID: 17599306. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Stabholz 2024 meta-analysis: initial treatment failure was higher with metronidazole (RR 1.58), but no antibiotic showed a mortality difference
cards.summary: Stabholz 2024 meta-analysis: initial treatment failure was higher with metronidazole (RR 1.58), but no antibiotic showed a mortality difference
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 randomised controlled trials of antibiotic therapy (metronidazole, glycopeptides — vancomycin or teicoplanin — and fidaxomicin) in adults with primary or recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection, searched to August 2023, with all-cause mortality as the focus outcome and Risk of Bias 2 assessment.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in all-cause mortality between vancomycin and metronidazole (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.32; 4 RCTs, 808 patients; very low certainty) or between vancomycin and fidaxomicin (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.14; 8 RCTs, 1,951 patients; low certainty). Initial treatment failure did not differ between fidaxomicin and vancomycin, but was higher with metronidazole (RR 1.58, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.27; 5 RCTs, 843 patients). Among initially cured patients, symptomatic recurrence needing re-treatment was lower with fidaxomicin than vancomycin (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.71; 6 RCTs, 1,617 patients). No study reported CDI complications or burden on daily activities.
cards.watchOut: The mortality comparisons rest on low to very low certainty evidence and the trials were not powered for death; the review's own warning is that guideline confidence built on recurrence rates may not translate into patient-relevant benefit. The metronidazole failure signal (RR 1.58) pools trials across eras and severities — it supports, but does not by itself reproduce, Zar's severity split.
cards.source: Stabholz Y et al. The effect of antibiotic therapy for Clostridioides difficile infection on mortality and other patient-relevant outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Microbiology and Infection. 2024. PMID: 37690610. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one severity-stratified trial and one meta-analysis agree — metronidazole's weakness is failure to cure, concentrated where disease is severe
cards.summary: Synthesis: one severity-stratified trial and one meta-analysis agree — metronidazole's weakness is failure to cure, concentrated where disease is severe
cards.people: One randomised double-blind trial (172 enrolled, 150 completing) directly comparing oral vancomycin with oral metronidazole by severity stratum, plus a 13-trial meta-analysis (up to 1,951 patients in its largest comparison) of CDI antibiotic therapy.
cards.result: Mild disease: cure 90% (metronidazole) vs 98% (vancomycin), P=.36. Severe disease: cure 76% vs 97%, P=.02. Recurrence in the trial: 15% vs 14%. Across trials: initial failure higher with metronidazole (RR 1.58, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.27); mortality not significantly different for any pairing. PROPOSED SPLIT (severity).
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the severe-disease gap (97% vs 76%) as if it came from a large modern trial — it is one small stratum of a 1994–2002 trial, and modern practice has largely moved to fidaxomicin or vancomycin first-line regardless (shelf #170). The durable lesson is narrower: where metronidazole is still used, severity is the variable that should govern the choice. Tier C is set because the direct evidence is a single older trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zar FA et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2007 (PMID: 17599306); Stabholz Y et al. Clinical Microbiology and Infection. 2024 (PMID: 37690610).

shelves.title: EPIC: once-daily plazomicin matched meropenem for complicated UTI — and was ahead at test of cure, 81.7% versus 70.1%, with more creatinine rises
shelves.question: In adults with complicated urinary tract infection, is once-daily plazomicin non-inferior to meropenem for clinical and microbiological cure?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage*/adverse effects · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Resistance, Multiple, Bacterial · Enterobacteriaceae/drug effects · Enterobacteriaceae Infections/drug therapy* · Female · Humans · Male · Meropenem/administration & dosage*/adverse effects · Microbial Sensitivity Tests · Middle Aged · Patient Acuity · Sisomicin/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives* · Urinary Tract Infections/drug therapy*/microbiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — EPIC (Wagenlehner FME et al., PMID: 30786187) randomised 609 patients with complicated urinary tract infection or acute pyelonephritis and met its non-inferiority objective at both primary time points: composite cure (clinical cure plus microbiological eradication) at day 5 was 88.0% (168/191) on once-daily plazomicin versus 91.4% (180/197) on meropenem (difference −3.4 points, 95% CI −10.0 to 3.1), and at the test-of-cure visit plazomicin was ahead, 81.7% versus 70.1% (difference 11.6 points, 95% CI 2.7 to 20.3), with fewer microbiological recurrences (3.7% vs 8.1%) and clinical relapses (1.6% vs 7.1%) at late follow-up. The aminoglycoside price tag showed in the expected place: creatinine rises of 0.5 mg/dL or more occurred in 7.0% versus 4.0%. The 2023 meta-analysis of novel antibiotics for complicated UTI (Hung KC et al., PMID: 37100354) supports the class direction — higher clinical cure at test of cure (83.6% vs 80.3%; OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.74) with similar adverse events — while warning its own clinical-cure evidence remains inconclusive. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): plazomicin is a credible once-daily meropenem alternative for complicated UTI caused by Enterobacteriaceae, including multidrug-resistant strains, with kidney monitoring as the condition.

cards.headline: EPIC 2019: plazomicin non-inferior to meropenem — composite cure 88.0% vs 91.4% at day 5, and ahead at test of cure, 81.7% vs 70.1%
cards.summary: EPIC 2019: plazomicin non-inferior to meropenem — composite cure 88.0% vs 91.4% at day 5, and ahead at test of cure, 81.7% vs 70.1%
cards.people: 609 patients with complicated urinary tract infection, including acute pyelonephritis, randomised 1:1 to intravenous plazomicin 15 mg/kg once daily or meropenem 1 g every 8 hours, with optional oral step-down after at least 4 days of intravenous therapy, for 7 to 10 days total. The primary (microbiologic modified intention-to-treat) population was 191 plazomicin and 197 meropenem patients; the non-inferiority margin was 15 percentage points.
cards.result: Composite cure (clinical cure and microbiologic eradication) at day 5: 88.0% (168/191) on plazomicin versus 91.4% (180/197) on meropenem (difference −3.4 percentage points, 95% CI −10.0 to 3.1). At the test-of-cure visit (15 to 19 days after starting therapy): 81.7% (156/191) versus 70.1% (138/197) (difference 11.6 points, 95% CI 2.7 to 20.3). Microbiologic eradication at test of cure favoured plazomicin, including for aminoglycoside-non-susceptible Enterobacteriaceae (78.8% vs 68.6%) and extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producers (82.4% vs 75.0%). At late follow-up (24 to 32 days), microbiologic recurrence was 3.7% versus 8.1% and clinical relapse 1.6% versus 7.1%. Serum creatinine increases of 0.5 mg/dL or more above baseline occurred in 7.0% versus 4.0% of patients.
cards.watchOut: A 15-point non-inferiority margin is wide — 'non-inferior' here tolerates a meaningfully worse drug — although the test-of-cure result (difference 11.6 points in plazomicin's favour, interval excluding zero) is stronger than the margin required. The trial covers complicated UTI and pyelonephritis due to Enterobacteriaceae; it is not evidence for uncomplicated cystitis, for non-urinary sources, or for patients in whom aminoglycoside kidney and ear toxicity cannot be monitored. Industry-funded (Achaogen, with BARDA support).
cards.source: Wagenlehner FME et al. Once-Daily Plazomicin for Complicated Urinary Tract Infections. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 30786187. Registry ID: NCT02486627. cards.headline: Hung 2023 meta-analysis: novel antibiotics beat conventional therapy on eradication (OR 1.79) and test-of-cure clinical cure (OR 1.37), with no excess adverse events
cards.summary: Hung 2023 meta-analysis: novel antibiotics beat conventional therapy on eradication (OR 1.79) and test-of-cure clinical cure (OR 1.37), with no excess adverse events
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 randomised controlled trials (3,514 participants for clinical cure at test of cure; 4,347 for microbiological eradication; 5,790 for adverse events) of novel antibiotics — new beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones and cefiderocol — versus conventional therapy for complicated urinary tract infection, searched to 20 October 2022, with trial sequential analysis.
cards.result: Clinical cure at test of cure was higher with novel antibiotics (83.6% vs 80.3%; OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.74; P=0.01; I²=35%). Microbiological eradication was higher (77.7% vs 67.2%; OR 1.79, 95% CI 1.46 to 2.20; P<0.00001). At end of treatment, clinical cure did not differ (OR 0.96, P=0.81), and treatment-emergent adverse events did not differ (OR 0.95, P=0.57). Trial sequential analysis judged the eradication and adverse-event evidence robust, but the clinical-cure evidence — at both test of cure and end of treatment — inconclusive.
cards.watchOut: A class-level pool: plazomicin is one aminoglycoside among several unlike drugs, so the pooled odds ratios describe 'novel versus conventional' strategy, not plazomicin's own effect — EPIC's card above carries that. The reviewers' own trial sequential analysis calls the clinical-cure evidence inconclusive, which is why this shelf's stamp stays at possible.
cards.source: Hung KC et al. Clinical efficacy and safety of novel antibiotics for complicated urinary tract infection: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. International Journal of Antimicrobial Agents. 2023. PMID: 37100354. Registry ID: none in the record. systematic review and meta-analysis, 11 rcts (hung 2023) systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 randomised controlled trials (3,514 participants for clinical cure at test of cure; 4,347 for microbiological eradication; 5,790 for adverse events) of novel antibiotics — new beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones and cefiderocol — versus conventional therapy for complicated urinary tract infection, searched to 20 october 2022, with trial sequential analysis. clinical cure at test of cure was higher with novel antibiotics (83.6% vs 80.3%; or 1.37, 95% ci 1.08 to 1.74; p=0.01; i²=35%). microbiological eradication was higher (77.7% vs 67.2%; or 1.79, 95% ci 1.46 to 2.20; p<0.00001). at end of treatment, clinical cure did not differ (or 0.96, p=0.81), and treatment-emergent adverse events did not differ (or 0.95, p=0.57). trial sequential analysis judged the eradication and adverse-event evidence robust, but the clinical-cure evidence — at both test of cure and end of treatment — inconclusive. a class-level pool: plazomicin is one aminoglycoside among several unlike drugs, so the pooled odds ratios describe 'novel versus conventional' strategy, not plazomicin's own effect — epic's card above carries that. the reviewers' own trial sequential analysis calls the clinical-cure evidence inconclusive, which is why this shelf's stamp stays at possible. hung kc et al. clinical efficacy and safety of novel antibiotics for complicated urinary tract infection: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. international journal of antimicrobial agents. 2023. pmid: 37100354. registry id: none in the record. mesh: humans · anti-bacterial agents*/adverse effects · randomized controlled trials as topic · urinary tract infections*/drug therapy/microbiology · beta-lactamase inhibitors/therapeutic use · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: one well-run non-inferiority trial puts plazomicin level with meropenem early and ahead at test of cure — the class literature agrees on eradication, and the kidney signal is the condition of use
cards.summary: Synthesis: one well-run non-inferiority trial puts plazomicin level with meropenem early and ahead at test of cure — the class literature agrees on eradication, and the kidney signal is the condition of use
cards.people: One randomised trial (609 patients; 388 in the primary population) of once-daily plazomicin versus meropenem for complicated UTI/pyelonephritis, plus an 11-trial meta-analysis (up to 5,790 participants) of novel antibiotics for complicated UTI.
cards.result: Day-5 composite cure 88.0% vs 91.4% (difference −3.4 points, 95% CI −10.0 to 3.1); test-of-cure composite cure 81.7% vs 70.1% (difference 11.6 points, 2.7 to 20.3); late relapse 1.6% vs 7.1%; creatinine rise ≥0.5 mg/dL in 7.0% vs 4.0%. Class level: eradication OR 1.79 (1.46 to 2.20), adverse events OR 0.95. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against meropenem in a trial with a 15-point margin is a licence to consider plazomicin where meropenem-sparing matters — it is not proof of superiority, despite the favourable test-of-cure point estimate, which was not the primary non-inferiority test. Aminoglycoside harms (kidney, hearing, balance) accumulate with duration and vulnerability in ways a 7-to-10-day trial in selected patients only partly captures. Tier C is set because the direct evidence is a single trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wagenlehner FME et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 30786187); Hung KC et al. International Journal of Antimicrobial Agents. 2023 (PMID: 37100354).

shelves.title: Antibiotics at catheter removal: a meta-analysis finds about 6 fewer symptomatic urine infections per 100 removals (NNT 17) — a real gain with an uncounted resistance cost
shelves.question: In patients having a urinary catheter removed, does antibiotic prophylaxis at removal reduce subsequent urinary tract infection?
shelves.mesh: Antibiotic Prophylaxis*/methods · Catheters, Indwelling/microbiology* · Device Removal/adverse effects/methods* · Female · Guidelines as Topic · Humans · Male · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Urinary Catheterization/adverse effects* · Urinary Catheters/microbiology* · Urinary Tract Infections/drug therapy/microbiology/prevention & control*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — across seven controlled studies (six randomised) of short-term catheterisation, antibiotic prophylaxis at catheter removal was associated with fewer subsequent symptomatic urinary tract infections: risk ratio 0.45 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.72), an absolute risk reduction of 5.8%, and a number needed to treat of 17 (95% CI 12 to 30). That is a 55% relative risk reduction, stated alongside the 5.8% absolute reduction. The limits are real: five of the seven studies were in surgical patients, the antibiotics and observation periods varied, and the review could not weigh the harms that decide policy in practice — side effects, cost, and antimicrobial resistance — against a modest absolute gain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prophylaxis at removal probably prevents some symptomatic infections after short-term catheterisation, most clearly in surgical patients, but which patients benefit enough to justify routine antibiotic use remains unresolved.

cards.headline: Marschall 2013 (meta-analysis): prophylaxis at catheter removal cut symptomatic UTI risk — risk ratio 0.45, absolute reduction 5.8%, NNT 17
cards.summary: Marschall 2013 (meta-analysis): prophylaxis at catheter removal cut symptomatic UTI risk — risk ratio 0.45, absolute reduction 5.8%, NNT 17
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled studies (Marschall 2013)
cards.people: Seven controlled studies (six randomised controlled trials and one non-randomised controlled intervention study) of antibiotic prophylaxis given to prevent symptomatic urinary tract infection after removal of a short-term urinary catheter (14 days or less); five of the seven studies were in surgical patients. Studies were published before November 2012 and identified through PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library.
cards.result: Antibiotic prophylaxis was associated with benefit: risk ratio 0.45 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.72) for symptomatic urinary tract infection after catheter removal — a 55% relative risk reduction — with an absolute risk reduction of 5.8% between intervention and control groups and a number needed to treat of 17 (95% CI 12 to 30) to prevent one urinary tract infection. Studies were heterogeneous in the type and duration of antimicrobial prophylaxis and in the period of observation.
cards.watchOut: A pooled result across different antibiotics, durations, and follow-up windows, drawn mostly from surgical patients — it does not identify which antibiotic, which dose, or which patient. The authors themselves flag the unmeasured other side of the ledger: side effects, cost, and antimicrobial resistance from more widespread prophylaxis.
cards.source: Marschall J et al. Antibiotic prophylaxis for urinary tract infections after removal of urinary catheter: meta-analysis. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2013. PMID: 23757735. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but modest absolute benefit — about 6 fewer symptomatic UTIs per 100 catheter removals — with the resistance cost uncounted
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but modest absolute benefit — about 6 fewer symptomatic UTIs per 100 catheter removals — with the resistance cost uncounted
cards.people: Seven controlled studies of prophylaxis at removal of a short-term urinary catheter, five in surgical patients (Marschall 2013).
cards.result: Symptomatic UTI: risk ratio 0.45 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.72); absolute risk reduction 5.8%; number needed to treat 17 (95% CI 12 to 30). Harms, cost, and resistance: not pooled in this review. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Do not read the 0.45 risk ratio as a case for universal prophylaxis: 94 of every 100 patients given antibiotics at removal would not have developed a symptomatic infection anyway or develop one despite prophylaxis, and every extra antibiotic course carries resistance pressure the trials did not measure. The evidence supports targeted use in higher-risk removals far better than a blanket rule.
cards.source: Synthesis of Marschall J et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2013 (PMID: 23757735).

shelves.title: Doravirine for first HIV treatment: non-inferior suppression to darunavir and efavirenz regimens in two phase 3 trials, with far fewer brain and sleep side effects than efavirenz
shelves.question: In antiretroviral-naive adults with HIV-1, is doravirine-based therapy non-inferior to ritonavir-boosted darunavir or to efavirenz-based therapy for viral suppression, with better tolerability?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-HIV Agents/administration & dosage* · Antiretroviral Therapy, Highly Active/methods* · Darunavir/administration & dosage* · Double-Blind Method · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions/epidemiology/pathology · Female · HIV Infections/drug therapy*/virology · HIV-1/isolation & purification · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pyridones/administration & dosage* · RNA, Viral/blood · Ritonavir/administration & dosage* · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles/administration & dosage*
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 non-inferiority trials point the same way. Against ritonavir-boosted darunavir (DRIVE-FORWARD), doravirine-based therapy suppressed HIV-1 RNA below 50 copies/mL in 84% versus 80% at week 48 (difference 3.9%, 95% CI −1.6 to 9.4). Against efavirenz-based therapy (DRIVE-AHEAD), the fixed-dose doravirine combination suppressed 84.3% versus 80.8% (difference 3.5%, 95% CI −2.0 to 9.0), with significantly less dizziness (8.8% vs 37.1%), fewer sleep disorders (12.1% vs 25.2%), and essentially flat lipids where efavirenz raised them. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the randomised record likewise ranked doravirine 100 mg highest for efficacy among the strategies compared, with no significant pairwise difference against boosted darunavir. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): doravirine-based initial therapy is non-inferior for viral suppression with a tolerability advantage over efavirenz — benefit here means an equally effective, better-tolerated option, not superior suppression.

cards.headline: Molina 2018 (DRIVE-FORWARD): doravirine non-inferior to boosted darunavir — 84% vs 80% suppressed at week 48
cards.summary: Molina 2018 (DRIVE-FORWARD): doravirine non-inferior to boosted darunavir — 84% vs 80% suppressed at week 48
cards.people: 769 antiretroviral-naive adults with HIV-1 (plasma HIV-1 RNA at least 1000 copies/mL) at 125 centres in 15 countries, randomised to oral doravirine 100 mg or darunavir 800 mg plus ritonavir 100 mg once daily, each with two investigator-selected nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, for up to 96 weeks; 383 per group received treatment and were analysed.
cards.result: At week 48, 321 (84%) participants in the doravirine group and 306 (80%) in the darunavir group achieved HIV-1 RNA below 50 copies/mL (difference 3.9%, 95% CI −1.6 to 9.4), establishing non-inferiority (margin −10 percentage points). Diarrhoea was less common with doravirine (5% vs 13%); nausea 7% vs 8%; headache 6% vs 3%. Discontinuation for adverse events: 2% vs 3%; serious adverse events 5% vs 6%.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against a strong comparator at 48 weeks is the claim — not superiority, and not yet the long-term resistance and durability record that older regimens carry. Discontinuations were mostly loss to follow-up (56 doravirine, 71 darunavir), which snapshot analysis counts as failure in both arms.
cards.source: Molina JM et al. Doravirine versus ritonavir-boosted darunavir in antiretroviral-naive adults with HIV-1 (DRIVE-FORWARD): 48-week results of a randomised, double-blind, phase 3, non-inferiority trial. The lancet. cards.headline: Orkin 2019 (DRIVE-AHEAD): doravirine combination non-inferior to efavirenz combination — 84.3% vs 80.8% — with far fewer neuropsychiatric effects
cards.summary: Orkin 2019 (DRIVE-AHEAD): doravirine combination non-inferior to efavirenz combination — 84.3% vs 80.8% — with far fewer neuropsychiatric effects
cards.people: 734 antiretroviral treatment-naive adults with HIV-1 RNA at least 1000 copies/mL randomised (728 treated, 364 per group) to once-daily fixed-dose doravirine/lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or efavirenz/emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for 96 weeks.
cards.result: At week 48, 84.3% (307/364) on doravirine combination and 80.8% (294/364) on efavirenz combination achieved HIV-1 RNA below 50 copies/mL (difference 3.5%, 95% CI −2.0 to 9.0), meeting the 10% non-inferiority margin. Doravirine recipients had significantly lower rates of dizziness (8.8% vs 37.1%), sleep disorders/disturbances (12.1% vs 25.2%), and altered sensorium (4.4% vs 8.2%). Mean fasting LDL cholesterol changed by −1.6 vs +8.7 mg/dL and non-HDL cholesterol by −3.8 vs +13.3 mg/dL, favouring doravirine.
cards.watchOut: The tolerability contrast is against efavirenz, whose neuropsychiatric profile is the weakest of modern comparators — the advantage over boosted darunavir in DRIVE-FORWARD was narrower and mostly gastrointestinal. Week 48 is the horizon here.

cards.headline: Afify 2021 (meta-analysis): doravirine 100 mg ranked highest for efficacy among compared strategies, with no significant pairwise difference versus boosted darunavir
cards.summary: Afify 2021 (meta-analysis): doravirine 100 mg ranked highest for efficacy among compared strategies, with no significant pairwise difference versus boosted darunavir
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Afify 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of doravirine in adults with HIV-1; six papers were included, covering doravirine doses (25, 100, 200 mg), efavirenz, ritonavir-boosted darunavir, and placebo strategies.
cards.result: In network estimates, doravirine 100 mg had the highest efficacy ranking (P score 0.786), ahead of doravirine 25 mg (0.684), efavirenz 600 mg (0.574), doravirine 200 mg (0.532), ritonavir plus darunavir (0.416), and placebo (0.009). For drug-related adverse events doravirine 100 mg ranked second only to placebo (P score 0.720 vs 0.927). Pairwise direct comparisons showed no significant difference between doravirine 100 mg and boosted darunavir (OR 1.14, 95% CI 0.23 to 5.74) or efavirenz (OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.17 to 1.98).
cards.watchOut: Rankings (P scores) from a six-paper network are fragile and the pairwise confidence intervals are very wide — this review corroborates the two phase 3 trials rather than adding precision, and its journal is outside the HIV specialty literature.
cards.source: Afify et al. Efficacy and safety of doravirine in treatment-naive HIV-1-infected adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Environmental science and pollution research international. 2021. PMID: 33098001. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: non-inferior suppression in two phase 3 trials (84% vs 80%; 84.3% vs 80.8%), with the clearest gain in tolerability over efavirenz
cards.summary: Synthesis: non-inferior suppression in two phase 3 trials (84% vs 80%; 84.3% vs 80.8%), with the clearest gain in tolerability over efavirenz
cards.people: Two phase 3 non-inferiority trials (769 and 734 randomised participants) plus a six-paper systematic review and meta-analysis of doravirine in treatment-naive HIV-1.
cards.result: Viral suppression below 50 copies/mL at week 48: 84% vs 80% against boosted darunavir (difference 3.9%, 95% CI −1.6 to 9.4) and 84.3% vs 80.8% against efavirenz combination (difference 3.5%, 95% CI −2.0 to 9.0) — non-inferior in both. Tolerability: dizziness 8.8% vs 37.1% and sleep disorders 12.1% vs 25.2% versus efavirenz; diarrhoea 5% vs 13% versus darunavir. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Both trials were industry phase 3 non-inferiority designs with 10-point margins — a regimen can pass and still be a few points worse in truth. The case for doravirine rests on equal suppression with fewer neuropsychiatric and lipid effects, not on better virology.
cards.source: Synthesis of Molina JM et al. The lancet. HIV. 2018 (PMID: 29592840); Orkin C et al. cards.search: synthesis: non-inferior suppression in two phase 3 trials (84% vs 80%; 84.3% vs 80.8%), with the clearest gain in tolerability over efavirenz synthesis: non-inferior suppression in two phase 3 trials (84% vs 80%; 84.3% vs 80.8%), with the clearest gain in tolerability over efavirenz in antiretroviral-naive adults with hiv-1, is doravirine-based therapy non-inferior to ritonavir-boosted darunavir or to efavirenz-based therapy for viral suppression, with better tolerability? synthesis two phase 3 non-inferiority trials (769 and 734 randomised participants) plus a six-paper systematic review and meta-analysis of doravirine in treatment-naive hiv-1. viral suppression below 50 copies/ml at week 48: 84% vs 80% against boosted darunavir (difference 3.9%, 95% ci −1.6 to 9.4) and 84.3% vs 80.8% against efavirenz combination (difference 3.5%, 95% ci −2.0 to 9.0) — non-inferior in both. tolerability: dizziness 8.8% vs 37.1% and sleep disorders 12.1% vs 25.2% versus efavirenz; diarrhoea 5% vs 13% versus darunavir. proposed likely (benefit). both trials were industry phase 3 non-inferiority designs with 10-point margins — a regimen can pass and still be a few points worse in truth. the case for doravirine rests on equal suppression with fewer neuropsychiatric and lipid effects, not on better virology. synthesis of molina jm et al. the lancet. hiv. 2018 (pmid: 29592840); orkin c et al. clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the infectious diseases society of america. 2019 (pmid: 30184165); afify et al. environmental science and pollution research international. 2021 (pmid: 33098001).

shelves.title: Fostemsavir for multidrug-resistant HIV: a clear 8-day randomised effect and suppression in about half of salvage patients at 48 weeks in the single BRIGHTE trial
shelves.question: In heavily treatment-experienced adults with multidrug-resistant HIV-1, does fostemsavir added to optimised background therapy achieve viral suppression?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Retroviral Agents/therapeutic use* · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · Drug Resistance, Multiple, Viral · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · HIV Infections/drug therapy* · HIV-1*/genetics · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Organophosphates/therapeutic use* · Piperazines/therapeutic use* · Prodrugs/therapeutic use · RNA, Viral/blood · Viral Load/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in BRIGHTE, a phase 3 trial in multidrug-resistant HIV-1, adding fostemsavir to a failing regimen cut HIV-1 RNA by a mean 0.79 log10 copies/mL in 8 days versus 0.17 log10 on placebo (P<0.001), in the cohort that still had at least one fully active drug available. By week 48, 54% of that randomised cohort and 38% of the cohort with no remaining options had HIV-1 RNA below 40 copies/mL, with mean CD4 gains of 139 and 64 cells respectively. An indirect-comparison analysis found significantly higher odds of suppression than optimised background therapy alone from an older trial programme (OR 3.26, 95% CI 2.08 to 5.11), but non-significant differences against ibalizumab-based therapy. Seven percent stopped fostemsavir for adverse events, and gp120 substitutions appeared in 43% of randomised-cohort virologic failures. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuinely new mechanism with sustained responses in about half of a salvage population — meaningful where options are exhausted, on single-trial evidence. Tier C is set for that reason.

cards.headline: Kozal 2020 (BRIGHTE): fostemsavir beat placebo over 8 days (−0.79 vs −0.17 log10) and 54% of the randomised cohort were suppressed at week 48
cards.summary: Kozal 2020 (BRIGHTE): fostemsavir beat placebo over 8 days (−0.79 vs −0.17 log10) and 54% of the randomised cohort were suppressed at week 48
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised (8-day) plus open-label trial (BRIGHTE, Kozal 2020)
cards.people: 371 adults with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 in 23 countries, in two cohorts: a randomised cohort of 272 patients who had at least one fully active approved drug in one or two classes (assigned 3:1 to fostemsavir 600 mg twice daily or placebo added to their failing regimen for 8 days, then open-label fostemsavir plus optimised background therapy), and a non-randomised cohort of 99 patients with no remaining antiretroviral options, started directly on open-label fostemsavir plus optimised background therapy.
cards.result: At day 8, the mean decrease in HIV-1 RNA was 0.79 log10 copies/mL in the fostemsavir group and 0.17 log10 copies/mL in the placebo group (P<0.001). At week 48, a virologic response (HIV-1 RNA below 40 copies/mL) had occurred in 54% of the randomised cohort and 38% of the non-randomised cohort; mean CD4+ T-cell increases were 139 and 64 cells per cubic millimeter respectively. Adverse events led to discontinuation of fostemsavir in 7% of patients. In the randomised cohort, gp120 substitutions were found in 20 of 47 patients (43%) with virologic failure.
cards.watchOut: Only the first 8 days were placebo-controlled; everything after that is open-label fostemsavir plus an optimised background regimen that itself contributes suppression, and the non-randomised cohort had no comparator at all. The 54% and 38% week-48 figures cannot be separated into fostemsavir's share versus the background regimen's.

cards.headline: Anderson 2022 (indirect comparison): fostemsavir-based therapy had significantly higher suppression odds than background therapy alone from BENCHMRK, but not versus ibalizumab
cards.summary: Anderson 2022 (indirect comparison): fostemsavir-based therapy had significantly higher suppression odds than background therapy alone from BENCHMRK, but not versus ibalizumab
cards.type: Matching-adjusted indirect comparison / systematic literature review (Anderson 2022)
cards.people: Matching-adjusted indirect comparison reweighting individual participant data from BRIGHTE against three comparator trials in heavily treatment-experienced people with multidrug-resistant HIV-1: TMB-301 (ibalizumab plus optimised background therapy, N=40), BENCHMRK-1/-2 (optimised background therapy alone, N=237), and VIKING-3 (optimised background therapy alone, N=183).
cards.result: Versus ibalizumab plus background therapy, fostemsavir plus background therapy (adjusted N=236) had numerically higher, non-significant odds of virologic suppression (OR 1.44, 95% CI 0.74 to 2.80; P=0.284) and a similar CD4 increase (mean difference 7.05 cells/mm3, 95% CI −60.88 to 74.98). Versus background therapy alone from BENCHMRK-1/-2 (adjusted N=126), odds of suppression were significantly higher (OR 3.26, 95% CI 2.08 to 5.11; P<0.001) with a CD4 advantage of 135.78 cells/mm3 (95% CI 91.93 to 179.63) at week 96. Versus VIKING-3 background therapy, differences were non-significant (OR 1.34, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.30).
cards.watchOut: Indirect comparisons across trials from different eras, reweighted statistically, are hypothesis-supporting rather than confirmatory — the one significant contrast is against background therapy alone, which is the weakest comparator, and the head-to-head question against ibalizumab remains unanswered by any randomised trial.
cards.source: Anderson et al. Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Fostemsavir in Heavily Treatment-Experienced People With HIV-1. Clinical therapeutics. 2022. PMID: 35610081. cards.headline: Synthesis: a new attachment mechanism, a clear 8-day randomised effect, and week-48 suppression in 54% (some options left) and 38% (none left)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a new attachment mechanism, a clear 8-day randomised effect, and week-48 suppression in 54% (some options left) and 38% (none left)
cards.people: 371 heavily treatment-experienced adults with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 (BRIGHTE), plus a matching-adjusted indirect comparison against three salvage trials.
cards.result: Day-8 HIV-1 RNA change: −0.79 vs −0.17 log10 copies/mL (P<0.001). Week-48 suppression below 40 copies/mL: 54% randomised cohort, 38% no-options cohort. Discontinuation for adverse events 7%; gp120 substitutions in 43% of randomised-cohort failures. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

shelves.title: Ibalizumab for multidrug-resistant HIV: 83% responded within a week of the loading dose — in one single-arm study of 40 patients with no control group
shelves.question: In adults with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 failing current therapy, does ibalizumab added to an optimised regimen suppress viral load?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-HIV Agents/therapeutic use* · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use* · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Drug Resistance, Multiple, Viral* · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · HIV Fusion Inhibitors/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use* · HIV Infections/drug therapy*/immunology/virology · HIV-1*/drug effects/isolation & purification · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Viral Load · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the entire case rests on one single-arm, open-label phase 3 study of 40 adults with multidrug-resistant HIV-1. After a 7-day control period on their failing therapy, a single loading dose of ibalizumab was followed by a decrease of at least 0.5 log10 copies/mL in 33 of 40 patients (83%) by day 14 (P<0.001 against the control period), with a mean fall of 1.1 log10. By week 25 on ibalizumab plus an optimised background regimen, the mean fall was 1.6 log10, 43% were below 50 copies/mL and 50% below 200 copies/mL. But there was no parallel control group, the background regimen (which had to include at least one fully active agent) shares credit for every later result, 9 of 10 patients with failure or rebound showed reduced ibalizumab susceptibility in vitro, and the commonest adverse event was diarrhoea (20%). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): real antiviral activity in a desperate population, demonstrated only against each patient's own control week. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single-arm study.

cards.headline: Emu 2018 (TMB-301): in a single-arm study of 40 patients, 83% achieved a ≥0.5 log10 viral-load fall 7 days after the ibalizumab loading dose
cards.summary: Emu 2018 (TMB-301): in a single-arm study of 40 patients, 83% achieved a ≥0.5 log10 viral-load fall 7 days after the ibalizumab loading dose
cards.people: 40 adults with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 in whom multiple antiretroviral therapies had failed, all with viral load above 1000 copies/mL (mean baseline 4.5 log10 copies/mL, mean CD4 count 150 per microliter). After a 7-day control period on current therapy, patients received a 2000 mg ibalizumab loading infusion, then 800 mg every 14 days through week 25 combined with an individually optimised background regimen including at least one fully active agent; 31 patients completed the study.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — a decrease in viral load of at least 0.5 log10 copies/mL from baseline (day 7) to day 14 — was met by 33 of 40 patients (83%) in the intention-to-treat population (P<0.001 for the comparison with the control period); the mean decrease was 1.1 log10 copies/mL. During the control period, only 1 patient (who received the optimised background regimen prematurely) had such a decrease. At week 25, the mean decrease from baseline was 1.6 log10 copies/mL; 43% had a viral load below 50 copies/mL and 50% below 200 copies/mL. Among 10 patients with virologic failure or rebound, 9 had a lower degree of susceptibility to ibalizumab than at baseline in vitro. The most common adverse event was diarrhoea (20%); four patients died from causes related to underlying illnesses, and one serious adverse event (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome) was deemed related to ibalizumab.
cards.watchOut: There is no randomised comparator: the day-14 result is measured against each patient's own preceding control week, and every result after the background regimen was optimised is a joint effect of ibalizumab plus that regimen. Nine of 40 enrolled patients did not complete the study, in a population with advanced disease (mean CD4 150).
cards.source: Emu B et al. Phase 3 Study of Ibalizumab for Multidrug-Resistant HIV-1. The New England journal of medicine. 2018. PMID: 30110589. Registry ID: NCT02475629. shelves.title: Point-of-care HIV testing for exposed infants: treatment started within 60 days for 90% versus 13% with laboratory referral in one Mozambican cluster trial
shelves.question: In HIV-exposed infants in low-resource settings, does point-of-care early infant diagnosis increase antiretroviral initiation and retention versus standard laboratory testing?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Retroviral Agents/therapeutic use* · Early Diagnosis · Female · HIV Infections/diagnosis*/drug therapy* · Humans · Infant · Male · Mozambique · Point-of-Care Systems* · Prospective Studies · Retention in Care/statistics & numerical data* · Drug Monitoring*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in one cluster-randomised trial across 16 primary health centres in Mozambique, point-of-care early infant diagnosis transformed the treatment cascade: 89.7% of HIV-positive infants started antiretroviral therapy within 60 days of sample collection versus 12.8% with standard laboratory referral (adjusted relative risk 7.34; P<0.001), median time to initiation was under 1 day versus 127 days, and retention at 90 days among those who started was 61.6% versus 42.9% (adjusted relative risk 1.40; P<0.027). The effect sizes are unusually large for a delivery intervention, which is itself a caution: a single programme, in one country's clinic system, where the standard-care arm performed exceptionally poorly (only 13 of 102 infants started within 60 days). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): same-day infant testing very probably speeds treatment and improves early retention where laboratory referral leaks patients, with the size of the gain depending on how weak the referral system is. Tier C is set because this is a single trial programme.

cards.headline: Jani 2018: point-of-care infant testing — 89.7% started treatment within 60 days vs 12.8% with laboratory referral; median under 1 day vs 127 days
cards.summary: Jani 2018: point-of-care infant testing — 89.7% started treatment within 60 days vs 12.8% with laboratory referral; median under 1 day vs 127 days
cards.people: HIV-exposed infants tested at 16 primary healthcare centres in Mozambique, cluster-randomised (8 centres on-site point-of-care testing, 8 centres referred laboratory standard-of-care testing). Primary outcomes were antiretroviral initiation within 60 days of sample collection (175 HIV-positive infants in the point-of-care arm, 102 in the standard arm) and retention at 90 days among those who initiated.
cards.result: The proportion of HIV-positive infants initiating antiretroviral therapy within 60 days was 89.7% (157 of 175) for point-of-care versus 12.8% (13 of 102) for standard care [adjusted relative risk 7.34; P<0.001]. Retention at 90 days among initiators was 61.6% (101 of 164) versus 42.9% (21 of 49) [adjusted relative risk 1.40; P<0.027]. Median time from sample collection to treatment initiation was less than 1 day (interquartile range 0–1) for point-of-care versus 127 days (44–154; P<0.001) for standard care.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen clusters is a small number for a cluster trial, and the standard-care arm's 12.8% initiation rate is the engine of the huge relative effect — in a system with a functioning laboratory network the absolute gain would be far smaller. Retention was still only 61.6% at 90 days even with same-day results, so testing speed solves only the first leak in the cascade.

shelves.title: Ibrexafungerp for an acute yeast infection: one day of tablets cured 50.5% versus 28.6% on placebo in VANISH 303 — effective, with no fluconazole comparison
shelves.question: In women with acute vulvovaginal candidiasis, is oral ibrexafungerp superior to placebo for clinical cure?
shelves.mesh: Antifungal Agents/adverse effects · Azoles/therapeutic use · Candidiasis, Vulvovaginal*/drug therapy · Female · Glycosides/therapeutic use · Humans · Triterpenes*/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in VANISH 303, a phase 3 randomised superiority trial, one day of oral ibrexafungerp (300 mg twice for 1 day) beat placebo on every efficacy endpoint at test-of-cure (day 11): clinical cure 50.5% versus 28.6% (P=0.001) — a 21.9 percentage-point absolute gain — mycological eradication 49.5% versus 19.4% (P<0.001), and overall success 36.0% versus 12.6% (P<0.001), with symptom resolution at follow-up (day 25) of 59.6% versus 44.9% (P=0.009). Adverse events were primarily gastrointestinal and mild. The honest framing: half of treated patients were not clinically cured at day 11, and placebo itself produced a 28.6% cure rate, so the drug adds about one extra cure for every five women treated over doing nothing. There is no comparison here against fluconazole, the standard oral treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ibrexafungerp is an effective oral option for acute vulvovaginal candidiasis versus placebo, with its place relative to azole therapy untested in this trial.

cards.headline: Schwebke 2022 (VANISH 303): ibrexafungerp clinical cure 50.5% vs 28.6% on placebo at day 11; mycological eradication 49.5% vs 19.4%
cards.summary: Schwebke 2022 (VANISH 303): ibrexafungerp clinical cure 50.5% vs 28.6% on placebo at day 11; mycological eradication 49.5% vs 19.4%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised controlled superiority trial (VANISH 303, Schwebke 2022)
cards.people: Patients with acute vulvovaginal candidiasis randomised 2:1 to ibrexafungerp 300 mg twice for 1 day (188 patients in the efficacy counts) or placebo (98 patients), in a phase 3 randomised controlled superiority trial. The primary endpoint was clinical cure (complete resolution of vulvovaginal signs and symptoms, score 0) at test-of-cure (day 11 ± 3); secondary endpoints included mycological eradication, overall success, clinical improvement, and symptom resolution at follow-up (day 25 ± 4).
cards.result: Clinical cure: 50.5% (95/188) with ibrexafungerp versus 28.6% (28/98) with placebo (P=0.001). Mycological eradication: 49.5% (93/188) versus 19.4% (19/98) (P<0.001). Overall success (clinical cure plus mycological eradication): 36.0% (64/178) versus 12.6% (12/95) (P<0.001). Symptom resolution at follow-up: 59.6% (112/188) versus 44.9% (44/98) (P=0.009). Post hoc analyses showed similar clinical cure rates in Black patients (54.8%, 40/73) and in patients with body mass index above 35 (54.5%, 24/44). Ibrexafungerp was well tolerated; adverse events were primarily gastrointestinal and mild in severity.
cards.watchOut: A placebo comparator in a condition with an effective standard oral therapy (fluconazole) proves the drug works, not where it fits. The record carries no registry ID, and the miner programme's second VANISH trial is not this record — only VANISH 303 is carded here. Clinical cure required a sign-and-symptom score of exactly zero, a strict bar that partly explains the 50.5% figure.
cards.source: Schwebke JR et al. Ibrexafungerp Versus Placebo for Vulvovaginal Candidiasis Treatment: A Phase 3, Randomized, Controlled Superiority Trial (VANISH 303). Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2022. PMID: 34467969. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Toxoplasmic encephalitis in AIDS: the one head-to-head trial stopped early and found no significant difference — the cheaper, available regimen remains unproven, not disproven
shelves.question: In patients with HIV-associated toxoplasmic encephalitis, is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as effective as pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine for clinical and radiological response?
shelves.mesh: AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections/drug therapy · Adult · Antiprotozoal Agents/administration & dosage · Drug Therapy, Combination · Encephalitis/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrimethamine/administration & dosage · Sulfadiazine/administration & dosage · Toxoplasmosis, Cerebral/drug therapy · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination/adverse effects
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the randomised record for this comparison is a single Thai trial (Kongsaengdao S et al., PMID: 17517949) that randomised AIDS patients with toxoplasmic encephalitis to six weeks of pyrimethamine 50 mg/day plus sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine 100 mg/day plus sulfadiazine, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and was terminated prematurely; its abstract reports that failure rates were not significantly different among the three groups and that the 50 mg pyrimethamine combination gave the best primary outcome (death in the first six weeks), while its authors themselves call for further evaluation of intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. The systematic review of randomised toxoplasmosis trials (Rajapakse S et al., PMID: 23816507) likewise found the efficacy of pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole similar for toxoplasmic encephalopathy, while grading most encephalitis trials as high risk of bias and poor methodological quality, with adverse effects seemingly more common on pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine. 'No significant difference' in a small, stopped-early trial is not demonstrated equivalence, and the abstract of the anchor record reports no arm sizes or event rates to extract. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a plausible alternative where pyrimethamine is unavailable or unaffordable, but equivalence is a hope the trials have not yet earned. Tier C is set because the evidence base is one prematurely terminated trial and a low-quality trial literature.

cards.headline: Kongsaengdao 2008: three-arm RCT stopped prematurely — failure rates not significantly different between trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and either pyrimethamine dose, with the 50 mg pyrimethamine arm rated best on the primary outcome
cards.summary: Kongsaengdao 2008: three-arm RCT stopped prematurely — failure rates not significantly different between trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and either pyrimethamine dose, with the 50 mg pyrimethamine arm rated best on the primary outcome
cards.people: AIDS patients with toxoplasmic encephalitis in Thailand, randomised to a 6-week course of pyrimethamine (50 mg/day or 100 mg/day) plus sulfadiazine (4 g/day) with folinic acid (25 mg/day), or trimethoprim (10 mg/kg/day) plus sulfamethoxazole (50 mg/kg/day). The record's abstract does not state the number randomised or arm-level event rates.
cards.result: The primary outcome was death in the first 6-week period; the secondary outcome was successful treatment within 6 weeks without severe adverse events, bone marrow suppression, drug-induced rash, or any other event causing a change of regimen. The authors report that toxoplasmic encephalitis was most successfully treated with pyrimethamine 50 mg/day plus sulfadiazine 4 g/day and folinic acid 25 mg/day, that failure rates were not significantly different among the three treatment groups, and that the study was terminated prematurely; they suggest intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole be further evaluated. No numerical event rates are given in the record.
cards.watchOut: Premature termination plus unreported arm sizes in the abstract means this trial cannot support an equivalence claim — absence of a significant difference in an underpowered comparison is expected even when real differences exist. Treat any secondary-source numbers for this trial with suspicion; none are used here because the fetched record does not contain them.

cards.headline: Rajapakse 2013 (systematic review of 14 randomised trials): for toxoplasmic encephalopathy the two regimens looked similar — in a literature the reviewers grade as mostly high risk of bias and poor quality
cards.summary: Rajapakse 2013 (systematic review of 14 randomised trials): for toxoplasmic encephalopathy the two regimens looked similar — in a literature the reviewers grade as mostly high risk of bias and poor quality
cards.people: Fourteen randomised trials of antibiotic regimens across all clinical syndromes of human toxoplasmosis (encephalitis, ocular disease, lymphadenopathy, pregnancy and congenital disease), identified through MEDLINE, EMBASE and SCOPUS with no date limits.
cards.result: For toxoplasmic encephalopathy, the efficacy of pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine and trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole was similar, and pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine versus pyrimethamine plus clindamycin also showed no difference, irrespective of outcome. Adverse effects seemed more common with pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine. Most trials for encephalitis and ocular manifestations had a high risk of bias and were of poor methodological quality; there were no trials in pregnancy or congenital toxoplasmosis. The reviewers conclude that overall trial evidence for these drugs is poor and further well-designed trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: A narrative systematic review without a pooled estimate for the encephalitis comparison: 'similar' summarises small heterogeneous trials rather than a meta-analytic equivalence bound. It corroborates the anchor trial's direction but cannot raise the certainty above weak.
cards.source: Rajapakse S et al. Antibiotics for human toxoplasmosis: a systematic review of randomized trials. Pathogens and Global Health. 2013. PMID: 23816507. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two sources, one message — no demonstrated difference, and no demonstrated equivalence either
cards.summary: Synthesis: two sources, one message — no demonstrated difference, and no demonstrated equivalence either
cards.people: One prematurely terminated three-arm RCT in AIDS patients with toxoplasmic encephalitis (Kongsaengdao 2008) plus a systematic review of 14 randomised toxoplasmosis trials (Rajapakse 2013).
cards.result: Failure rates: not significantly different among pyrimethamine 50 mg, pyrimethamine 100 mg (each plus sulfadiazine) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole arms. Review verdict: efficacy similar for encephalopathy; adverse effects seemingly more common with pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine; evidence quality poor, high risk of bias throughout. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: The practical stakes are asymmetric: pyrimethamine is often unavailable or very expensive, so trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is widely used on exactly this thin evidence. This shelf records that the substitution is reasonable but unproven — it should not be quoted as showing the regimens are interchangeable at equal efficacy. Tier C is set for the single small stopped-early trial at the centre of the evidence.

shelves.title: Typhoid in children: cure in 91% on oral azithromycin versus 97% on ceftriaxone in a 64-child culture-positive trial — close on cure, and all four relapses fell in the ceftriaxone arm
shelves.question: In children with uncomplicated typhoid fever, is azithromycin as effective as ceftriaxone for fever clearance and cure?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Azithromycin/therapeutic use · Ceftriaxone/therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Humans · Male · Salmonella typhi/drug effects · Treatment Outcome · Typhoid Fever/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the head-to-head trial (Frenck RW et al., PMID: 11073741) randomised 108 children aged 4 to 17 years with uncomplicated typhoid fever to 7 days of oral azithromycin (10 mg/kg/day) or ceftriaxone (75 mg/kg/day); among the 64 with Salmonella typhi isolated from blood, cure was achieved in 31 of 34 (91 percent) on azithromycin and 29 of 30 (97 percent) on ceftriaxone (P>.05) — a 6-percentage-point gap the trial was far too small to resolve. All 64 isolates were susceptible to both drugs, no serious side effects occurred in either arm, and the one asymmetry was relapse: 4 ceftriaxone-treated patients subsequently relapsed, none reported on azithromycin. The Cochrane review of azithromycin for enteric fever (Effa EE et al., PMID: 18843701; 7 trials, 773 participants) points the same way on relapse: versus ceftriaxone, azithromycin significantly reduced relapse (odds ratio 0.09, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.70; 132 participants, 2 trials) with no significant difference in other outcomes, and versus fluoroquinolones it reduced clinical failure (odds ratio 0.48, 0.26 to 0.89). Those pooled estimates rest on few participants and open-label trials from 2008 and earlier — before today's extensively drug-resistant strains. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): once-daily oral azithromycin is a credible, more convenient alternative to ceftriaxone for uncomplicated childhood typhoid where isolates are susceptible. Tier C is set because the direct comparison is a single small older trial.

cards.headline: Frenck 2000: among 64 culture-positive children, cure in 31/34 (91%) on azithromycin versus 29/30 (97%) on ceftriaxone (P>.05); 4 relapses, all after ceftriaxone; no serious side effects
cards.summary: Frenck 2000: among 64 culture-positive children, cure in 31/34 (91%) on azithromycin versus 29/30 (97%) on ceftriaxone (P>.05); 4 relapses, all after ceftriaxone; no serious side effects
cards.people: 108 children aged 4 to 17 years with uncomplicated typhoid fever, randomised to 7 days of azithromycin (10 mg/kg/day, maximum 500 mg/day, oral) or ceftriaxone (75 mg/kg/day, maximum 2.5 g/day); Salmonella typhi was isolated from initial blood cultures in 64 patients (34 azithromycin, 30 ceftriaxone), and all 64 isolates were susceptible to both agents.
cards.result: Cure was achieved in 31 of 34 patients (91 percent) treated with azithromycin and 29 of 30 (97 percent) treated with ceftriaxone (P>.05). Of the patients treated with ceftriaxone, 4 subsequently had relapse of their infection; no relapses are reported for the azithromycin arm. No serious side effects occurred in any study subject. The authors conclude that once-daily oral azithromycin appears effective for uncomplicated typhoid fever in children and could be a convenient alternative where medical resources are scarce.
cards.watchOut: Sixty-four informative patients cannot establish equivalence: the cure difference (91 versus 97 percent) has a confidence interval wide enough to include a clinically important disadvantage for azithromycin. The trial predates widespread fluoroquinolone and emerging azithromycin resistance in Salmonella typhi; its susceptibility findings (all isolates susceptible to both drugs) describe Egypt at the turn of the century, not current South Asian strains.
cards.source: Frenck RW et al. Azithromycin versus ceftriaxone for the treatment of uncomplicated typhoid fever in children. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2000. PMID: 11073741. cards.summary: Effa 2008 (Cochrane, 7 trials, 773 participants): versus ceftriaxone, azithromycin cut relapse (odds ratio 0.09, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.70) with no difference in other outcomes; versus fluoroquinolones it cut clinical failure (0.48, 0.26 to 0.89)
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Effa 2008, Cochrane)
cards.people: Seven randomised trials involving 773 hospital inpatients — three exclusively in adults, two in children, two mixed — comparing azithromycin with other antibiotics for culture-confirmed uncomplicated enteric fever (Salmonella Typhi or Paratyphi); trials used adequate sequence generation and allocation concealment but were open label.
cards.result: Against chloramphenicol (77 participants, 1 trial) no difference was shown for any outcome. Against fluoroquinolones (4 trials), azithromycin significantly reduced clinical failure (odds ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.89; 564 participants) and duration of hospital stay (mean difference −1.04 days, 95% CI −1.73 to −0.34; 213 participants, 2 trials), with no significant difference in other outcomes; all four trials included multidrug-resistant or nalidixic-acid-resistant strains. Against ceftriaxone (132 participants, 2 trials), azithromycin significantly reduced relapse (odds ratio 0.09, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.70) and not other outcome measures. Few adverse events were reported, most mild and self-limiting.
cards.watchOut: The relapse advantage rests on 132 participants in 2 trials — a handful of events drives an odds ratio of 0.09, and the interval (0.01 to 0.70) is correspondingly wide. All trials were open label and the search closed in August 2008; neither this review nor the anchor trial speaks to extensively drug-resistant typhoid.

cards.headline: Synthesis: azithromycin matches ceftriaxone closely on cure in susceptible strains and may relapse less — convenience is real, equivalence is approximate
cards.summary: Synthesis: azithromycin matches ceftriaxone closely on cure in susceptible strains and may relapse less — convenience is real, equivalence is approximate
cards.people: One head-to-head trial in 108 children (64 culture-positive; Frenck 2000) plus a Cochrane review of 7 trials and 773 participants with enteric fever (Effa 2008).
cards.result: Cure (culture-positive children): 91 percent on azithromycin versus 97 percent on ceftriaxone, P>.05. Relapse: 4 cases after ceftriaxone versus none reported after azithromycin in the trial; pooled odds ratio 0.09 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.70) favouring azithromycin across 2 trials. Serious side effects: none in the anchor trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Everything on this shelf assumes susceptible isolates and uncomplicated disease. Complicated typhoid, suspected resistance, or inability to take oral therapy changes the question entirely, and local resistance surveillance — not a 2000 trial — should govern empiric choice today. Tier C is set for the single small direct trial.

shelves.title: Severe leptospirosis: ceftriaxone and penicillin G performed identically (median fever 3 days, 5 deaths in each arm) — while the Cochrane review finds antibiotics themselves unproven against placebo
shelves.question: In adults with severe leptospirosis, is intravenous ceftriaxone as effective as intravenous penicillin G — and has antibiotic therapy itself been shown to improve outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Ceftriaxone/therapeutic use · Cephalosporins/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Leptospirosis/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Penicillin G/therapeutic use · Penicillins/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Thailand · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two different uncertainties sit inside this question. The head-to-head part is settled as far as one trial can settle it: Panaphut T et al. (PMID: 12802748) randomised 173 patients with severe leptospirosis in Thailand to intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily or sodium penicillin G 1.5 million units every 6 hours, each for 7 days; the median duration of fever was 3 days in both groups, 10 patients died (5 in each group), and there were no statistically significant differences in the duration of organ dysfunction — the authors conclude the two are equally effective, with once-daily dosing and broader spectrum as ceftriaxone's practical advantages. The deeper part is unsettled: the Cochrane review of antibiotics for leptospirosis (Brett-Major DM et al., PMID: 22336839; 7 trials) found, across the four placebo-controlled trials, deaths of 16/200 (8.0 percent) on antibiotics versus 11/203 (5.4 percent) on placebo — fixed-effect odds ratio 1.56 (95% CI 0.70 to 3.46), random-effects 1.16 (0.23 to 5.95) — with all trials at high risk of bias and no significant effect on hospital stay in the one trial reporting it (8.9 versus 8.8 days). Note the miner question's framing (antibiotics versus no therapy, anchored on Panaphut) does not match the anchor trial, which compares two antibiotics; this shelf answers both parts with the records that actually address them. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): choose between ceftriaxone and penicillin on logistics, not efficacy — and recognise that antibiotic benefit in severe leptospirosis, though standard practice, has never been cleanly demonstrated in randomised trials. Tier C is set for the single head-to-head trial and the high-bias placebo literature.

cards.headline: Panaphut 2003: median fever duration 3 days in both arms, 5 deaths in each (of 87 ceftriaxone, 86 penicillin G), no difference in organ dysfunction duration — ceftriaxone equals penicillin G for severe leptospirosis
cards.summary: Panaphut 2003: median fever duration 3 days in both arms, 5 deaths in each (of 87 ceftriaxone, 86 penicillin G), no difference in organ dysfunction duration — ceftriaxone equals penicillin G for severe leptospirosis
cards.people: 173 patients with severe leptospirosis at Khon Kaen Hospital, Thailand (July 2000 to December 2001), randomised open-label to intravenous ceftriaxone (1 g daily for 7 days; n=87) or intravenous sodium penicillin G (1.5 million units every 6 hours for 7 days; n=86); the primary outcome was time to fever resolution.
cards.result: Survival analysis showed the median duration of fever was 3 days for both groups. Ten patients (5 in each group) died of leptospirosis infection. There were no statistically significant differences in the duration of organ dysfunction between the groups. The authors conclude that ceftriaxone and sodium penicillin G were equally effective, and that once-daily administration and the extended spectrum of ceftriaxone provide additional benefits over intravenous penicillin.
cards.watchOut: An open-label trial of 173 patients with 10 deaths cannot exclude moderate mortality differences between the regimens, and 'severe leptospirosis' case mix in one Thai hospital may not travel. Crucially, with no placebo or no-treatment arm, this trial says nothing about whether antibiotics change the course of severe disease at all — that question belongs to the Cochrane card.
cards.source: Panaphut T et al. Ceftriaxone compared with sodium penicillin g for treatment of severe leptospirosis. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2003. PMID: 12802748. cards.headline: Brett-Major 2012 (Cochrane, 7 trials): antibiotics versus placebo — deaths 8.0% versus 5.4% (fixed-effect odds ratio 1.56, 95% CI 0.70 to 3.46); all trials at high risk of bias
cards.summary: Brett-Major 2012 (Cochrane, 7 trials): antibiotics versus placebo — deaths 8.0% versus 5.4% (fixed-effect odds ratio 1.56, 95% CI 0.70 to 3.46); all trials at high risk of bias
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Brett-Major 2012, Cochrane)
cards.people: Seven randomised trials of antibiotics for leptospirosis: four trials with 403 patients compared an antibiotic with placebo or no intervention (all using parenteral penicillin for the mortality analysis), and three compared antibiotic regimens against each other; trial populations varied in disease severity.
cards.result: Across the placebo-controlled trials, deaths were 16/200 (8.0 percent) in the antibiotic arms versus 11/203 (5.4 percent) in the placebo arms, giving a fixed-effect odds ratio of 1.56 (95% CI 0.70 to 3.46) and a random-effects odds ratio of 1.16 (95% CI 0.23 to 5.95), with moderate heterogeneity (I²=50 percent); two of the four trials had no deaths and could not contribute to the estimate. Only one trial (253 patients) reported hospitalisation: parenteral penicillin versus placebo showed no significant effect (8.9 versus 8.8 days; mean difference 0.10 days, 95% CI −0.83 to 1.03). All included trials had high risk of bias.
cards.watchOut: A point estimate above 1.0 with an interval spanning 0.70 to 3.46 is inconclusive, not evidence of harm — the placebo-controlled trials are small, old, and at high risk of bias, and they largely predate modern supportive care. This card grades the randomised proof; it is not an argument to withhold antibiotics, which remain standard care on physiological and observational grounds.
cards.source: Brett-Major DM et al. Antibiotics for leptospirosis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012. PMID: 22336839. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: regimen choice is a logistics question (settled, one trial); antibiotic efficacy itself is an open question (unsettled, high-bias trials)
cards.summary: Synthesis: regimen choice is a logistics question (settled, one trial); antibiotic efficacy itself is an open question (unsettled, high-bias trials)
cards.people: One head-to-head trial in 173 patients with severe leptospirosis (Panaphut 2003) plus a Cochrane review of 7 randomised trials including 403 placebo-controlled patients (Brett-Major 2012).
cards.result: Ceftriaxone versus penicillin G: fever duration median 3 days in both; deaths 5 versus 5; no significant differences in organ dysfunction. Antibiotics versus placebo (Cochrane): mortality odds ratio 1.56 (95% CI 0.70 to 3.46, fixed-effect); hospital stay difference 0.10 days (−0.83 to 1.03). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the two halves of this shelf into a claim that 'antibiotics don't work in leptospirosis': the placebo trials are too weak to show that, and the shelved doxycycline-prophylaxis question (prevention in exposed soldiers) is a different question again. What the record supports is narrower — the two intravenous regimens perform alike, and efficacy against no treatment is unproven. Tier C is set accordingly.
