shelves.title: Brucellosis: the all-oral doxycycline-rifampin regimen is NOT as effective — relapse 16% versus 5.3%, and combined failure 24% versus 7.45%, with a meta-analysis agreeing (odds ratio 3.17)
shelves.question: In human brucellosis, is doxycycline plus rifampin as effective as doxycycline plus streptomycin for cure without relapse?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Brucella melitensis* · Brucellosis/drug therapy · Child · Doxycycline/adverse effects · Drug Therapy, Combination/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Rifampin/adverse effects · Spain · Streptomycin/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — the answer to this shelf's question is no, and two independent sources say so consistently. In the GECMEI multicentre trial (Solera J et al., PMID: 8540716), 194 patients with acute brucellosis (without endocarditis or neurobrucellosis) received doxycycline for 45 days plus either rifampin 900 mg/day for 45 days or streptomycin 1 g/day intramuscularly for 14 days. Initial lack of efficacy occurred in 8 of 100 (8 percent) on doxycycline-rifampin versus 2 of 94 (2 percent) on doxycycline-streptomycin (P=0.10); relapses occurred in 16 of 100 (16 percent) versus 5 of 94 (5.3 percent) (P=0.02); and the combined failure outcome — the number that matters to patients — was 26 of 100 (24 percent) versus 7 of 94 (7.45 percent) (P=0.0016). Tolerability did not rescue the oral regimen: adverse effects forcing discontinuation occurred in 4 percent versus 2 percent (P>0.2). The systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised brucellosis trials (Solís García del Pozo J et al., PMID: 22393379 — the record's first author; the miner entry cites it as Skalsky et al.) pooled the same comparison and found it favoured doxycycline-streptomycin (odds ratio 3.17, 95% CI 2.05 to 4.91 for relapse/failure with the rifampin regimen), while finding no significant difference between doxycycline-streptomycin and doxycycline-gentamicin (odds ratio 1.89, 0.81 to 4.39). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): the convenience of an all-oral regimen is bought with roughly triple the failure rate; where injections are feasible, an aminoglycoside partner is the better-evidenced choice. Tier C is not set — a consistent trial-plus-meta-analysis record is above the weak tier.

cards.headline: Solera 1995 (GECMEI): combined failure in 24% on doxycycline-rifampin versus 7.45% on doxycycline-streptomycin (P=0.0016); relapses 16% versus 5.3% (P=0.02)
cards.summary: Solera 1995 (GECMEI): combined failure in 24% on doxycycline-rifampin versus 7.45% on doxycycline-streptomycin (P=0.0016); relapses 16% versus 5.3% (P=0.02)
cards.people: 194 ambulatory or hospitalised patients with acute brucellosis due to Brucella melitensis in five Spanish general hospitals, without endocarditis or neurobrucellosis; diagnosis by isolation of Brucella from blood or other tissues (120 patients) or a standard tube agglutination titre of 1/160 or more with compatible clinical findings (74). Both groups received doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 45 days, plus rifampin 900 mg/day in a single morning dose for 45 days (100 patients) or streptomycin 1 g/day intramuscularly for 14 days (94).
cards.result: Lack of therapeutic efficacy developed in 8 of 100 patients (8 percent) in the doxycycline-rifampin group and 2 of 94 (2 percent) in the doxycycline-streptomycin group (P=0.10). Relapses occurred in 16 of 100 (16 percent) versus 5 of 94 (5.3 percent) (P=0.02). Combining relapse with initial lack of efficacy, 26 patients (24 percent) on doxycycline-rifampin and 7 (7.45 percent) on doxycycline-streptomycin failed to respond (P=0.0016). Therapy was generally well tolerated; adverse effects necessitating discontinuation occurred in 4 patients (4 percent) versus 2 (2 percent) (P>0.2). The authors conclude the doxycycline-rifampin regimen is less effective.
cards.watchOut: An open trial from 1995 in Brucella melitensis infection, excluding the complicated forms (endocarditis, neurobrucellosis) where regimen choice matters most and evidence is thinnest. Relapse ascertainment depends on follow-up intensity and duration, which the abstract does not detail; the meta-analysis card is what protects this shelf from single-trial fragility.

cards.headline: Solís García del Pozo 2012 (systematic review and meta-analysis): doxycycline-rifampin versus doxycycline-streptomycin favours streptomycin (odds ratio 3.17, 95% CI 2.05 to 4.91); doxycycline-gentamicin looks similar to streptomycin (1.89, 0.81 to 4.39)
cards.summary: Solís García del Pozo 2012 (systematic review and meta-analysis): doxycycline-rifampin versus doxycycline-streptomycin favours streptomycin (odds ratio 3.17, 95% CI 2.05 to 4.91); doxycycline-gentamicin looks similar to streptomycin (1.89, 0.81 to 4.39)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Solís García del Pozo 2012)
cards.people: Randomised clinical trials published from 1985 onwards assessing antimicrobial regimens in documented acute uncomplicated human brucellosis, identified in MEDLINE and the Cochrane Central Register; primary outcomes were relapse, therapeutic failure, their combination, and adverse effects, pooled as odds ratios (fixed-effect model, random-effects where heterogeneity was significant). The miner entry cites this review as Skalsky et al.; the fetched record's first author is Solís García del Pozo J.
cards.result: Comparison of combined doxycycline and rifampicin with doxycycline and streptomycin favoured the streptomycin regimen (odds ratio 3.17; 95% CI 2.05 to 4.91, for the rifampin regimen's worse outcome). There were no significant differences between doxycycline-streptomycin and doxycycline-gentamicin (odds ratio 1.89; 0.81 to 4.39). Rifampicin plus quinolones was similar to doxycycline-rifampicin (odds ratio 1.23; 0.63 to 2.40). Only one study assessed triple therapy, so it cannot be considered the treatment of choice. The authors conclude the preferred treatment in uncomplicated brucellosis is a doxycycline-aminoglycoside combination, while noting oral regimens should be better studied rather than rejected outright.
cards.watchOut: The pooled odds ratio aggregates trials of varying size and era, and the outcome direction (odds of relapse/failure on the rifampin regimen) must be read with the anchor trial's absolute rates — 24 percent versus 7.45 percent — to keep the size of the problem in view. Uncomplicated acute brucellosis only; complicated disease was outside the included trials.

cards.headline: Synthesis: trial and meta-analysis agree — the all-oral regimen fails about three times as often; an aminoglycoside partner is the evidence-backed default
cards.summary: Synthesis: trial and meta-analysis agree — the all-oral regimen fails about three times as often; an aminoglycoside partner is the evidence-backed default
cards.people: One multicentre trial of 194 patients (Solera 1995) plus a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised brucellosis trials from 1985 onwards (Solís García del Pozo 2012).
cards.result: Relapse: 16 percent versus 5.3 percent (P=0.02). Combined relapse or initial failure: 24 percent versus 7.45 percent (P=0.0016). Meta-analytic odds ratio for the rifampin regimen's worse outcome: 3.17 (95% CI 2.05 to 4.91). Discontinuations for adverse effects: 4 percent versus 2 percent (not significant). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) — for doxycycline plus rifampin relative to doxycycline plus streptomycin.
cards.watchOut: 'Harm' here is comparative, not absolute: doxycycline-rifampin still cured about three-quarters of patients and remains a fallback where aminoglycoside injections, monitoring, or patient acceptance rule out the better regimen — with relapse surveillance doing the safety work. Doxycycline-gentamicin may offer the aminoglycoside benefit with a shorter injection course, but its pooled interval (0.81 to 4.39) is too wide to claim equality on this record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Solera J et al. Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. 1995 (PMID: 8540716); Solís García del Pozo J et al. PLoS One. 2012 (PMID: 22393379).

shelves.title: Single-dose azithromycin for cholera: clinical success 73% versus 27% and bacteriological success 78% versus 10% against single-dose ciprofloxacin — a rout driven by ciprofloxacin's lost potency against local strains
shelves.question: In adults with severe cholera, does a single dose of azithromycin match a single dose of ciprofloxacin for clinical and bacteriological cure?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Azithromycin/administration & dosage · Bangladesh · Cholera/complications · Ciprofloxacin/administration & dosage · Combined Modality Therapy · Diarrhea/etiology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Resistance, Bacterial · Fluid Therapy · Humans · Male · Treatment Outcome · Vibrio cholerae/classification · Vomiting/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — note first a correction to the miner question, which asked about multi-day tetracycline: the anchor trial (Saha D et al., PMID: 16760445) actually compared single 1-gram doses of azithromycin and ciprofloxacin in 195 men hospitalised with severe cholera caused by Vibrio cholerae O1 or O139 in Bangladesh, alongside fluid therapy. The result was one-sided: clinical success (cessation of watery stools within 48 hours) in 71 of 97 patients (73 percent) on azithromycin versus 26 of 98 (27 percent) on ciprofloxacin (P<0.001), and bacteriological success in 76 of 97 (78 percent) versus 10 of 98 (10 percent) (P<0.001). Azithromycin patients also had shorter diarrhoea (median 30 versus 78 hours), less vomiting (43 percent versus 67 percent), fewer stools (median 36 versus 52), and lower stool volume (median 114 versus 322 ml per kilogram). The explanation sits in the microbiology: the median ciprofloxacin minimum inhibitory concentration for the 177 O1 isolates was 0.25 micrograms per milliliter, 11 to 83 times higher than in previous studies at the site — ciprofloxacin had not become a bad drug everywhere, it had stopped working against these strains. The Cochrane review of antimicrobials for cholera (Leibovici-Weissman Y et al., PMID: 24944120; 39 trials, 4,623 participants) supplies the class context: antimicrobial therapy shortened diarrhoea by about a day and a half versus placebo or no treatment (mean difference −36.77 hours, 95% CI −43.51 to −30.03; moderate quality evidence), halved stool volume, and cut rehydration fluid needs by 40 percent. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): where ciprofloxacin susceptibility has eroded, single-dose azithromycin is the better-evidenced single-dose choice — an inherently local verdict that susceptibility surveillance must keep re-earning. Tier C is set because the head-to-head evidence is a single trial in men at one site.

cards.headline: Saha 2006 (NEJM): single-dose azithromycin beat single-dose ciprofloxacin decisively — clinical success 73% versus 27%, bacteriological success 78% versus 10% (both P<0.001); diarrhoea 30 versus 78 hours
cards.summary: Saha 2006 (NEJM): single-dose azithromycin beat single-dose ciprofloxacin decisively — clinical success 73% versus 27%, bacteriological success 78% versus 10% (both P<0.001); diarrhoea 30 versus 78 hours
cards.people: 195 men hospitalised for five days with severe cholera caused by Vibrio cholerae O1 or O139 in Bangladesh, randomised double-blind to a single 1-gram dose (two 500-mg tablets) of azithromycin (97 patients) or ciprofloxacin (98), with daily stool cultures and fluid therapy as combined care. The miner question named tetracycline as comparator; the record's comparator is ciprofloxacin, and this shelf follows the record.
cards.result: Clinical success (cessation of watery stools within 48 hours): 71 of 97 patients (73 percent) on azithromycin versus 26 of 98 (27 percent) on ciprofloxacin (P<0.001). Bacteriological success (no isolation of V. cholerae after 48 hours): 76 of 97 (78 percent) versus 10 of 98 (10 percent) (P<0.001). Azithromycin patients had a shorter duration of diarrhoea (median 30 versus 78 hours), lower frequency of vomiting (43 percent versus 67 percent), fewer stools (median 36 versus 52), and lower stool volume (median 114 versus 322 ml per kilogram of body weight). The median ciprofloxacin minimum inhibitory concentration for the 177 V. cholerae O1 isolates was 0.25 micrograms per milliliter, 11 to 83 times as high as in previous studies at this site.
cards.watchOut: All participants were men, at one site, during a period of documented local ciprofloxacin resistance: the trial measures azithromycin against a comparator whose potency had locally collapsed, so its margins must not be exported to settings where ciprofloxacin remains fully susceptible — nor assumed to hold if azithromycin resistance rises. Antibiotics are adjuncts in cholera; rehydration is the life-saving treatment, as the trial's own combined-modality design reflects.
cards.source: Saha D et al. Single-dose azithromycin for the treatment of cholera in adults. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2006. PMID: 16760445. Registry ID: NCT00229944. cards.headline: Leibovici-Weissman 2014 (Cochrane, 39 trials, 4,623 participants): antimicrobials shortened diarrhoea by about 36.8 hours versus placebo or no treatment and halved stool volume (ratio of means 0.5)
cards.summary: Leibovici-Weissman 2014 (Cochrane, 39 trials, 4,623 participants): antimicrobials shortened diarrhoea by about 36.8 hours versus placebo or no treatment and halved stool volume (ratio of means 0.5)
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Leibovici-Weissman 2014, Cochrane)
cards.people: Thirty-nine randomised and quasi-randomised trials in adults and children with cholera comparing any antimicrobial with placebo or no treatment, different antimicrobials head-to-head, or different dosing schedules/durations; primary outcomes were diarrhoea duration and stool volume, pooled with random-effects meta-analysis and graded with GRADE.
cards.result: Versus placebo or no treatment, antimicrobial therapy shortened the mean duration of diarrhoea by about a day and a half (mean difference −36.77 hours, 95% CI −43.51 to −30.03; 19 trials, 1,013 participants; moderate quality evidence), reduced total stool volume by 50 percent (ratio of means 0.5, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.56; 18 trials, 1,042 participants; moderate quality evidence), reduced rehydration fluid requirements by 40 percent (ratio of means 0.60, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.68; 11 trials, 1,201 participants), and shortened faecal excretion of vibrios by almost three days.
cards.watchOut: The review pools many drug classes and eras; its placebo comparison establishes that antimicrobials as a class help, not that any single agent or single-dose schedule is best. Head-to-head differences between agents in cholera are dominated by local resistance — the review's averages cannot substitute for current susceptibility data at the place of treatment.
cards.source: Leibovici-Weissman Y et al. Antimicrobial drugs for treating cholera. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 24944120. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Strong Treat 1 to 4: four doses of ivermectin cured no more than one dose (85% versus 86% at 12 months) and caused more adverse events — the trial was stopped early for futility
shelves.question: In Strongyloides stercoralis infection, are multiple doses of ivermectin superior to a single dose for parasitological cure?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Animals · Anthelmintics/administration & dosage · Antibodies, Helminth/blood · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions/epidemiology · Feces/parasitology · Female · Humans · Italy · Ivermectin/administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · Spain · Strongyloides stercoralis/drug effects · Strongyloidiasis/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the answer to this shelf's question is no: more doses did not cure more people. Strong Treat 1 to 4 (Buonfrate D et al., PMID: 31558376) randomised 309 patients older than 5 years with non-disseminated Strongyloides stercoralis infection at centres in Italy, Spain and the UK to a single dose of ivermectin 200 micrograms/kg or four doses (days 1, 2, 15 and 16). At 12 months, clearance in the modified full-analysis set was 86 percent (102 of 118) on a single dose versus 85 percent (96 of 113) on four doses (risk difference 1.48 percent, 95% CI −7.55 to 10.52; p=0.75), with similar per-protocol results; adverse events were generally mild but more frequent with multiple doses, and the trial was terminated early due to futility — continuing could not plausibly reveal the superiority it was designed to detect. The Cochrane review of ivermectin for strongyloidiasis (Henriquez-Camacho C et al., PMID: 26778150) is consistent on dosing: in its dosage comparison, a second dose of ivermectin was not associated with higher cure (risk ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.11; 94 participants), while ivermectin beat albendazole on parasitological cure (risk ratio 1.79, 1.55 to 2.08; moderate quality evidence). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for non-disseminated infection, one dose does the work of four — fewer adverse events, simpler delivery, same cure. Tier C is set because the dose comparison rests on this single trial, stopped early with about a quarter of randomised patients outside the modified analysis set.

cards.headline: Buonfrate 2019 (Strong Treat 1 to 4): clearance at 12 months 86% (102/118) on one dose versus 85% (96/113) on four doses (risk difference 1.48 percent, 95% CI −7.55 to 10.52; p=0.75) — stopped early for futility
cards.summary: Buonfrate 2019 (Strong Treat 1 to 4): clearance at 12 months 86% (102/118) on one dose versus 85% (96/113) on four doses (risk difference 1.48 percent, 95% CI −7.55 to 10.52; p=0.75) — stopped early for futility
cards.type: Multicentre randomised superiority trial (Strong Treat 1 to 4, Buonfrate 2019)
cards.people: 309 patients older than 5 years and weighing more than 15 kg, resident in areas not endemic for Strongyloides stercoralis, enrolled at four centres in Italy, three in Spain and two in the UK (2013–2017); eligibility required a positive faecal test plus serology at any titre, or positive serology at high titres regardless of faecal results. Randomisation: single dose of ivermectin 200 micrograms/kg (155 patients) versus four doses of 200 micrograms/kg on days 1, 2, 15 and 16 (154).
cards.result: The primary end point — clearance of S. stercoralis infection at 12 months — was reached by 86 percent (95% CI 79 to 91; 102 of 118 participants) in the single-dose group and 85 percent (77 to 90; 96 of 113) in the four-dose group in the modified full-analysis set (risk difference 1.48 percent, 95% CI −7.55 to 10.52; p=0.75); per-protocol results were similar. Adverse events were generally of mild intensity and more frequent in the multiple-dose group. The trial was terminated early due to futility. The authors conclude multiple doses did not show higher efficacy and were tolerated less well, so a single dose should be preferred for non-disseminated strongyloidiasis.
cards.watchOut: A superiority trial stopped for futility is not a formal non-inferiority trial: the interval (−7.55 to 10.52 percent) still allows a modest true advantage for four doses, and 78 of 309 randomised patients were outside the modified full-analysis set at 12 months. Participants were non-endemic-area residents with non-disseminated disease — hyperinfection and disseminated strongyloidiasis in immunocompromised patients are different, life-threatening questions this trial does not touch.

cards.headline: Henriquez-Camacho 2016 (Cochrane): a second ivermectin dose was not associated with higher cure (risk ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.11; 94 participants); ivermectin beat albendazole (1.79, 1.55 to 2.08)
cards.summary: Henriquez-Camacho 2016 (Cochrane): a second ivermectin dose was not associated with higher cure (risk ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.11; 94 participants); ivermectin beat albendazole (1.79, 1.55 to 2.08)
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Henriquez-Camacho 2016, Cochrane)
cards.people: Seven trials enrolling 1,147 participants (1994–2011, in Africa, Southeast Asia, America and Europe) comparing ivermectin with albendazole or thiabendazole for chronic Strongyloides stercoralis infection, including a subgroup comparing different ivermectin dosages.
cards.result: Against albendazole, parasitological cure was higher with ivermectin (risk ratio 1.79, 95% CI 1.55 to 2.08; 478 participants, four trials; moderate quality evidence), with no statistically significant difference in adverse events (risk ratio 0.80, 0.59 to 1.09; 518 participants; low quality evidence). Against thiabendazole, cure differed little (risk ratio 1.07, 0.96 to 1.20; 467 participants; low quality evidence) but adverse events were less common with ivermectin (risk ratio 0.31, 0.20 to 0.50; moderate quality evidence). In the dosage subgroup, taking a second dose of ivermectin 200 micrograms/kg was not associated with higher cure (risk ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.11; 94 participants).
cards.watchOut: The dosage subgroup is small (94 participants) and compares one versus two doses, not the one-versus-four schedule of Strong Treat — it corroborates a flat dose-response rather than directly confirming the anchor trial. Cure definitions across the older trials mix faecal and serological criteria, which is why the review's quality grades are moderate at best.

cards.summary: Synthesis: the dose-response is flat — one dose cures as many as four, with fewer adverse events; extra doses buy nothing measurable
cards.people: One multicentre trial of 309 patients randomised to one versus four ivermectin doses (Buonfrate 2019) plus a Cochrane review of 7 trials and 1,147 participants (Henriquez-Camacho 2016).
cards.result: Clearance at 12 months: 86 percent (single dose) versus 85 percent (four doses); risk difference 1.48 percent (95% CI −7.55 to 10.52). Second-dose effect (Cochrane subgroup): risk ratio 1.02 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.11). Adverse events: more frequent with multiple doses in the trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the single-dose regimen.
cards.watchOut: Both sources concern chronic, non-disseminated infection in largely immunocompetent or screened populations. Nothing here should be read into disseminated disease or hyperinfection, where prolonged ivermectin courses are standard on entirely different grounds. Tier C is set for the single dose-comparison trial at the centre of the shelf.

shelves.title: Giardiasis in children: single-dose tinidazole cured MORE than 3 days of nitazoxanide — 90.5% versus 78.4% parasitological cure in a 137-child trial (P<0.05)
shelves.question: In children with giardiasis, is single-dose tinidazole as effective as 3 days of nitazoxanide for clinical and parasitological cure?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain/parasitology · Adolescent · Antiparasitic Agents/administration & dosage · Child · Child, Preschool · Cuba · Diarrhea/drug therapy · Feces/parasitology · Female · Giardiasis/complications · Humans · Nitro Compounds · Thiazoles/administration & dosage · Tinidazole/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the head-to-head trial (Escobedo AA et al., PMID: 18348774) randomised 166 Cuban children with microscopically proven Giardia lamblia infection to a single dose of tinidazole 50 mg/kg or nitazoxanide 7.5 mg/kg twice daily for 3 days; among the 137 children who completed the study, parasitological cure — no Giardia in either of two faecal samples collected 5 to 10 days after treatment — was significantly more frequent after tinidazole (90.5 percent) than after nitazoxanide (78.4 percent) (P<0.05). Both schedules were well accepted and well tolerated, with only mild, transient, self-limited side effects, and diarrhoea generally cleared 2 to 6 days after starting treatment. The Cochrane review of drugs for giardiasis (Granados CE et al., PMID: 23235648; 19 trials, 1,817 participants) puts this result in a sobering frame: its best-supported comparison is albendazole versus metronidazole (parasitological cure risk ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.03; moderate quality evidence), while the shortened regimens — single-dose tinidazole, single-dose metronidazole, 3-day nitazoxanide — were evaluated in trials at high risk of bias and too small to reliably detect or exclude important differences (very low quality evidence). So the direct answer favours tinidazole, on one open trial with a per-protocol analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single supervised dose that cures at least as many children is operationally attractive, and nitazoxanide remains, in the trial authors' own words, a good candidate where tinidazole is unsuitable. Tier C is not set — the miner entry graded this trial-plus-Cochrane base above the weak tier — but the stamp stays at POSSIBLE for the single small open trial.

cards.headline: Escobedo 2008: parasitological cure 90.5% after single-dose tinidazole versus 78.4% after 3 days of nitazoxanide (P<0.05) among 137 children completing the study; side effects mild in both arms
cards.summary: Escobedo 2008: parasitological cure 90.5% after single-dose tinidazole versus 78.4% after 3 days of nitazoxanide (P<0.05) among 137 children completing the study; side effects mild in both arms
cards.people: 166 children in Cuba, each proven infected with Giardia lamblia by microscopical examination of a faecal sample, randomised open-label to nitazoxanide 7.5 mg/kg twice a day for 3 days or a single dose of tinidazole 50 mg/kg; 137 children completed the study (74 nitazoxanide, 63 tinidazole) and provided two faecal samples 5 to 10 days after completing treatment, with cure defined as no Giardia found in both samples.
cards.result: Parasitological cure following a single dose of tinidazole was significantly higher than following six doses of nitazoxanide (90.5 percent versus 78.4 percent; P<0.05). Both treatment schedules were well accepted and well tolerated, with only mild, transient and self-limited side effects reported. The commonest symptom on enrolment, diarrhoea, generally cleared 2 to 6 days after the initiation of treatment. The authors conclude that although apparently less efficacious than tinidazole, nitazoxanide remains a good candidate for treating children with Giardia lamblia infection.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with results reported for the 137 of 166 children who completed the study and provided samples — a per-protocol framing that can flatter either arm if dropouts differ by response. Cure was parasitological at 5 to 10 days; later relapse or reinfection, common where exposure continues, was not captured. One trial, one country, one era's strains.
cards.source: Escobedo AA et al. The treatment of giardiasis in children: single-dose tinidazole compared with 3 days of nitazoxanide. Annals of Tropical Medicine and Parasitology. 2008. PMID: 18348774. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Granados 2012 (Cochrane, 19 trials, 1,817 participants): shortened regimens including single-dose tinidazole and 3-day nitazoxanide rest on very low quality evidence; albendazole matches metronidazole on cure (risk ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.03)
cards.summary: Granados 2012 (Cochrane, 19 trials, 1,817 participants): shortened regimens including single-dose tinidazole and 3-day nitazoxanide rest on very low quality evidence; albendazole matches metronidazole on cure (risk ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.03)
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Granados 2012, Cochrane)
cards.people: Nineteen randomised trials involving 1,817 participants (1,441 of them children) comparing metronidazole given for 5 to 10 days with single-dose metronidazole, tinidazole, albendazole, mebendazole, or nitazoxanide for symptomatic giardiasis; studies were generally small with poor methods reporting, and most reported parasitological rather than clinical outcomes.
cards.result: Albendazole (400 mg once daily for 5 to 10 days) was probably equivalent to metronidazole for parasitological cure (risk ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.03; 932 participants, 10 trials; moderate quality evidence) and symptom improvement (risk ratio 0.98, 0.93 to 1.04; 483 participants, 5 trials), with fewer gastrointestinal (risk ratio 0.29, 0.13 to 0.63) and neurological (0.34, 0.18 to 0.64) side effects, over short (2 to 3 week) follow-up. Mebendazole comparisons were too small and biased for reliable conclusions (very low quality evidence). Five further trials evaluated shortened regimens of tinidazole (single dose; 179 participants, 3 trials), metronidazole (single dose; 55 participants, 1 trial) and nitazoxanide (3 days; 55 participants, 1 trial) — again at high risk of bias and too small to reliably detect or exclude important differences (very low quality evidence).
cards.watchOut: The Cochrane review does not pool the exact tinidazole-versus-nitazoxanide comparison this shelf asks about — the anchor trial stands alone for that pairing, and the review's role here is to grade how fragile shortened-regimen evidence generally is. Its albendazole finding also means the practical choice set is wider than the two drugs in the question.
cards.source: Granados CE et al. Drugs for treating giardiasis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012. PMID: 23235648. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the only direct trial favours single-dose tinidazole; the review literature says all shortened-regimen evidence is fragile — prefer tinidazole, hold the conclusion loosely
cards.summary: Synthesis: the only direct trial favours single-dose tinidazole; the review literature says all shortened-regimen evidence is fragile — prefer tinidazole, hold the conclusion loosely
cards.people: One open randomised trial in 166 children (137 completing; Escobedo 2008) plus a Cochrane review of 19 trials and 1,817 participants (Granados 2012).
cards.result: Parasitological cure: 90.5 percent (single-dose tinidazole) versus 78.4 percent (3-day nitazoxanide), P<0.05. Tolerability: mild, transient side effects in both arms of the trial. Cochrane grading of shortened regimens generally: very low quality evidence; the review's firmest result is albendazole's equivalence to metronidazole (risk ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.03). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: A 12-percentage-point cure gap from 137 completers is compatible with a much smaller true difference. Where the clinical priority is a directly observed single dose (adherence, school or outbreak settings), tinidazole's showing here supports it; where nitroimidazole intolerance or refractory infection is in play, this shelf's evidence does not reach. Watch for refractory giardiasis, which neither source addresses.
cards.source: Synthesis of Escobedo AA et al. Annals of Tropical Medicine and Parasitology. 2008 (PMID: 18348774); Granados CE et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012 (PMID: 23235648).

shelves.title: Natamycin beats voriconazole for fungal eye ulcers overall — but the win is Fusarium's: outside Fusarium the two drops performed the same
shelves.question: In fungal keratitis, is natamycin superior to voriconazole for visual acuity and perforation — especially in Fusarium infection?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Adult · Antifungal Agents/administration & dosage+adverse effects+therapeutic use · Corneal Perforation/microbiology · Corneal Ulcer/drug therapy+microbiology+physiopathology · Double-Blind Method · Eye Infections, Fungal/drug therapy+microbiology+physiopathology · Female · Fungi/isolation & purification · Humans · Keratoplasty, Penetrating · Male · Middle Aged · Mycoses/drug therapy+microbiology+physiopathology · Natamycin/administration & dosage+adverse effects+therapeutic use · Ophthalmic Solutions · Pyrimidines/administration & dosage+adverse effects+therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles/administration & dosage+adverse effects+therapeutic use · Visual Acuity/physiology · Voriconazole · Wound Healing/drug effects
shelves.balance: SPLIT — natamycin was the better drug overall in the Mycotic Ulcer Treatment Trial (Prajna NV et al., PMID: 23710492), with better 3-month visual acuity and fewer perforations or therapeutic keratoplasties, and a systematic summary of the randomised trials (Retamal J et al., PMID: 30562337) reached the same conclusion. But the advantage was concentrated almost entirely in Fusarium infection: in Fusarium cases the acuity and perforation differences were large, while in non-Fusarium cases acuity and perforation were essentially identical between the drugs. The practical reading is therefore organism-dependent, not a blanket verdict — natamycin first for filamentous keratitis, especially where Fusarium is likely, and no demonstrated natamycin advantage once a non-Fusarium organism is established. PROPOSED SPLIT: natamycin superior, driven by Fusarium; the two drugs look similar for non-Fusarium keratitis.

cards.headline: Prajna 2013 (MUTT I): natamycin beat voriconazole on 3-month acuity (difference 0.18 logMAR) and halved perforation/keratoplasty odds (OR 0.42) — in Fusarium the perforation OR was 0.06, in non-Fusarium 1.08
cards.summary: Prajna 2013 (MUTT I): natamycin beat voriconazole on 3-month acuity (difference 0.18 logMAR) and halved perforation/keratoplasty odds (OR 0.42) — in Fusarium the perforation OR was 0.06, in non-Fusarium 1.08
cards.people: 323 patients enrolled (940 screened) with smear-positive filamentous fungal corneal ulcers and visual acuity 20/40 to 20/400, randomised double-masked to topical voriconazole 1% or natamycin 5% hourly while awake until re-epithelialisation, then four times daily for at least 3 weeks. Causative organisms: Fusarium 128 (40%), Aspergillus 54 (17%), other filamentous fungi 141 (43%).
cards.result: Natamycin-treated cases had significantly better 3-month best spectacle-corrected visual acuity (regression coefficient 0.18 logMAR, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.30 in the direction favouring natamycin as reported; P=.006) and were less likely to have corneal perforation or require therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty (odds ratio 0.42, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.80; P=.009). In Fusarium cases natamycin was clearly better (acuity coefficient 0.41 logMAR, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.61; P<.001; perforation odds ratio 0.06, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.28; P<.001), while non-Fusarium cases fared similarly on both drugs (acuity coefficient 0.02 logMAR, 95% CI −0.17 to 0.13 as reported; P=.81; perforation odds ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.48 to 2.43; P=.86). The authors conclude voriconazole should not be used as monotherapy in filamentous keratitis.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, conducted where Fusarium predominates — the organism mix (40% Fusarium) drives the headline result, so settings where Aspergillus or other fungi dominate should expect a smaller natamycin advantage. Smear-positive filamentous ulcers only; yeast keratitis is a different question.
cards.source: Prajna NV et al. The mycotic ulcer treatment trial: a randomized trial comparing natamycin vs voriconazole. JAMA Ophthalmology. 2013. PMID: 23710492. Registry ID: NCT00996736. cards.headline: Retamal 2018: systematic summary of three randomised trials concluded natamycin probably gives better visual acuity and prevents perforation/keratoplasty versus voriconazole
cards.summary: Retamal 2018: systematic summary of three randomised trials concluded natamycin probably gives better visual acuity and prevents perforation/keratoplasty versus voriconazole
cards.people: A systematic review (Epistemonikos-based, with re-analysis of primary studies, meta-analysis and GRADE summary of findings) that identified three systematic reviews including three randomised trials overall comparing natamycin with voriconazole for fungal keratitis.
cards.result: The reviewers concluded that natamycin probably is associated with better visual acuity after infection, and that it prevents corneal perforation and/or the need to perform therapeutic keratoplasty compared with voriconazole in fungal keratitis. No pooled numeric estimate is given in the record's abstract; the direction and the GRADE-qualified wording ('probably') are what the record supports.
cards.watchOut: The review rests on the same small trial base dominated by MUTT I — it confirms rather than independently extends the evidence, and its abstract reports conclusions without pooled numbers, so it cannot sharpen the size of the effect.

cards.summary: Synthesis: natamycin first for filamentous keratitis — a large advantage in Fusarium, no measurable advantage in non-Fusarium disease
cards.people: One phase 3 trial of 323 patients (MUTT I) plus a systematic summary of three randomised trials — the randomised record for natamycin versus voriconazole in fungal keratitis.
cards.result: Overall: better 3-month acuity with natamycin (0.18 logMAR) and lower perforation/keratoplasty odds (OR 0.42). By organism: Fusarium acuity difference 0.41 logMAR and perforation OR 0.06; non-Fusarium acuity difference 0.02 logMAR and perforation OR 1.08. PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit is organism-dependent.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the overall result as if it applied evenly: a clinician facing culture-proven non-Fusarium keratitis has no trial evidence here that natamycin outperforms voriconazole, and combination or organism-directed therapy questions are outside this shelf. Tier C is set because the evidence is essentially one trial.

shelves.title: Six months of valganciclovir for symptomatic congenital CMV: no hearing gain at 6 months, but better hearing and language by age two
shelves.question: In neonates with symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus disease, does 6 months of oral valganciclovir improve hearing and developmental outcomes versus 6 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents/administration & dosage+adverse effects · Audiometry · Child Development · Cytomegalovirus Infections/complications+congenital+drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Evoked Potentials, Auditory, Brain Stem · Ganciclovir/administration & dosage+adverse effects+analogs & derivatives · Gestational Age · Hearing Loss, Sensorineural/prevention & control+virology · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Neutropenia/chemically induced · Valganciclovir
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised trial (Kimberlin DW et al., PMID: 25738669) is a study in two halves: on its primary endpoint, best-ear hearing at 6 months, six months of valganciclovir did not beat six weeks (P=0.41). The benefit appeared later and on broader measures — total-ear hearing more often improved or stayed normal at 12 months (73% vs 57%) and 24 months (77% vs 64%), with better language-composite and receptive-communication scores at 24 months. A systematic review of (val)ganciclovir and hearing in congenital CMV (De Cuyper E et al., PMID: 35072277) supports treatment of symptomatic children with hearing loss, while stressing the lack of randomised evidence for asymptomatic or isolated-hearing-loss presentations. Grade 3 or 4 neutropenia affected about one in five infants in the first 6 weeks in both arms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): longer treatment modestly improves longer-term hearing and developmental outcomes in symptomatic congenital CMV, at the price of months of drug exposure and monitoring.

cards.headline: Kimberlin 2015: 6 months of valganciclovir did not improve best-ear hearing at 6 months (P=0.41), but total-ear hearing was better at 12 months (73% vs 57%) and 24 months (77% vs 64%), with better language scores
cards.summary: Kimberlin 2015: 6 months of valganciclovir did not improve best-ear hearing at 6 months (P=0.41), but total-ear hearing was better at 12 months (73% vs 57%) and 24 months (77% vs 64%), with better language scores
cards.people: 96 neonates with symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus disease randomised to oral valganciclovir for 6 months versus 6 weeks (followed by placebo); 86 had evaluable follow-up data at 6 months. Endpoints were adjusted for central nervous system involvement at baseline.
cards.result: Best-ear hearing at 6 months was similar (improvement in 2 participants in the 6-month group and 3 in the 6-week group; no change in 36 and 37; worsening in 5 and 3; P=0.41). Total-ear hearing was more likely to be improved or remain normal at 12 months in the 6-month group (73% vs 57%, P=0.01) and at 24 months (77% vs 64%, P=0.04). At 24 months the 6-month group had better Bayley-III language-composite (P=0.004) and receptive-communication (P=0.003) scores. Grade 3 or 4 neutropenia occurred in 19% during the first 6 weeks; during the next 4.5 months it occurred in 21% of the 6-month group and 27% of the 6-week group (P=0.64).
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint was null — the positive findings are secondary, longer-term endpoints in a 96-infant trial, so they are hypothesis-strengthening rather than definitive. Symptomatic congenital CMV only; this trial says nothing about treating asymptomatic infants.
cards.source: Kimberlin DW et al. Valganciclovir for symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2015. PMID: 25738669. Registry ID: NCT00466817. cards.headline: De Cuyper 2022: systematic review of 18 studies (682 treated children) — treated symptomatic children had more hearing improvement (Peto OR 7.72) and less deterioration (Peto OR 0.23) than untreated children
cards.summary: De Cuyper 2022: systematic review of 18 studies (682 treated children) — treated symptomatic children had more hearing improvement (Peto OR 7.72) and less deterioration (Peto OR 0.23) than untreated children
cards.people: Systematic review (PRISMA) of studies providing ear-specific hearing results after (val)ganciclovir treatment of children with congenital CMV-related hearing loss; 18 studies with 682 treated patients, with a Peto odds-ratio meta-analysis against untreated children.
cards.result: Treating symptomatic children with hearing loss resulted in more hearing improvement (Peto OR 7.72, 95% CI 3.08 to 19.34) and less hearing deterioration (Peto OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.57). Against untreated-group rates of 9.4% improvement and 28.2% deterioration, treated-group rates were 44.5% and 6.3% respectively. The reviewers found sufficient evidence to support treatment of symptomatic congenital CMV with hearing loss, but insufficient evidence for isolated hearing loss, late-onset hearing loss, or asymptomatic infection, and called for prospective randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: Mostly non-randomised comparisons — treated-versus-untreated contrasts in observational cohorts are vulnerable to confounding by severity and era, so the large odds ratios should be read as supportive, not as the effect size a trial would find.
cards.source: De Cuyper E et al. The Effect of (Val)ganciclovir on Hearing in Congenital Cytomegalovirus: A Systematic Review. The Laryngoscope. 2022. PMID: 35072277. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Synthesis: treat symptomatic congenital CMV for 6 months — no short-term hearing gain, modest longer-term hearing and language gains, neutropenia in about one in five
cards.people: One randomised duration trial (96 neonates) plus a systematic review of 18 studies (682 treated children) — the evidence for valganciclovir duration and hearing in symptomatic congenital CMV.
cards.result: Duration: 6 months vs 6 weeks — best-ear hearing at 6 months null (P=0.41); total-ear hearing improved/normal 73% vs 57% at 12 months and 77% vs 64% at 24 months; language scores better at 24 months. cards.watchOut: Families should be counselled on the actual shape of this result: the trial did not show better hearing at 6 months, and the longer-term gains, while consistent across hearing and language, come from secondary endpoints. Tier C is set because the duration evidence is a single trial.

shelves.title: Ceftriaxone for neurosyphilis: similar responses and shorter hospital stay in a French cohort — but no real trial has ever tested it against penicillin
shelves.question: In neurosyphilis, is ceftriaxone as effective as benzylpenicillin for clinical and serological outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Ceftriaxone/therapeutic use · Female · France · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neurosyphilis/drug therapy · Penicillin G/therapeutic use · Retrospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — there is no adequate randomised comparison. The largest dataset is a French retrospective multicentre cohort (Bettuzzi T et al., PMID: 34051142) in which overall clinical response at one month was higher with ceftriaxone than benzylpenicillin in crude and propensity-weighted analyses, serological response at 6 months did not differ, and hospital stay was shorter with ceftriaxone — but only 42 of 208 patients received ceftriaxone, and confounding by who gets which drug is exactly what a retrospective design cannot remove. The Cochrane review (Buitrago-Garcia D et al., PMID: 31132142) found a single trial of 36 participants, graded very low quality, with inconclusive serological and clinical cure results. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): ceftriaxone is a plausible alternative where benzylpenicillin is impractical, but equivalence has not been shown by a design that can show it.

cards.headline: Bettuzzi 2021: retrospective cohort — overall clinical response 98% with ceftriaxone versus 76% with benzylpenicillin, serological response similar (88% vs 82%), hospital stay shorter with ceftriaxone
cards.summary: Bettuzzi 2021: retrospective cohort — overall clinical response 98% with ceftriaxone versus 76% with benzylpenicillin, serological response similar (88% vs 82%), hospital stay shorter with ceftriaxone
cards.people: 208 patients with neurosyphilis treated at eight French tertiary centres, 1997–2017 (42 ceftriaxone, 166 benzylpenicillin); mean age 44.4 years, 93% men. Neurosyphilis required positive treponemal and non-treponemal tests plus otic/ocular syphilis, neurological symptoms with positive CSF-VDRL or CSF-PCR, or CSF leukocytes above five. Primary outcome was overall (complete or partial) clinical response one month after treatment initiation.
cards.result: Overall clinical response occurred in 41 (98%) ceftriaxone patients versus 125 (76%) benzylpenicillin patients (crude odds ratio 13.02, 95% CI 1.73 to 97.66; p=0.017), remaining different after propensity score weighting (OR 1.22, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.33; p<0.0001, as reported). Complete response was 52% versus 33% crude (OR 2.26, 95% CI 1.12 to 4.41) but not significant after weighting (OR 1.08, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.24; p=0.269). Serological response at 6 months did not differ (21 [88%] of 24 vs 76 [82%] of 93; crude OR 1.56, 95% CI 0.42 to 5.86; p=0.50). Hospital stay was significantly shorter in the ceftriaxone group (p<0.0001). No major adverse effects were reported in either group.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and heavily unbalanced (42 vs 166) — clinicians chose the drug, so ceftriaxone patients may have differed systematically, and the very wide crude confidence interval (1.73 to 97.66) shows how fragile the headline contrast is. The propensity-weighted odds ratio is reported on a different scale and should not be compared directly with the crude figure.
cards.source: Bettuzzi T et al. Ceftriaxone compared with benzylpenicillin in the treatment of neurosyphilis in France: a retrospective multicentre study. The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 2021. PMID: 34051142. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Buitrago-Garcia 2019 (Cochrane): the entire randomised record is one 36-person trial — serological cure 16% versus 11%, clinical cure 44% versus 18%, both inconclusive, very low quality
cards.summary: Buitrago-Garcia 2019 (Cochrane): the entire randomised record is one 36-person trial — serological cure 16% versus 11%, clinical cure 44% versus 18%, both inconclusive, very low quality
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised trials of any antibiotic regimen versus any other for adults with neurosyphilis (including people with HIV), searching to April 2019. One trial was identified, with 36 participants with syphilis and HIV (mainly men, median age 34), comparing ceftriaxone 2 g daily for 10 days (18 participants) with penicillin G 4 million units intravenously every 4 hours for 10 days (18 participants).
cards.result: Serological cure: 3 of 18 (16%) with ceftriaxone versus 2 of 18 (11%) with penicillin G (risk ratio 1.50, 95% CI 0.28 to 7.93; very low-quality evidence). Clinical cure: 8 of 18 (44%) versus 2 of 18 (18%) (RR 4.00, 95% CI 0.98 to 16.30; very low-quality evidence). The reviewers judged the results incomplete and inconclusive — insufficient to determine whether any difference exists between ceftriaxone and penicillin G. The trial was funded by a pharmaceutical company.
cards.watchOut: A 36-person trial cannot settle equivalence for an uncommon, slowly evolving disease — its confidence intervals span from substantial harm to large benefit on both cure measures. Absence of randomised evidence is not evidence that the drugs differ, either.
cards.source: Buitrago-Garcia D et al. Antibiotic therapy for adults with neurosyphilis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019. PMID: 31132142. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ceftriaxone looks at least comparable in observational data and shortens hospital stay, but no study capable of proving equivalence exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: ceftriaxone looks at least comparable in observational data and shortens hospital stay, but no study capable of proving equivalence exists
cards.people: One retrospective cohort of 208 patients and one 36-person randomised trial (Cochrane 2019) — the entire comparative record for ceftriaxone versus benzylpenicillin in neurosyphilis.
cards.result: Clinical response at 1 month favoured ceftriaxone in the cohort (98% vs 76% crude); complete response and serological response did not differ after adjustment/weighting or in the trial; hospital stay was shorter with ceftriaxone. Randomised cure estimates: serological RR 1.50 (0.28–7.93), clinical RR 4.00 (0.98–16.30), very low quality. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Benzylpenicillin remains the reference treatment on guideline and historical grounds that this shelf does not re-litigate; the honest claim for ceftriaxone is practical (once-daily, shorter stay) with no demonstrated inferiority in weak data — not proven equivalence. Tier C is set because the best evidence is observational.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — thalidomide works for erythema nodosum leprosum, and the dose question is about tapering, not just the starting dose. In the double-blind dose-comparison trial (Villahermosa LG et al., PMID: 15891124; 22 men), a 300 mg starting dose and a 100 mg starting dose produced comparable improvement by day 7 (7 of 10 versus 12 of 12 improved; P=0.08), but the slower taper from the higher dose showed significantly less re-emergence of ENL through week 7 (P=0.02) — while most patients in both groups developed new lesions soon after treatment stopped. The Cochrane review of ENL interventions (Van Veen NH et al., PMID: 19588412) found thalidomide significantly increased remission of skin lesions versus aspirin (RR 2.43) in one 92-participant trial, and that mild-to-moderate adverse events were significantly fewer at 100 mg than 300 mg daily (RR 0.46). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): thalidomide controls ENL; a higher start with a slow taper holds the reaction longer, at the cost of more adverse events, and relapse after stopping is the rule.

cards.headline: Villahermosa 2005: dose comparison in 22 men — day-7 improvement comparable (12/12 on 100 mg start vs 7/10 on 300 mg start), but slower taper from 300 mg gave less ENL re-emergence through week 7 (P=0.02)
cards.summary: Villahermosa 2005: dose comparison in 22 men — day-7 improvement comparable (12/12 on 100 mg start vs 7/10 on 300 mg start), but slower taper from 300 mg gave less ENL re-emergence through week 7 (P=0.02)
cards.people: 22 men with erythema nodosum leprosum in a randomised, double-blind, double-dummy trial: group A (12) received 100 mg thalidomide daily for one week, then 50 mg/day in weeks 2–3, then dummy capsules in weeks 4–7; group B (10) received 300 mg daily for one week, then a six-week taper of four capsules daily with gradual decrements every two weeks.
cards.result: Both regimens caused comparable improvement in 19 patients at day 7 (group A 12 of 12 versus group B 7 of 10; P=0.08), but slower tapering in group B showed less re-emergence of ENL through week 7 (P=0.02 versus group A). Most patients developed new lesions soon after stopping treatment. The authors conclude slower tapering from a higher initial dose may improve clinical ENL responses, but high recurrence after discontinuation means better tapering regimens still need to be identified.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-two men, one week of full-dose treatment, and a taper comparison confounded by design — the higher-dose group also tapered more slowly, so dose and taper speed cannot be separated. Men only: thalidomide's teratogenicity shapes who can receive it at all, a constraint this trial's population hides.
cards.source: Villahermosa LG et al. A randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, controlled dose comparison of thalidomide for treatment of erythema nodosum leprosum. The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. 2005. PMID: 15891124. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Van Veen 2009 (Cochrane): thalidomide beat aspirin for skin-lesion remission (RR 2.43, 92 participants); adverse events fewer at 100 mg than 300 mg (RR 0.46) — but the 13 ENL trials were generally poor quality
cards.summary: Van Veen 2009 (Cochrane): thalidomide beat aspirin for skin-lesion remission (RR 2.43, 92 participants); adverse events fewer at 100 mg than 300 mg (RR 0.46) — but the 13 ENL trials were generally poor quality
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised trials of interventions for erythema nodosum leprosum in people with leprosy: 13 studies, 445 participants, generally poor quality, with no pooling possible because treatments were heterogeneous.
cards.result: Thalidomide showed a significant remission of skin lesions compared with aspirin (risk ratio 2.43, 95% CI 1.28 to 4.59; 1 trial, 92 participants). Clofazimine was superior to prednisolone for treatment successes (RR 3.67, 95% CI 1.36 to 9.91; 1 trial, 24 participants) and to thalidomide for fewer recurrences (RR 0.08, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.56; 1 trial, 72 participants). Mild-to-moderate adverse events were significantly lower with 100 mg thalidomide than 300 mg daily (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.93), while minor adverse events were more frequent with clofazimine than prednisolone (RR 1.92, 95% CI 1.10 to 3.35). No significant benefit was found for several other interventions, and no study assessed quality of life or economic outcomes. The reviewers found some evidence of benefit for thalidomide and clofazimine but no clear evidence overall, and called for larger, better trials.
cards.watchOut: Every positive contrast in this review rests on a single small trial, and the clofazimine-versus-thalidomide recurrence result cuts against any simple 'thalidomide is best' reading — thalidomide's edge is speed of remission, not durability.
cards.source: Van Veen NH et al. Interventions for erythema nodosum leprosum. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2009. PMID: 19588412. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: thalidomide switches ENL off reliably and quickly; keeping it off after the taper ends is the unsolved problem
cards.summary: Synthesis: thalidomide switches ENL off reliably and quickly; keeping it off after the taper ends is the unsolved problem
cards.people: One 22-patient dose-comparison trial plus a Cochrane review of 13 trials (445 participants) — the evidence for thalidomide in erythema nodosum leprosum.
cards.result: Remission vs aspirin RR 2.43; day-7 improvement comparable between 100 mg and 300 mg starts; slower taper from 300 mg reduced re-emergence through week 7 (P=0.02); adverse events lower at 100 mg (RR 0.46); relapse after stopping was common in both arms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Thalidomide is teratogenic and its use is tightly restricted in many settings — efficacy here does not translate into availability, and this shelf's all-male trial evidence cannot speak to use in women of childbearing potential. Tier C is set because the dose evidence is a single 22-patient trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Villahermosa LG et al. The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. 2005 (PMID: 15891124); Van Veen NH et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2009 (PMID: 19588412).

shelves.title: Decolonising nasal S. aureus carriers: hospital S. aureus infection 3.4% versus 7.7% with mupirocin–chlorhexidine after rapid screening — the benefit lives in carriers, not in everyone
shelves.question: In hospital patients who carry Staphylococcus aureus in the nose, does screening plus mupirocin–chlorhexidine decolonisation prevent hospital-acquired S. aureus infection, including surgical-site infection?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Anti-Infective Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Carrier State/drug therapy · Cause of Death · Chlorhexidine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Cross Infection/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Length of Stay · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Mupirocin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Nasal Cavity/microbiology · Ointments · Polymerase Chain Reaction · Skin/microbiology · Soaps/therapeutic use · Staphylococcal Infections/prevention & control · Staphylococcus aureus/genetics/isolation & purification · Surgical Wound Infection/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials converge on the same point: the benefit is in confirmed carriers. In Bode (Bode LG et al., PMID: 20054045), carriers identified by rapid PCR screening and treated with mupirocin nasal ointment plus chlorhexidine soap had a hospital S. aureus infection rate of 3.4% (17/504) versus 7.7% (32/413) on placebo — a relative risk of 0.42 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.75), a 58% relative reduction with the absolute rates printed alongside — and the effect was strongest for deep surgical-site infections (relative risk 0.21, 0.07 to 0.62). In Perl (Perl TM et al., PMID: 12063371), intranasal mupirocin given to all-comers did not reduce S. aureus surgical-site infection overall (2.3% versus 2.4%), but among the 891 confirmed nasal carriers, nosocomial S. aureus infections fell from 7.7% to 4.0% (odds ratio 0.49, 0.25 to 0.92). Neither trial showed a mortality difference, and Bode's strains were all methicillin- and mupirocin-susceptible — a condition that cannot be assumed where resistance is common. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): screen-and-decolonise works for carriers; blanket mupirocin for unscreened surgical patients does not, on this record.

cards.headline: Bode 2010: S. aureus infection 3.4% (17/504) versus 7.7% (32/413) — relative risk 0.42; deep surgical-site infection relative risk 0.21
cards.summary: Bode 2010: S. aureus infection 3.4% (17/504) versus 7.7% (32/413) — relative risk 0.42; deep surgical-site infection relative risk 0.21
cards.people: Hospital patients screened on admission by real-time PCR for nasal S. aureus carriage: 6,771 screened, 1,251 patients positive, 917 carriers in the intention-to-treat analysis, of whom 808 (88.1%) underwent surgery. Carriers received mupirocin nasal ointment plus chlorhexidine soap or placebo. All identified strains were susceptible to methicillin and mupirocin.
cards.result: The rate of hospital S. aureus infection was 3.4% (17 of 504) in the mupirocin–chlorhexidine group versus 7.7% (32 of 413) in the placebo group — relative risk 0.42 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.75), i.e. a 58% relative reduction with absolute rates of 3.4% and 7.7% alongside. The effect was most pronounced for deep surgical-site infections (relative risk 0.21, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.62). All-cause in-hospital mortality did not differ significantly, and time to onset of nosocomial infection was shorter in the placebo group (p=0.005).
cards.watchOut: The strategy needs the whole chain — rapid screening, a susceptible organism, and treatment completed before the operation — and the trial's ecology (universal methicillin and mupirocin susceptibility) flatters it. Widespread mupirocin use selects for resistance, which a single trial in a low-resistance setting cannot price in.
cards.source: Bode LG et al. Preventing surgical-site infections in nasal carriers of Staphylococcus aureus. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20054045. Registry ID: ISRCTN56186788. cards.headline: Perl 2002: no overall benefit of mupirocin for all surgical patients (2.3% versus 2.4%) — but among nasal carriers, nosocomial S. aureus infection 4.0% versus 7.7% (odds ratio 0.49)
cards.summary: Perl 2002: no overall benefit of mupirocin for all surgical patients (2.3% versus 2.4%) — but among nasal carriers, nosocomial S. aureus infection 4.0% versus 7.7% (odds ratio 0.49)
cards.people: 4,030 patients undergoing general, gynaecologic, neurologic or cardiothoracic surgery were enrolled and 3,864 analysed, receiving intranasal mupirocin or placebo regardless of carriage status; 891 (23.1%) were nasal carriers of S. aureus (444 mupirocin, 447 placebo).
cards.result: Overall, S. aureus surgical-site infection occurred in 2.3% of mupirocin recipients and 2.4% of placebo recipients — not significantly different. Among confirmed nasal carriers, nosocomial S. aureus infections occurred in 4.0% on mupirocin versus 7.7% on placebo (odds ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.92; p=0.02), with the absolute rates printed alongside.
cards.watchOut: The carrier result is a subgroup of an overall-null trial — exactly the pattern that can mislead — though here the subgroup is the biologically pre-specified target (the drug can only help patients who carry the organism) and Bode's screening-based trial later confirmed it prospectively. Mupirocin alone, without chlorhexidine body washing, is also a weaker intervention than Bode's bundle.
cards.source: Perl TM et al. Intranasal mupirocin to prevent postoperative Staphylococcus aureus infections. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2002. PMID: 12063371. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: treat the carrier, not the crowd — screening-targeted decolonisation halves S. aureus infection; blanket prophylaxis does not
cards.summary: Synthesis: treat the carrier, not the crowd — screening-targeted decolonisation halves S. aureus infection; blanket prophylaxis does not
cards.people: Two randomised placebo-controlled trials: a screening-based decolonisation bundle in 917 confirmed carriers (Bode 2010) and intranasal mupirocin in 3,864 unselected surgical patients including 891 carriers (Perl 2002).
cards.result: In carriers: hospital S. aureus infection 3.4% versus 7.7% (relative risk 0.42) with the bundle; nosocomial S. aureus infection 4.0% versus 7.7% (odds ratio 0.49) with mupirocin alone. In unselected patients: surgical-site infection 2.3% versus 2.4%, no benefit. Mortality: no difference in either trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate current resistance patterns, neither tests universal decolonisation without screening, and neither measures the population-level cost of mupirocin resistance that routine use can generate. The evidence supports a targeted programme in settings where susceptibility holds — not an assumption that it holds everywhere. Tier C is not set: two randomised trials agree.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bode LG et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2010 (PMID: 20054045); Perl TM et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2002 (PMID: 12063371).

shelves.title: Mailed FIT outreach in underserved care: screening in 40.7% versus 12.1% on usual care at one year — and colonoscopy outreach wins the three-year process while FIT wins the single test
shelves.question: In underserved primary-care populations, does mailed FIT outreach with reminders increase colorectal cancer screening completion versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Colonoscopy/methods · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnosis · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Immunohistochemistry · Male · Mass Screening/methods · Medically Underserved Area · Middle Aged · Occult Blood · Patient Compliance · Reproducibility of Results · Retrospective Studies
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two large pragmatic trials in safety-net systems agree that mailing the test beats waiting for a clinic visit. In the first, screening participation within a year was 40.7% with mailed FIT outreach versus 12.1% with usual care (colonoscopy outreach reached 24.6%) (Gupta S et al., PMID: 23921906). In the second, completion of the full three-year screening process was 28.0% with FIT outreach and 38.4% with colonoscopy outreach versus 10.7% with usual care — FIT outreach's absolute advantage over usual care was 17.3 percentage points (95% CI 14.8 to 19.8) (Singal AG et al., PMID: 28873161). The honest nuance is inside the second trial: a mailed colonoscopy invitation completed the multi-year process more often than repeated FIT, even though FIT wins any single round. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): mailed FIT outreach roughly triples screening completion versus usual care in underserved populations, on two concordant randomised trials — not Tier C.

cards.headline: Gupta 2013: one-year screening participation 40.7% with FIT outreach versus 24.6% with colonoscopy outreach and 12.1% with usual care (P<0.001)
cards.summary: Gupta 2013: one-year screening participation 40.7% with FIT outreach versus 24.6% with colonoscopy outreach and 12.1% with usual care (P<0.001)
cards.people: Uninsured patients aged 54–64 not up to date with colorectal screening in the John Peter Smith Health Network, a Texas safety-net system: 1,593 assigned to mailed FIT outreach (invitation plus enclosed no-cost FIT), 479 to mailed colonoscopy outreach, and 3,898 to usual care (opportunistic visit-based screening); outreach groups also received telephone follow-up. Mean age 59 years; 64% women; 41% white, 24% black, 29% Hispanic.
cards.result: Screening participation within one year was 40.7% for FIT outreach and 24.6% for colonoscopy outreach versus 12.1% for usual care (P<0.001 for both comparisons with usual care), and FIT outreach beat colonoscopy outreach (P<0.001), consistently across white, black and Hispanic subgroups. Colorectal cancer identification was 0.4% (FIT), 0.4% (colonoscopy) and 0.2% (usual care); advanced adenoma detection 0.8%, 1.3% and 0.4%. Eleven of 60 patients with abnormal FIT results did not complete colonoscopy. Registry ID: NCT01191411.
cards.watchOut: One safety-net system and a one-year horizon: a single FIT round is the easiest version of screening to complete, and the 11 of 60 abnormal results without completed colonoscopy show where the pathway leaks. Effects in insured, already-engaged populations will be smaller because usual-care completion starts higher.
cards.source: Gupta S et al. cards.headline: Singal 2017: three-year screening-process completion 38.4% colonoscopy outreach, 28.0% FIT outreach, 10.7% usual care — FIT's absolute gain over usual care 17.3 points (95% CI 14.8–19.8)
cards.summary: Singal 2017: three-year screening-process completion 38.4% colonoscopy outreach, 28.0% FIT outreach, 10.7% usual care — FIT's absolute gain over usual care 17.3 points (95% CI 14.8–19.8)
cards.people: 5,999 participants aged 50–64 receiving primary care in the Parkland Health and Hospital System safety-net institution and not up to date with screening (median age 56; 61.9% women): 2,400 assigned to mailed FIT outreach (with repeat annual testing processes), 2,400 to mailed colonoscopy outreach, and 1,199 to usual clinic-based care, followed from 2013 to 2016.
cards.result: Screening-process completion within three years (colonoscopy completed, or annual FIT adherence after a normal result, or diagnostic colonoscopy after an abnormal result, or treatment evaluation if cancer was found) was 38.4% for colonoscopy outreach, 28.0% for FIT outreach and 10.7% for usual care. Absolute differences versus usual care were 27.7 points (95% CI 25.1 to 30.4) for colonoscopy outreach and 17.3 points (95% CI 14.8 to 19.8) for FIT outreach (P<0.001 for all comparisons). Adenoma and advanced-neoplasia detection differences versus usual care were larger for colonoscopy outreach (10.3% and 3.1%) than for FIT outreach (1.3% and 0.7%, the latter two not significant). There were no screening-related harms in any group. Registry ID: NCT01710215.
cards.watchOut: Over three years the ranking flips: colonoscopy outreach completes the process more often because a single colonoscopy discharges the obligation, while FIT demands annual repetition. A programme choosing FIT outreach is choosing the better first round and the harder long game — both facts are in this trial.
cards.source: Singal AG et al. Effect of Colonoscopy Outreach vs Fecal Immunochemical Test Outreach on Colorectal Cancer Screening Completion: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 28873161. cards.headline: Synthesis: mailing the kit is one of the most reliable screening interventions ever trialled — the open question is sustaining it
cards.summary: Synthesis: mailing the kit is one of the most reliable screening interventions ever trialled — the open question is sustaining it
cards.people: Two pragmatic randomised trials in US safety-net systems, 5,970 and 5,999 participants respectively, comparing mailed FIT outreach (with telephone follow-up processes) against usual care, with colonoscopy outreach as a third arm in both.
cards.result: Versus usual care: one-year participation 40.7% versus 12.1%; three-year process completion 28.0% versus 10.7% (absolute gain 17.3 points). Colonoscopy outreach: 24.6% at one year but 38.4% process completion at three years. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), not Tier C: two large concordant randomised trials carry the claim.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are US safety-net systems with very low usual-care baselines (about 11–12%); the relative gain is transportable, the absolute gain is not. Neither trial reports a mortality endpoint — screening completion is the outcome, and its link to cancer death runs through the screening tests themselves.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gupta S et al. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2013 (PMID: 23921906); Singal AG et al. JAMA. 2017 (PMID: 28873161).

shelves.title: Patient navigation after an abnormal screening test: resolution came faster in the randomised trial, and the multisite programme's benefit appeared after day 90 (adjusted HR 1.51 for resolution by one year)
shelves.question: After an abnormal cancer screening test, does patient navigation shorten time to diagnostic resolution versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Breast Neoplasms/diagnosis · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnosis · Early Detection of Cancer · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Navigation · Prostatic Neoplasms/diagnosis · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — navigation speeds resolution, but the benefit is delayed and uneven across abnormality types. In the individually randomised Denver trial, time to diagnostic resolution was significantly shorter with lay patient navigation across breast, colorectal and prostate abnormalities combined (stratified log-rank P<0.001), with clear gains for mammographic BI-RADS 3 (P=0.0003) and colorectal abnormalities (P=0.0017) but not for BI-RADS 4/5 or abnormal clinical breast examinations (Raich PC et al., PMID: 23045537). The multisite Patient Navigation Research Program's pooled analysis of 10,521 participants found no benefit in the first 90 days, then a benefit from day 91 to 365 for both diagnostic resolution (adjusted hazard ratio 1.51, 95% CI 1.23 to 1.84) and treatment initiation (adjusted HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.86), largest in centres whose usual-care delays were greatest (Freund KM et al., PMID: 24938303). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): navigation shortens time to resolution mainly for the patients usual care is slowest to resolve — Tier C, because the pooled effect is a modest hazard ratio assembled across heterogeneous centres.

cards.headline: Raich 2012 randomised trial: time to resolution significantly shorter with navigation (P<0.001) — driven by BI-RADS 3 (P=0.0003) and colorectal (P=0.0017), not by BI-RADS 4/5
cards.summary: Raich 2012 randomised trial: time to resolution significantly shorter with navigation (P<0.001) — driven by BI-RADS 3 (P=0.0003) and colorectal (P=0.0017), not by BI-RADS 4/5
cards.people: 993 eligible patients with abnormal screening tests at Denver Health, a safety-net system (one of ten Patient Navigation Research Program sites), randomised to lay patient navigation or no navigation: 628 with abnormal breast screens (66 abnormal clinical examinations, 304 BI-RADS 0, 200 BI-RADS 3, 58 BI-RADS 4 or 5), 235 colorectal and 130 prostate. Participants were 72% minority, 49% with household income under $10,000, and 36% uninsured.
cards.result: Time to diagnostic resolution was significantly shorter in the navigated group (stratified log-rank test, P<0.001). By abnormality: navigation improved resolution for mammographic BI-RADS 3 (P=0.0003) and BI-RADS 0 (P=0.09), but not for BI-RADS 4/5 or abnormal breast examinations; it shortened time for colorectal resolution (P=0.0017) and prostate resolution (P=0.06). The abstract reports significance levels rather than median days gained — a declared gap in the record.
cards.watchOut: The abnormalities where navigation did not help (BI-RADS 4/5, abnormal examinations) are the ones usual care already fast-tracks because cancer is likely; navigation's value concentrates in the ambiguous middle, where patients are most easily lost. Single-site, lay-navigator model.
cards.source: Raich PC et al. Patient navigation improves cancer diagnostic resolution: an individually randomized clinical trial in an underserved population. Cancer Epidemiology, Biomarkers & Prevention. 2012. PMID: 23045537. cards.headline: Freund 2014 (Patient Navigation Research Program): no benefit in the first 90 days, then resolution adjusted HR 1.51 (95% CI 1.23–1.84) and treatment initiation HR 1.43 from day 91 to 365
cards.summary: Freund 2014 (Patient Navigation Research Program): no benefit in the first 90 days, then resolution adjusted HR 1.51 (95% CI 1.23–1.84) and treatment initiation HR 1.43 from day 91 to 365
cards.type: Multisite programme meta-analysis of controlled trials (Freund 2014)
cards.people: 10,521 participants with abnormal screening tests and 2,105 with a cancer or precancer diagnosis across the US Patient Navigation Research Program (2007–2010), covering breast, cervical, colorectal and prostate abnormalities; 73% from racial/ethnic minority groups, 40% publicly insured and 31% uninsured.
cards.result: There was no benefit during the first 90 days of care. From 91 to 365 days, navigation improved diagnostic resolution (adjusted hazard ratio 1.51, 95% CI 1.23 to 1.84; P<0.001) and initiation of cancer therapy (adjusted HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.86; P<0.007). Metaregression showed navigation's greatest benefits in the centres with the greatest delays under usual care.
cards.watchOut: A pooled programme analysis, not a single randomised trial, with centre-level heterogeneity as a headline finding: in a well-functioning system with short usual-care delays, this record predicts little or no gain. The 90-day null also means navigation is not an emergency accelerator — it is a rescue for the stalled.
cards.source: Freund KM et al. Impact of patient navigation on timely cancer care: the Patient Navigation Research Program. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2014. PMID: 24938303. cards.headline: Synthesis: navigation works where usual care stalls — after 90 days, and for ambiguous abnormalities
cards.summary: Synthesis: navigation works where usual care stalls — after 90 days, and for ambiguous abnormalities
cards.people: One individually randomised trial (993 patients, single safety-net system) and one multisite programme analysis (10,521 participants with screening abnormalities) of lay/professional patient navigation versus usual care.
cards.result: Randomised trial: significantly shorter time to resolution overall (P<0.001), with gains concentrated in BI-RADS 3 and colorectal abnormalities. Programme analysis: adjusted HR 1.51 for resolution and 1.43 for treatment initiation between days 91 and 365, no benefit before day 90. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the direction is consistent but the effect is conditional on a slow usual-care baseline.
cards.watchOut: Neither record reports median days saved in its abstract, so the size of the prize in days — the number a patient would ask for — cannot be stated from these records; the stamp rests on hazard ratios and significance tests.
cards.source: Synthesis of Raich PC et al. Cancer Epidemiology, Biomarkers & Prevention. 2012 (PMID: 23045537); Freund KM et al. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2014 (PMID: 24938303).
