shelves.title: A lung screening decision aid for people who smoke: 67.4% felt well prepared to decide versus 48.2% with standard information — knowledge and values clarity up, screening uptake unchanged
shelves.question: In people who smoke and are eligible for lung screening, does a patient decision aid improve knowledge and decision quality about low-dose CT screening versus standard information?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Decision Support Techniques · Early Detection of Cancer/methods/psychology · Female · Humans · Lung Neoplasms/diagnosis · Male · Mass Screening/psychology/statistics & numerical data · Middle Aged · Patient Participation/psychology/statistics & numerical data · Smokers/psychology/statistics & numerical data · Tomography, X-Ray Computed/psychology/statistics & numerical data · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for decision quality, which is what a decision aid is for; it did not change behaviour. In the randomised trial among tobacco-quitline clients eligible for lung screening, the video decision aid left 67.4% of viewers well prepared to make a screening decision versus 48.2% with standard educational material (odds ratio 2.31, 95% CI 1.56 to 3.44); 50.0% versus 28.3% felt informed (OR 2.56, 95% CI 1.72 to 3.79) and 68.0% versus 47.4% were clear about their values on the harms and benefits (OR 2.37, 95% CI 1.60 to 3.51), and the aid group was more knowledgeable at every follow-up (Volk RJ et al., PMID: 32003822). Intentions to be screened and actual screening within six months did not differ between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a decision aid measurably improves knowledge, preparedness and values clarity without steering uptake either way — a single trial, so Tier C.

cards.headline: Volk 2020: well prepared to decide in 67.4% with the decision aid versus 48.2% with standard material (OR 2.31, 95% CI 1.56–3.44); informed 50.0% versus 28.3%; uptake unchanged
cards.summary: Volk 2020: well prepared to decide in 67.4% with the decision aid versus 48.2% with standard material (OR 2.31, 95% CI 1.56–3.44); informed 50.0% versus 28.3%; uptake unchanged
cards.people: 516 current or recent clients of 13 US state tobacco quitlines who met age and smoking-history eligibility for lung cancer screening, randomised to the video decision aid 'Lung Cancer Screening: Is It Right for Me?' (n=259) or standard educational material (n=257), enrolled 2015–2016 and followed for 6 months; 71.7% were under 65, 62.0% women, 26.7% black, 9.1% uninsured.
cards.result: Well prepared to make a screening decision: 153 of 227 (67.4%) with the decision aid versus 108 of 224 (48.2%) with standard material (OR 2.31, 95% CI 1.56 to 3.44; P<0.001). Feeling informed: 117 of 234 (50.0%) versus 66 of 233 (28.3%) (OR 2.56, 95% CI 1.72 to 3.79; P<0.001). Clear about personal values on harms and benefits: 159 of 234 (68.0%) versus 110 of 232 (47.4%) (OR 2.37, 95% CI 1.60 to 3.51; P<0.001). The aid group was more knowledgeable at each follow-up assessment. Intentions to be screened and screening behaviour within 6 months did not differ between groups. Registry ID: NCT02286713.
cards.watchOut: Outcomes are self-reported decision-quality measures at one week (with knowledge to six months) in quitline clients — people already motivated enough to call a quitline. A decision aid that does not change uptake is succeeding by its own lights, but a service buying it to raise screening rates would be buying the wrong tool.
cards.source: Volk RJ et al. Effect of a Patient Decision Aid on Lung Cancer Screening Decision-Making by Persons Who Smoke: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Network Open. 2020. PMID: 32003822. Registry ID: NCT02286713. cards.people: One randomised trial of 516 screening-eligible quitline clients comparing a video decision aid with standard educational material.
cards.result: Preparation for decision-making 67.4% versus 48.2%; feeling informed 50.0% versus 28.3%; values clarity 68.0% versus 47.4%; knowledge higher at every follow-up; screening intentions and completion unchanged at 6 months. shelves.title: Paying people $24 to vaccinate against COVID-19: uptake rose 4.2 percentage points from a 71.6% baseline in an 8,286-person Swedish randomised trial — nudges moved intentions only
shelves.question: Do small monetary incentives increase COVID-19 vaccination uptake versus no incentive?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · COVID-19/prevention & control · COVID-19 Vaccines · Female · Humans · Intention · Male · Middle Aged · Records · Reimbursement, Incentive · Sweden · Vaccination/economics/methods/statistics & numerical data · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a modest payment produced a modest, real increase, verified in records rather than self-report. In the preregistered Swedish randomised trial of 8,286 participants, a guaranteed payment of 200 Swedish kronor (about US $24) increased vaccination by 4.2 percentage points from a baseline rate of 71.6% (P=0.005), with uptake measured in population-wide administrative vaccination records (Campos-Mercade P et al., PMID: 34618594). Behavioural nudges in the same trial raised stated intentions but had only small, non-significant effects on actual vaccination. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): small guaranteed payments increase vaccination uptake by a few percentage points — a single trial in a high-baseline setting, so Tier C, and the absolute gain will differ where baseline uptake differs.

cards.headline: Campos-Mercade 2021: +4.2 percentage points in vaccination from a 71.6% baseline (P=0.005) for a 200-kronor payment; nudges changed intentions, not vaccinations
cards.summary: Campos-Mercade 2021: +4.2 percentage points in vaccination from a 71.6% baseline (P=0.005) for a 200-kronor payment; nudges changed intentions, not vaccinations
cards.people: 8,286 participants in Sweden randomised to a guaranteed monetary payment of 200 Swedish kronor (US $24) for vaccinating, to behavioural-nudge conditions, or to control, with vaccination ascertained by linkage to population-wide administrative vaccination records rather than self-report.
cards.result: The monetary payment increased vaccination rates by 4.2 percentage points (P=0.005) from a baseline rate of 71.6% — that is, to roughly three-quarters of participants. Behavioural nudges increased stated intentions to vaccinate but had only small and not statistically significant impacts on vaccination rates. The authors concluded that modest monetary incentives can raise vaccination rates.
cards.watchOut: One country, one vaccine campaign, and a high baseline: at 71.6% baseline the remaining unvaccinated were the harder-to-reach, yet the absolute gain was still only 4.2 points. The record does not test larger payments, lotteries, or effects on later doses or other vaccines, and paying for vaccination remains contested on fairness grounds the trial does not address.

shelves.title: Adding the GP's name to a bowel scope reminder letter: attendance 4% versus 3% — no significant effect (adjusted OR 1.30, 95% CI 0.69–2.43) in previous non-participants
shelves.question: Does a GP-endorsed reminder letter increase uptake of bowel cancer screening among previous non-participants versus a standard reminder?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Colorectal Neoplasms · Early Detection of Cancer · Female · Humans · London · Male · Mass Screening · Reminder Systems · Sigmoidoscopy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the endorsement, at least in this unpersonalised form, did not move attendance. In the North West London randomised trial, previous non-participants who received a GP-endorsed reminder letter a year after their original bowel scope (flexible sigmoidoscopy) invitation attended in 4% of cases versus 3% with the standard reminder letter — an adjusted odds ratio of 1.30 (95% CI 0.69 to 2.43), not statistically significant (Kaushal A et al., PMID: 33022321). The authors' own reading is that the endorsement may not have been personalised enough. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): a GP endorsement added to a reminder letter did not significantly increase bowel scope attendance among previous non-participants — a single trial, so Tier C, and the null applies to this endorsement format, not to every form of GP involvement.

cards.headline: Kaushal 2020: attendance 4% with GP-endorsed reminder versus 3% with standard reminder (adjusted OR 1.30, 95% CI 0.69–2.43) — not significant
cards.summary: Kaushal 2020: attendance 4% with GP-endorsed reminder versus 3% with standard reminder (adjusted OR 1.30, 95% CI 0.69–2.43) — not significant
cards.people: 1,200 screening-eligible men and women in North West London, UK, who had not responded to their initial bowel scope screening (flexible sigmoidoscopy) invitation at least 12 months earlier, randomised 1:1 to a GP-endorsed reminder letter (n=600) or a standard reminder letter (n=600) in June–August 2019; the analysis adjusted for sex, clinical commissioning group and local deprivation.
cards.result: Those who received the GP-endorsed reminder were only slightly more likely to attend bowel scope screening than those who received the standard letter (4% versus 3%), and the difference was not statistically significant (adjusted OR 1.30, 95% CI 0.69 to 2.43). The authors concluded that adding a GP endorsement to the annual reminder letter did not have an effect on attendance, suggesting the endorsement used was not personalised enough.
cards.watchOut: Attendance was very low in both arms (3–4%) — this was a hard-to-reach population of persistent non-participants, and the screening test was one-off flexible sigmoidoscopy, not a home stool test. The trial rules out a large effect of this letter format; it does not test personalised endorsements, GP endorsement of first invitations, or endorsement in stool-test programmes.
cards.source: Kaushal A et al. Use of a GP-endorsed non-participant reminder letter to promote uptake of bowel scope screening: A randomised controlled trial in a hard-to-reach population. shelves.title: Contacting at-risk relatives directly instead of relying on the patient: cascade testing uptake 62% versus 40% in first-degree relatives in the meta-analysis — from non-randomised comparisons
shelves.question: For hereditary cancer and familial hypercholesterolaemia families, does direct contact of at-risk relatives by health services increase cascade testing uptake versus family-mediated contact?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Genetic Predisposition to Disease · Genetic Counseling · Privacy · Neoplastic Syndromes, Hereditary
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — direct contact reaches more relatives, on evidence that is comparative but not randomised. In the hereditary-cancer meta-analysis, direct relative contact by the medical team or laboratory produced genetic counselling uptake of 63% (95% CI 49 to 75) versus 35% (95% CI 24 to 48) with patient-mediated contact, and genetic testing in first-degree relatives of 62% (95% CI 49 to 73) versus 40% (95% CI 32 to 48); overall, only 48% of relatives underwent counselling and 41% testing by any route (Frey MK et al., PMID: 35960887). In familial hypercholesterolaemia, a systematic review of 24 non-comparative studies likewise found the direct strategy gave the largest yield of index cases participating in cascade testing (94%, 8 studies), while a combined strategy — letting the index case choose the contact method — produced the largest yields of relatives tested among those contacted (Leonardi-Bee J et al., PMID: 34753031). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): direct contact increases cascade uptake over family-mediated contact — Tier C, because the underlying studies are non-randomised and the reviewers themselves call for randomised confirmation.

cards.headline: Frey 2022 meta-analysis: direct contact — counselling 63% versus 35%, testing in first-degree relatives 62% versus 40%, versus patient-mediated contact
cards.summary: Frey 2022 meta-analysis: direct contact — counselling 63% versus 35%, testing in first-degree relatives 62% versus 40%, versus patient-mediated contact
cards.people: 87 studies of cascade genetic counselling and testing for hereditary cancer syndromes comparing patient-mediated (family) contact with direct contact of relatives by the medical team or testing laboratory, by telephone, letter or email.
cards.result: Among relatives in the meta-analysis, 48% (95% CI 38 to 58) underwent cascade genetic counselling and 41% (95% CI 34 to 48) cascade genetic testing overall. Direct contact produced significantly higher counselling uptake than patient-mediated contact (63%, 95% CI 49 to 75, versus 35%, 95% CI 24 to 48) and higher testing uptake in first-degree relatives (62%, 95% CI 49 to 73, versus 40%, 95% CI 32 to 48). Testing completion by direct-contact method was 61% (95% CI 51 to 70) for telephone, 48% (95% CI 37 to 59) for letters and 48% (95% CI 45 to 50) for emails.
cards.watchOut: The component studies were not randomised head-to-head trials — programmes that adopted direct contact may differ from those that did not, and the authors state the shift should be confirmed by randomised trials. Direct contact is also constrained by privacy law in many jurisdictions, which the uptake figures do not price in.
cards.source: Frey MK et al. Cascade Testing for Hereditary Cancer Syndromes: Should We Move Toward Direct Relative Contact? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2022. PMID: 35960887. MeSH: Humans · Genetic Predisposition to Disease · Genetic Counseling · Privacy · Neoplastic Syndromes, Hereditary

cards.headline: Leonardi-Bee 2021 (familial hypercholesterolaemia): direct strategy led index-case participation (94%); a combined, patient-chosen strategy led relative-testing yields (40% of those contacted)
cards.summary: Leonardi-Bee 2021 (familial hypercholesterolaemia): direct strategy led index-case participation (94%); a combined, patient-chosen strategy led relative-testing yields (40% of those contacted)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of non-comparative studies (Leonardi-Bee 2021)
cards.people: 24 non-comparative studies of cascade testing strategies in relatives of familial hypercholesterolaemia index cases: 11 used a direct strategy, 8 an indirect (family-mediated) strategy, and 5 a combination of both; searches ran to May 2020.
cards.result: The median number of new relatives with familial hypercholesterolaemia found per index case was approximately 1. The combination strategy gave the largest yields of relatives tested out of those contacted (40%, 95% CI 37 to 42; 1 study) and of relatives responding out of those contacted (54%; 1 study), while the direct strategy gave the largest yield of index cases participating in cascade testing out of those with confirmed familial hypercholesterolaemia (94%, 8 studies) compared with the other strategies (P≤0.01 for all comparisons). The authors conclude the evidence is limited, and that a combination strategy letting the index case choose the contact method appears to lead to better yields.
cards.watchOut: Non-comparative studies throughout — yields are compared across different programmes and countries, not within randomised comparisons, and the headline combination-strategy yields rest on single studies. This card corroborates the direction of the cancer meta-analysis; it does not independently prove it.
cards.source: Leonardi-Bee J et al. Effectiveness of cascade testing strategies in relatives for familial hypercholesterolemia: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Atherosclerosis. 2021. PMID: 34753031. MeSH: Cost-Benefit Analysis · Genetic Testing · Humans · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II/diagnosis/genetics · Mass Screening

cards.summary: Synthesis: direct contact roughly doubles counselling uptake over leaving it to the family — with a consent-shaped caveat
cards.people: A meta-analysis of 87 hereditary-cancer studies and a systematic review of 24 familial-hypercholesterolaemia studies, all non-randomised comparisons of contact strategies.
cards.result: Counselling uptake 63% versus 35%; first-degree-relative testing 62% versus 40%; in hypercholesterolaemia, direct contact led index-case participation (94%) while patient-chosen combined contact led relative-testing yield (40% of those contacted). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: consistent direction across two conditions, but no randomised confirmation and real privacy constraints on implementation.

shelves.title: Pay-for-performance and payment incentives in primary care: screening and process measures improve in some schemes, patient outcomes mostly do not — and cancer-screening incentives showed partial or no effects in most studies
shelves.question: Do pay-for-performance schemes in primary care improve preventive care quality and screening rates versus fee-for-service alone?
shelves.mesh: Breast Neoplasms/diagnosis · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnosis · Early Detection of Cancer/economics/statistics & numerical data · Female · General Practitioners/economics/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Motivation · Physician Incentive Plans/statistics & numerical data · Reimbursement, Incentive/statistics & numerical data · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms/diagnosis
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the reviews agree the effects are inconsistent and mostly confined to process measures. A systematic review focused on cancer screening found that most studies showed partial or no effects of financial incentives on breast and cervical screening delivery rates, with only a few positive or partial effects for colorectal screening (Mauro M et al., PMID: 31587819). A broader 2026 systematic review of randomised and cluster-randomised trials of payment and financial-incentive models in primary care (10 studies, including pay-for-performance) found that selected interventions may improve provider adherence, preventive screening, chronic-disease management and vaccination uptake, but that improvements in patient-centred clinical outcomes were less consistent, every included study carried some concerns or a high risk of bias, and certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate (Alrashed A et al., PMID: 42764853). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): pay-for-performance may lift some preventive process measures; a reliable improvement in screening rates or patient outcomes is not established — Tier C.

cards.headline: Mauro 2019: most studies showed partial or no effect of GP financial incentives on breast and cervical screening delivery; few positive or partial effects for colorectal screening
cards.summary: Mauro 2019: most studies showed partial or no effect of GP financial incentives on breast and cervical screening delivery; few positive or partial effects for colorectal screening
cards.people: 18 studies of financial incentives paid in general practice to improve delivery of breast, cervical and colorectal cancer screening programmes, identified under PRISMA guidance across Web of Science, PubMed, the Cochrane Library and Google Scholar.
cards.result: Most studies showed partial or no effects of financial incentives on breast and cervical cancer screening delivery rates. Few positive or partial effects were found for colorectal cancer screening. The authors conclude that the effects of these tools are still not clear and that ongoing monitoring of incentive programmes is critical to determining their effectiveness. The abstract reports directions of effect rather than pooled rates — a declared gap: no single effect size can be quoted for screening from this record.
cards.watchOut: A narrative systematic review without a pooled estimate, mixing scheme designs and countries. 'Partial or no effect in most studies' is the finding; it cannot distinguish a genuinely ineffective policy from well-designed schemes diluted by poorly designed ones.
cards.source: Mauro M et al. Effect of financial incentives on breast, cervical and colorectal cancer screening delivery rates: Results from a systematic literature review. Health Policy. 2019. PMID: 31587819. cards.headline: Alrashed 2026: across 10 randomised trials, selected payment models may improve preventive and process measures — patient outcomes less consistent; certainty very low to moderate; all studies at some or high risk of bias
cards.summary: Alrashed 2026: across 10 randomised trials, selected payment models may improve preventive and process measures — patient outcomes less consistent; certainty very low to moderate; all studies at some or high risk of bias
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised and cluster-randomised trials (Alrashed 2026)
cards.people: 10 studies meeting eligibility criteria for payment and financial-incentive interventions in primary healthcare, spanning pay-for-performance, performance-based financing, direct facility financing, physician financial incentives and patient-directed incentives, appraised with the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool and GRADE.
cards.result: Selected payment and financial-incentive interventions may improve provider adherence to evidence-based practice and strengthen preventive and process-of-care measures, including preventive screening, chronic disease management and vaccination uptake. Improvements in patient-centred clinical outcomes were less consistent. Methodological quality was variable — all studies showed either some concerns or a high risk of bias — and certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate. The authors call for high-quality multicentre randomised trials with longer follow-up and standardised outcomes.
cards.watchOut: This record has no MeSH terms in its PubMed record, and it pools unlike interventions (paying practices, facilities, physicians and patients are different policies). Its qualitative conclusion — 'may improve processes, outcomes inconsistent' — is the strongest statement the evidence supports, which is why the stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence).

systematic review of randomised and cluster-randomised trials (alrashed 2026) 10 studies meeting eligibility criteria for payment and financial-incentive interventions in primary healthcare, spanning pay-for-performance, performance-based financing, direct facility financing, physician financial incentives and patient-directed incentives, appraised with the cochrane risk of bias 2 tool and grade. selected payment and financial-incentive interventions may improve provider adherence to evidence-based practice and strengthen preventive and process-of-care measures, including preventive screening, chronic disease management and vaccination uptake. improvements in patient-centred clinical outcomes were less consistent. methodological quality was variable — all studies showed either some concerns or a high risk of bias — and certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate. the authors call for high-quality multicentre randomised trials with longer follow-up and standardised outcomes. this record has no mesh terms in its pubmed record, and it pools unlike interventions (paying practices, facilities, physicians and patients are different policies). its qualitative conclusion — 'may improve processes, outcomes inconsistent' — is the strongest statement the evidence supports, which is why the stamp is maybe (weak evidence). alrashed a et al. from volume to value: a systematic review of payment and financial incentive models for preventive care delivery in primary health care. cureus. 2026. pmid: 42764853. mesh: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: incentives reliably change what is counted, unreliably change what matters
cards.summary: Synthesis: incentives reliably change what is counted, unreliably change what matters
cards.people: A screening-specific systematic review (18 studies) and a randomised-trials systematic review of primary-care payment models (10 studies).
cards.result: Cancer screening: partial or no effect in most studies, few positive colorectal results. Broader preventive care: possible gains in screening, vaccination and chronic-disease process measures; patient-centred outcomes inconsistent; evidence certainty very low to moderate with universal risk-of-bias concerns. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: the claim rests on heterogeneous, low-certainty review evidence.
cards.watchOut: Neither review can separate the effect of paying for performance from the effect of measuring it — schemes bundle targets, feedback and money together, so 'pay-for-performance works' is not a conclusion either record licenses.

shelves.title: Text messages and bowel screening: adding an SMS reminder raised kit return to 82.6% versus 77.7% — but swapping the reminder letter for an SMS cut participation to 17.2% versus 21.9%
shelves.question: Does adding a text-message (SMS) component to screening invitations increase bowel cancer screening participation versus invitation alone?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Text Messaging/statistics & numerical data · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnosis · Reminder Systems · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Aged · Spain · Patient Acceptance of Health Care/statistics & numerical data · Occult Blood
shelves.balance: SPLIT — adding a text helps; replacing the letter with a text hurts. In the Catalan screening programme, people who had collected a FIT kit but not returned it within 14 days completed screening more often when an SMS reminder was added: 64.2% versus 53.7% at 30 days and 82.6% versus 77.7% at 126 days (Vives N et al., PMID: 39083331). But when an SMS was sent instead of the routine postal reminder to non-completers at six weeks, participation fell to 17.2% versus 21.9% on the letter (odds ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.82), and the trial was stopped early; only after a recovery postal reminder did the SMS group's final participation (29.3%) overtake the control group's (26.5%) (Vives N et al., PMID: 39742454). PROPOSED SPLIT: an SMS added to the standard pathway increases participation; an SMS substituted for the letter decreases it — Tier C, as both trials come from one programme.

cards.headline: Vives 2024 (M-TICS, SMS added): FIT completion 64.2% versus 53.7% at 30 days and 82.6% versus 77.7% at 126 days with an added SMS reminder (P<0.001)
cards.summary: Vives 2024 (M-TICS, SMS added): FIT completion 64.2% versus 53.7% at 30 days and 82.6% versus 77.7% at 126 days with an added SMS reminder (P<0.001)
cards.people: People in the Catalonia, Spain colorectal screening programme who had picked up a FIT kit at a pharmacy but not returned it within 14 days: 4,563 received an SMS reminder on day 14 and 4,806 received no reminder; both groups received a 30-day reminder letter if needed. Registry ID: NCT04343950.
cards.result: FIT completion was higher with the SMS reminder at every time point: 64.2% versus 53.7% at 30 days, 78.6% versus 72.0% at 60 days, and 82.6% versus 77.7% at 126 days (P<0.001 throughout), with higher participation independent of sex, age, socioeconomic level and previous screening behaviour. In a telephone survey, 89.2% of interviewees considered SMS reminders important and useful and 93.4% preferred them to postal letters; the intervention reduced invitation costs by US $2.4 per participant gained.
cards.watchOut: The population had already collected a kit — the SMS is rescuing the nearly-compliant, not recruiting the uninvited, so its effect cannot be read across to first invitations. One programme, one country, one test type.

JMIR Public Health and Surveillance. 2024. PMID: 39083331. Registry ID: NCT04343950. cards.headline: Vives 2025 (SMS instead of letter): participation 17.2% versus 21.9% (OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.62–0.82) — trial stopped early; a rescue letter later reversed the deficit
cards.summary: Vives 2025 (SMS instead of letter): participation 17.2% versus 21.9% (OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.62–0.82) — trial stopped early; a rescue letter later reversed the deficit
cards.people: Adults aged 50–69 in the same Catalan FIT programme who had not completed screening within 6 weeks of invitation: 12,167 randomised to an SMS reminder and 12,221 to the standard reminder letter. The trial was stopped early in September 2022 on interim results; the interim analysis covered 5,570 people with complete 18-week follow-up. Registry ID: NCT04343950 (same programme registration as the companion trial).
cards.result: At the interim analysis, participation was 17.2% (477 of 2,781) in the SMS group versus 21.9% (610 of 2,789) in the letter group (OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.82; P<0.001). As a recovery strategy, 7,591 non-participants in the SMS group received a second reminder by letter and reached 23% participation; the final analysis (N=24,388) showed 29.3% (3,561 of 12,167) in the intervention group, which had by then received two reminders, versus 26.5% (3,235 of 12,221) in controls (OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.23; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The final-analysis 'win' compares two reminders against one — it shows a second contact helps, not that SMS beats letters. The clean randomised comparison is the interim one, and it favours the letter. Both M-TICS trials share one programme and registration, so this is one programme's evidence, not two independent confirmations.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the channel is an addition, not a substitute — SMS on top of the letter helps, SMS instead of it harms
cards.summary: Synthesis: the channel is an addition, not a substitute — SMS on top of the letter helps, SMS instead of it harms
cards.people: Two randomised trials from one Catalan FIT screening programme: 9,369 kit-collectors (SMS added) and 24,388 invited non-completers (SMS substituted for the letter).
cards.result: Added SMS: completion +10.5 points at 30 days and +4.9 points at 126 days. Substituted SMS: participation −4.7 points at interim (OR 0.71), reversed only by adding a postal reminder afterwards. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the split is between two uses of the same tool, demonstrated within a single programme.
cards.watchOut: Programmes elsewhere differ in mobile coverage, letter design and baseline participation; the direction of the split (add, don't substitute) is the transportable lesson, not the exact percentages.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vives N et al. JMIR Public Health and Surveillance. 2024 (PMID: 39083331); Vives N et al. JMIR mHealth and uHealth. 2025 (PMID: 39742454).

shelves.title: Opt-out hepatitis C testing in emergency departments: programmes found 182 new cases in one Dublin series and linked 86.2% of new diagnoses to care — but a Canadian universal programme found new cases in only 0.23% and linked just two patients
shelves.question: In emergency departments, does opt-out universal hepatitis C screening identify more new infections and link more people to care than risk-based testing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Choice Behavior · Diagnostic Services/statistics & numerical data · Emergency Service, Hospital/organization & administration/statistics & numerical data · Female · HIV Infections/diagnosis · Hepatitis B/diagnosis · Hepatitis C/diagnosis · Humans · Ireland · Male · Mass Screening/methods/standards/statistics & numerical data · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — opt-out testing demonstrably finds new infections; no study here compares it head-to-head with risk-based testing, and linkage varied from excellent to poor. In Dublin's three-year opt-out programme, 61.7% of patients who had blood taken accepted screening, 267 of 41,535 individual patients screened (12.1% of all positives) were newly diagnosed — including 182 new hepatitis C diagnoses — and 86.2% of new diagnoses were linked to care (Grant C et al., PMID: 31806726). In a Canadian university emergency department's universal opt-out programme, 62.1% of eligible patients were tested, the prevalence of new hepatitis C cases was 0.23% (95% CI 0.12 to 0.45), and only two newly diagnosed hepatitis C patients were linked to care at three months (Martel-Laferriere V et al., PMID: 35042704). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): universal opt-out screening identifies new hepatitis C infections that risk-based testing is designed to miss, but the yield and linkage dividend depend entirely on local prevalence and follow-up infrastructure — Tier C, observational evidence with no direct comparator.

cards.headline: Grant 2020 (Dublin, 3 years): 61.7% accepted opt-out screening; 182 new hepatitis C diagnoses among 267 new diagnoses overall; 86.2% of new diagnoses linked to care
cards.summary: Grant 2020 (Dublin, 3 years): 61.7% accepted opt-out screening; 182 new hepatitis C diagnoses among 267 new diagnoses overall; 86.2% of new diagnoses linked to care
cards.people: Emergency department patients at a Dublin, Ireland hospital from July 2015 to June 2018 who underwent phlebotomy and could consent: of 140,550 visits, 88,854 patients (63.2%) had blood taken and 54,817 (61.7%) accepted opt-out testing for HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C, representing 41,535 individual patients, with follow-up of 1 to 36 months.
cards.result: 2,202 patients tested positive; 267 (12.1%) were newly diagnosed infections and 1,762 (80.0%) were known diagnoses. New diagnoses comprised 38 HIV, 47 hepatitis B and 182 hepatitis C cases. Of patients with known diagnoses who were not linked to care, 81.5% (95% CI 74.9 to 87.0) were relinked after screening; of the new diagnoses, 86.2% (95% CI 80.4 to 90.8) were linked to care.
cards.watchOut: No risk-based comparator arm: the counterfactual — how many of these 182 hepatitis C cases risk-based testing would have caught — is unknown, and four-fifths of positives were already diagnosed, so the programme's largest measurable service was relinkage, not new detection. Yield reflects Dublin's inner-city prevalence and will not transport to low-prevalence departments.
cards.source: Grant C et al. Opt-out screening for HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C: observational study of screening acceptance, yield and treatment outcomes. Emergency Medicine Journal. 2020. PMID: 31806726. cards.headline: Martel-Laferriere 2022 (Canada): 62.1% tested under universal opt-out; new hepatitis C prevalence 0.23%; only two new hepatitis C patients linked to care at 3 months
cards.summary: Martel-Laferriere 2022 (Canada): 62.1% tested under universal opt-out; new hepatitis C prevalence 0.23%; only two new hepatitis C patients linked to care at 3 months
cards.people: Adults born after 1945 attending a Canadian university-hospital emergency department for any condition on any shift; of 6,350 eligible patients informed of the programme, 62.1% were tested for at least one virus (3,910 for hepatitis C), 25% opted out and 12% were not tested for organisational reasons. Registry ID: NCT03595527.
cards.result: Overall prevalence was 1.9% for hepatitis C and 1.2% for HIV; the prevalence of new cases was 0.23% (95% CI 0.12 to 0.45) for hepatitis C and 0.05% (95% CI 0.01 to 0.20) for HIV, and 0.3% (18 patients) were coinfected. Among the new cases, only two hepatitis-C-infected and one HIV-infected patient were linked to care three months after diagnosis. The authors concluded that identification of new cases and linkage to care were both low.
cards.watchOut: The same opt-out design as the Dublin programme produced a fraction of the yield and near-failed linkage — the difference is setting and follow-up infrastructure, not the test offer. Any claim for universal screening that quotes only the high-yield programme is cherry-picking; this card is the corrective.
cards.source: Martel-Laferriere V et al. Opt-out universal HCV and HIV screening in a Canadian emergency room: a cross-sectional study. BMJ Open. 2022. PMID: 35042704. Registry ID: NCT03595527. cards.headline: Synthesis: the offer finds cases everywhere; whether it helps depends on prevalence and on what happens after the result
cards.summary: Synthesis: the offer finds cases everywhere; whether it helps depends on prevalence and on what happens after the result
cards.people: Two opt-out emergency-department screening programmes: Dublin (41,535 individual patients over 3 years) and a Canadian university department (6,350 eligible patients); neither included a risk-based-testing comparator.
cards.result: New hepatitis C diagnoses: 182 in Dublin, where 86.2% of all new diagnoses were linked to care; new-case prevalence 0.23% in Canada, where only two new hepatitis C patients were linked at 3 months. Testing uptake was near-identical (61.7% and 62.1%). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: the identification half of the question is answered affirmatively but observationally; the 'more than risk-based testing' half has never been directly tested in these records — a declared gap.
cards.watchOut: Screening that identifies infections without linking patients to treatment delivers cost without cure. These two programmes, read together, argue that the linkage pathway — not the opt-out offer — is the intervention that decides value.
cards.source: Synthesis of Grant C et al. Emergency Medicine Journal. 2020 (PMID: 31806726); Martel-Laferriere V et al. BMJ Open. 2022 (PMID: 35042704).

shelves.title: Home self-collection kits for chlamydia and gonorrhoea: testing uptake 2.61 times higher than clinic collection in a 15-trial meta-analysis — and mailing men a kit directly made testing 11.1 times as likely as usual care
shelves.question: Does offering home self-collection kits for chlamydia and gonorrhoea increase STI screening uptake versus clinic-based testing invitations?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Gonorrhea/diagnosis · Chlamydia Infections/diagnosis · Specimen Handling/methods · Chlamydia trachomatis/isolation & purification · Neisseria gonorrhoeae/isolation & purification · Self Care/methods · Mass Screening/methods
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — offering people a home kit gets substantially more of them tested, and those who test positive reach care at the same rate. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies, including 15 randomised trials with 62,369 participants, found uptake of chlamydia or gonorrhoea testing was 2.61 times higher with home self-collection than with clinic-based collection, with high concordance between home and clinic specimens and no significant difference in linkage to care (prevalence ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.01) (Smith AC et al., PMID: 39191483). In the largest single outreach trial pattern inside that evidence, mailing young men a sampling kit directly produced a relative risk of being tested of 11.1 (95% CI 7.3 to 16.9) versus usual care — though absolute return rates stayed low, at 7.8% (Scholes D et al., PMID: 17538514). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): home self-collection multiplies screening uptake severalfold over clinic invitations — a solid randomised-trial meta-analysis, so not Tier C; the caveat is that multiplied uptake can still be a small absolute number.

cards.headline: Smith 2024 meta-analysis: uptake 2.61 times higher at home than in clinic across 15 randomised trials; linkage to care not significantly different (PR 0.96, 95% CI 0.91–1.01)
cards.summary: Smith 2024 meta-analysis: uptake 2.61 times higher at home than in clinic across 15 randomised trials; linkage to care not significantly different (PR 0.96, 95% CI 0.91–1.01)
cards.people: 19 studies from 1998 to 2024 directly comparing specimens self-collected at home or in other non-clinical settings with collection at a healthcare facility for chlamydia and/or gonorrhoea testing: 15 randomised trials totalling 62,369 participants, plus four concordance studies with 906 participants; randomised trials were appraised with the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool.
cards.result: Uptake of chlamydia or gonorrhoea testing was 2.61 times higher at home compared with clinical settings. Concordance between specimens collected at home and in clinical settings was high, and linkage to care was not significantly different between the two settings (prevalence ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.01). The authors conclude that offering home self-collection as an additional strategy could increase sexually transmitted infection testing in countries that have not yet widely adopted it.
cards.watchOut: 'Additional strategy' is the authors' own framing: the trials mostly test home kits offered alongside or instead of clinic invitations in motivated study populations. The 2.61-fold figure is a relative effect — where clinic uptake is very low, home uptake can be several-fold higher and still leave most invitees untested, as the second card shows.

cards.headline: Scholes 2007 randomised trial in men: mailed kit — testing relative risk 11.1 (95% CI 7.3–16.9) versus usual care, but only 7.8% returned a specimen
cards.summary: Scholes 2007 randomised trial in men: mailed kit — testing relative risk 11.1 (95% CI 7.3–16.9) versus usual care, but only 7.8% returned a specimen
cards.people: 8,820 male health-plan enrollees aged 21–25 in Washington State, randomised to a letter plus a test-request card for a home urine sampling kit (n=2,940), a letter plus a directly mailed mail-back sampling kit (n=2,940), or usual care (n=2,940), with one reminder to the intervention arms; the outcome was chlamydia testing within four months.
cards.result: 105 of 2,940 men (3.6%) in the request-card arm and 230 of 2,940 (7.8%) in the direct-kit arm returned mailed specimens. Compared with usual care, the relative risk of being tested was 5.6 (95% CI 3.6 to 8.7) for the request-card arm and 11.1 (95% CI 7.3 to 16.9) for the direct-kit arm, and the direct kit beat the request card significantly. Chlamydia prevalence among returned specimens was 1.0% (1 of 105) and 2.6% (6 of 230); 70% of all positive intervention tests came from mailed samples. Overall intervention response was 5.7%.
cards.watchOut: The relative risks are spectacular because usual-care testing in young men was near zero; the absolute yield was 335 tests and 7 positives from 5,880 mailed invitations. Home kits solve the access problem, not the motivation problem — both facts belong on the shelf.
cards.source: Scholes D et al. Population-based outreach for Chlamydia screening in men: results from a randomized trial. Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 2007. PMID: 17538514. cards.headline: Synthesis: severalfold relative gains, honest absolute numbers, no linkage penalty
cards.summary: Synthesis: severalfold relative gains, honest absolute numbers, no linkage penalty
cards.people: A meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials (62,369 participants) comparing home self-collection with clinic collection, plus a three-arm randomised outreach trial in 8,820 young men.
cards.result: Uptake ratio 2.61 for home versus clinic collection; linkage to care prevalence ratio 0.96 (not significant); specimen concordance high. In the men's outreach trial, relative risks of testing were 5.6 (kit on request) and 11.1 (kit mailed directly) against absolute returns of 3.6% and 7.8%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), not Tier C: a large randomised-trial meta-analysis carries the claim.
cards.watchOut: Uptake is a process outcome: the records show more testing and equal linkage, not fewer complications of untreated infection. Programmes should budget for the low absolute returns the relative risks conceal.
cards.source: Synthesis of Smith AC et al. BMJ Global Health. 2024 (PMID: 39191483); Scholes D et al. Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 2007 (PMID: 17538514).

shelves.title: Community health workers and cancer screening in underserved communities: uptake odds 2.25 for colorectal screening in minority populations and 1.90 across breast, cervical and bowel screening in two randomised-trial meta-analyses
shelves.question: In underserved communities, do community health worker programmes increase cancer screening uptake versus usual outreach?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnosis/ethnology · Community Health Workers · Early Detection of Cancer/statistics & numerical data · Ethnic and Racial Minorities/statistics & numerical data · United States · Mass Screening/statistics & numerical data · Patient Acceptance of Health Care/statistics & numerical data/ethnology · Minority Groups/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two independent meta-analyses of randomised trials point the same way. For colorectal screening in racial and ethnic minority populations, community-health-worker-led interventions increased uptake versus no intervention with an odds ratio of 2.25 (95% CI 1.48 to 3.44; P<0.001) across 10 US randomised trials, and multicomponent interventions worked best across all groups (Rana T et al., PMID: 36927698). Across breast, cervical and bowel screening, a second meta-analysis of 30 randomised trials found participation associated with an odds ratio of 1.901 (95% CI 1.60 to 2.26; P<0.001), with larger effects in people previously non-adherent to screening schedules and 25 of 30 studies conducted in ethnic minority groups (Bellhouse S et al., PMID: 29080378). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): community health worker programmes increase cancer screening uptake in underserved communities — not Tier C, because two concordant randomised-trial meta-analyses carry it; the stamp stays at POSSIBLE because study quality in the larger review was generally poor.

cards.headline: Rana 2024: colorectal screening uptake OR 2.25 (95% CI 1.48–3.44) for community-health-worker interventions versus no intervention in 10 US randomised trials
cards.summary: Rana 2024: colorectal screening uptake OR 2.25 (95% CI 1.48–3.44) for community-health-worker interventions versus no intervention in 10 US randomised trials
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Rana 2024)
cards.people: 10 randomised controlled trials conducted in the United States of community-health-worker-led interventions to improve colorectal cancer screening uptake in racial and ethnic minority populations, identified from five databases searched in May 2022.
cards.result: Colorectal screening uptake was enhanced in participants receiving community-health-worker-led interventions compared with no intervention (odds ratio 2.25, 95% CI 1.48 to 3.44; P<0.001). Subgroup analyses by ethnic group and by intervention components showed multicomponent interventions were more effective in increasing uptake among all racial and ethnic groups. The authors conclude multicomponent community-health-worker interventions can improve colorectal screening uptake in minority populations and may transfer to other countries.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is 'no intervention', not an active outreach programme — the trials cannot say whether community health workers beat cheaper alternatives such as mailed kits, only that they beat doing nothing. All 10 trials are US-based.
cards.source: Rana T et al. Effectiveness of Community Health Worker-Led Interventions in Enhancing Colorectal Cancer Screening Uptake in Racial and Ethnic Minority Populations: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. cards.headline: Bellhouse 2018: screening receipt OR 1.901 (95% CI 1.60–2.26) across 30 randomised trials of community-based health workers — largest gains in the previously non-adherent
cards.summary: Bellhouse 2018: screening receipt OR 1.901 (95% CI 1.60–2.26) across 30 randomised trials of community-based health workers — largest gains in the previously non-adherent
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Bellhouse 2018)
cards.people: 30 eligible randomised trials with a cancer screening outcome (breast, cervical and bowel screening); 25 of the 30 studies were conducted with ethnic minority groups, and 15 (45%) explicitly reported a theoretical foundation for the intervention.
cards.result: Participation in community-based health worker interventions was associated with increased receipt of screening (OR 1.901, 95% CI 1.60 to 2.26; P<0.001) for breast, cervical and bowel cancer. Larger effect sizes were observed in participants previously non-adherent with recommended screening schedules. The number of behaviour-change techniques used showed only a trend-level association with effect size (P=0.08). Study quality was generally poor, with inadequate blinding and reliance on self-reported outcomes the common limitations.
cards.watchOut: Self-reported screening in unblinded trials inflates effects, and the review's own quality verdict is 'generally poor' — the OR of 1.90 should be read as an upper-middle estimate. Effects are concentrated in minority and previously non-adherent populations, which is the shelf's population, but says little about general-population programmes.
cards.source: Bellhouse S et al. Are community-based health worker interventions an effective approach for early diagnosis of cancer? A systematic review and meta-analysis. Psycho-Oncology. 2018. cards.people: Two meta-analyses of randomised trials: 10 US trials in minority populations (colorectal screening) and 30 trials across breast, cervical and bowel screening, 25 of them in ethnic minority groups.

shelves.title: Babesiosis: atovaquone plus azithromycin cleared parasites as completely as clindamycin plus quinine — with adverse effects in 15% versus 72% (tinnitus in 39% on the old regimen)
shelves.question: In non-life-threatening babesiosis, is atovaquone plus azithromycin as effective as clindamycin plus quinine — and how do the two regimens compare on adverse effects?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Animals · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antiprotozoal Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Atovaquone · Azithromycin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Babesia/genetics/isolation & purification · Babesiosis/drug therapy/parasitology · Clindamycin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · DNA, Protozoan/blood · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Naphthoquinones/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Quinine/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the benefit is tolerability at equal efficacy, in the only randomised trial. In that trial (Krause PJ et al., PMID: 11078770), 58 subjects with non-life-threatening babesiosis in southern New England received seven days of atovaquone plus azithromycin (40 subjects) or clindamycin plus quinine (18 subjects). Parasite clearance was complete in both groups: three months after treatment, no parasites were visible on microscopy and no Babesia microti DNA was detectable in any subject, and by six months no patient in either group had symptoms (symptom resolution at three months: 65% versus 73%, p=0.66). The difference was harm: adverse effects in 15% on atovaquone–azithromycin versus 72% on clindamycin–quinine (p<0.001) — on the older regimen, tinnitus in 39%, diarrhoea in 33% and decreased hearing in 28%, against diarrhoea and rash at 8% each on the newer one. The trial was small and nonblinded, and it excluded life-threatening disease, so it says nothing about severe babesiosis, exchange transfusion, or immunocompromised patients, where this evidence does not reach. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for non-severe babesiosis, atovaquone plus azithromycin is the regimen patients can actually finish — Tier C, a single small trial.

cards.headline: Krause 2000: parasite clearance complete in both arms at 3 months — adverse effects 15% on atovaquone–azithromycin versus 72% on clindamycin–quinine
cards.summary: Krause 2000: parasite clearance complete in both arms at 3 months — adverse effects 15% on atovaquone–azithromycin versus 72% on clindamycin–quinine
cards.people: 58 subjects with non-life-threatening babesiosis on Nantucket, Block Island and in southern Connecticut, assigned to atovaquone 750 mg every 12 hours plus azithromycin (500 mg on day 1, then 250 mg daily) for seven days (40 subjects) or clindamycin 600 mg every 8 hours plus quinine 650 mg every 8 hours for seven days (18 subjects); prospective, nonblinded.
cards.result: Adverse effects were reported by 15% of the atovaquone–azithromycin group versus 72% of the clindamycin–quinine group (p<0.001); the commonest on the newer regimen were diarrhoea and rash (8% each), and on the older regimen tinnitus (39%), diarrhoea (33%) and decreased hearing (28%). Symptoms had resolved by three months in 65% versus 73% (p=0.66), and by six months in all patients in both groups. Three months after treatment, microscopy showed no parasites and PCR detected no Babesia microti DNA in any subject in either group.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-eight patients, an unequal 40:18 allocation, no blinding, and a tolerability outcome that patients could hardly fail to notice on quinine — the adverse-effect gap is real in direction but its size is soft. Life-threatening babesiosis was excluded, so the shelf cannot be stretched to severe disease or to asplenic and immunocompromised patients.
cards.source: Krause PJ et al. Atovaquone and azithromycin for the treatment of babesiosis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2000. PMID: 11078770. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.question: For non-severe scrub typhus — and for the undifferentiated acute fever in Southeast Asia where scrub typhus and leptospirosis are the leading treatable causes — is azithromycin as effective as doxycycline, the standard drug?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on efficacy, with a tolerability edge to azithromycin; severe scrub typhus lives on its own shelf (INTREST) and is not this question. In South Korea (Kim YS et al., PMID: 15494910), 93 patients with mild scrub typhus were randomised open-label to a single 500 mg dose of azithromycin or doxycycline 200 mg daily for a week: cure was achieved in 47 (100%) of 47 on azithromycin and 43 (93.5%) of 46 on doxycycline (p=0.117), median time to defervescence 21 versus 29 hours (p=0.097), no serious adverse events and no relapses in either group over one month. In Thailand (Phimda K et al., PMID: 17638700), 296 adults with acute undifferentiated fever were randomised to 7 days of doxycycline or 3 days of azithromycin; among the 151 with a determined cause — 69 leptospirosis, 57 scrub typhus, 14 murine typhus, 11 mixed — azithromycin was not inferior to doxycycline for both leptospirosis and scrub typhus with comparable fever clearance times (the record reports no arm-specific cure rates, so none are quoted), and adverse events were less frequent with azithromycin (10.6% versus 27.6%; p=0.02), against which the authors set azithromycin's higher cost and lower availability. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in mild disease the drugs performed alike in both randomised comparisons — two small open-label trials, so the stamp stays POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Kim 2004 (South Korea, n=93, mild scrub typhus): single-dose azithromycin cure 100% (47/47) versus doxycycline 93.5% (43/46); defervescence 21 versus 29 hours; no relapses
cards.summary: Kim 2004 (South Korea, n=93, mild scrub typhus): single-dose azithromycin cure 100% (47/47) versus doxycycline 93.5% (43/46); defervescence 21 versus 29 hours; no relapses
cards.people: 93 patients with mild scrub typhus in South Korea (September 2002–November 2003), randomly assigned to a single 500-mg dose of azithromycin (n=47) or doxycycline 200 mg daily orally for one week (n=46); primary comparison was time to defervescence, with cure and one-month relapse assessed.
cards.result: Cure was achieved in 47 (100%) of 47 patients in the azithromycin group and 43 (93.5%) of 46 in the doxycycline group (p=0.117). Median time to defervescence was 21 hours with azithromycin and 29 hours with doxycycline (p=0.097). There were no serious adverse events, and no relapses occurred in either group during one month of follow-up. The authors concluded a single 500-mg dose of azithromycin was as effective as a week of doxycycline for mild scrub typhus acquired in South Korea.
cards.watchOut: Mild disease only, 93 patients, open-label, one country — the trial cannot speak to severe scrub typhus (a separate shelf), to doxycycline-resistant strains reported elsewhere, or to pregnancy, where the choice matters most and randomised data are absent.
cards.source: Kim YS et al. A comparative trial of a single dose of azithromycin versus doxycycline for the treatment of mild scrub typhus. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2004. PMID: 15494910. cards.headline: Phimda 2007 (Thailand, n=296 undifferentiated fever): azithromycin not inferior to doxycycline for leptospirosis and scrub typhus; adverse events 10.6% versus 27.6% (p=0.02)
cards.summary: Phimda 2007 (Thailand, n=296 undifferentiated fever): azithromycin not inferior to doxycycline for leptospirosis and scrub typhus; adverse events 10.6% versus 27.6% (p=0.02)
cards.people: 296 adults presenting with acute fever under 15 days without an obvious focus at four hospitals in Thailand (July 2003–January 2005), randomised to doxycycline for 7 days or azithromycin for 3 days; the cause of fever was determined in 151 patients (51%) — 69 leptospirosis, 57 scrub typhus, 14 murine typhus, 11 with both leptospirosis and a rickettsial infection.
cards.result: The efficacy of azithromycin was not inferior to that of doxycycline for the treatment of both leptospirosis and scrub typhus, with comparable fever clearance times in the two arms; the record reports no arm-specific cure percentages, so none are quoted. Adverse events occurred more frequently in the doxycycline group than the azithromycin group (27.6% versus 10.6%; p=0.02). The authors concluded doxycycline is an affordable and effective choice for both infections, while azithromycin was better tolerated but more expensive and less readily available.
cards.watchOut: Half the enrolled fevers never got a diagnosis, so the disease-specific claim rests on the 151 confirmed cases; severe leptospirosis and severe scrub typhus are different questions with their own shelves — this trial is about the ambulant, undifferentiated presentation.
cards.source: Phimda K et al. Doxycycline versus azithromycin for treatment of leptospirosis and scrub typhus. Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. 2007. PMID: 17638700. cards.headline: Synthesis: for mild scrub typhus and the fevers that mimic it, azithromycin is a genuine alternative — equal cures in both trials, gentler on patients, dearer and scarcer
cards.summary: Synthesis: for mild scrub typhus and the fevers that mimic it, azithromycin is a genuine alternative — equal cures in both trials, gentler on patients, dearer and scarcer
cards.people: Two randomised open-label trials: 93 patients with mild scrub typhus in South Korea and 296 adults with undifferentiated acute fever in Thailand (151 with confirmed leptospirosis, scrub typhus, murine typhus or mixed infection).
cards.result: Cure 100% versus 93.5% (single-dose azithromycin versus week-long doxycycline, mild scrub typhus); non-inferior efficacy with comparable fever clearance in the fever trial; adverse events 10.6% versus 27.6% favouring azithromycin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on efficacy — two concordant randomised trials, both small and open-label.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial enrolled severe disease, children as a defined group, or pregnant women — the populations where the doxycycline alternative is most wanted. Resistance patterns in Orientia vary by place and era; local guidance governs.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kim YS et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2004 (PMID: 15494910); Phimda K et al. Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. 2007 (PMID: 17638700).

shelves.title: Ibuprofen cut acute mountain sickness on rapid ascent in two trials (43% versus 69%; 24.4% versus 40.4% in intention-to-treat) — but the larger trial's per-protocol analysis went null, and ibuprofen can mask the headache that defines the diagnosis
shelves.question: In people ascending rapidly to high altitude, does ibuprofen prevent acute mountain sickness compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Altitude Sickness/prevention & control · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Ibuprofen/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Male · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two double-blind placebo-controlled trials, positive on their primary analyses, with an honest crack in the larger one. Lipman 2012 (PMID: 22440488) found acute mountain sickness in 43% on ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily versus 69% on placebo on ascent to 3,810 m (odds ratio 0.3, 95% CI 0.1 to 0.8; number needed to treat 3.9), with lower severity scores (3.2 versus 4.4). Gertsch 2012 (ASCENT, PMID: 23098412) found acute mountain sickness in 24.4% versus 40.4% in the intention-to-treat analysis (P=.01) and less high-altitude headache (42.3% versus 60.5%, P<.01) — but among the 183 of 294 recruits who completed the trial per protocol, the difference was not significant (22.7% versus 32.9%, P=.129). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ibuprofen probably reduces acute mountain sickness on rapid ascent, with the per-protocol null and the headache-masking problem printed on the face of the shelf.

cards.headline: Lipman 2012: acute mountain sickness in 43% on ibuprofen versus 69% on placebo (odds ratio 0.3) on ascent to 3,810 m
cards.summary: Lipman 2012: acute mountain sickness in 43% on ibuprofen versus 69% on placebo (odds ratio 0.3) on ascent to 3,810 m
cards.people: 86 healthy low-altitude adult volunteers who completed the study (44 ibuprofen, 42 placebo), randomised to ibuprofen 600 mg or placebo three times daily starting 6 hours before ascent from 1,240 m to 3,810 m in the White Mountains of California, July–August 2010; acute mountain sickness defined by Lake Louise Questionnaire score ≥3 with headache and at least one other symptom.
cards.result: Acute mountain sickness developed in 43% of the ibuprofen group versus 69% of the placebo group (odds ratio 0.3, 95% CI 0.1 to 0.8; number needed to treat 3.9, 95% CI 2 to 33). Severity was lower on ibuprofen (score 3.2 [SD 2.4] versus 4.4 [SD 2.6]). There were no differences in demographic characteristics between the groups.
cards.watchOut: A small, single-ascent volunteer study with a very high placebo event rate (69%) — the absolute benefit (26 percentage points) is unlikely to be this large on slower, real-world ascents. The outcome is a symptom questionnaire in which headache is compulsory, and ibuprofen is an analgesic: some of the 'prevention' may be masking.
cards.source: Lipman GS et al. Ibuprofen prevents altitude illness: a randomized controlled trial for prevention of altitude illness with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories. Annals of Emergency Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22440488. cards.headline: Gertsch 2012 (ASCENT): intention-to-treat acute mountain sickness 24.4% versus 40.4% (P=.01) — but per-protocol 22.7% versus 32.9% (P=.129, not significant)
cards.summary: Gertsch 2012 (ASCENT): intention-to-treat acute mountain sickness 24.4% versus 40.4% (P=.01) — but per-protocol 22.7% versus 32.9% (P=.129, not significant)
cards.people: 294 healthy Western trekkers recruited on the Everest approach at 4,280 m or 4,358 m, randomised to ibuprofen 600 mg or placebo three times daily before and during ascent to 4,928 m; 183 completed the trial per protocol (62 lost to follow-up, 49 broke protocol), with the intention-to-treat analysis covering 232 participants.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, ibuprofen reduced acute mountain sickness (24.4% versus 40.4%; P=.01) and high-altitude headache (42.3% versus 60.5%; P<.01), and reduced severe high-altitude headache (4.9% versus 14.7%; P=.01). Among the 183 per-protocol completers, acute mountain sickness incidence was 22.7% versus 32.9% (P=.129), not significant, with headache incidence and severity also non-significant.
cards.watchOut: Over a third of recruits did not complete the trial, and the result flips with the analysis population — the authors note sicker placebo patients may have complied less, biasing the per-protocol comparison. The authors also name the central artefact themselves: ibuprofen can mask headache, a compulsory criterion for diagnosing acute mountain sickness.
cards.source: Gertsch JH et al. Altitude Sickness in Climbers and Efficacy of NSAIDs Trial (ASCENT): randomized, controlled trial of ibuprofen versus placebo for prevention of altitude illness. Wilderness & Environmental Medicine. 2012. PMID: 23098412. shelves.title: School-located flu vaccination: programmes add about 7–12 percentage points of coverage (randomised programme trial and Oakland's city-wide rollout), with fewer illness absences and fewer community flu hospitalisations in seasons when the vaccine worked
shelves.question: Does school-located influenza vaccination increase children's vaccination coverage and reduce illness-related school absence?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Absenteeism · Adolescent · California · Child · Child, Preschool · Cohort Studies · Cross-Sectional Studies · Female · Humans · Influenza Vaccines · Influenza, Human · Male · School Health Services · Schools · Students · Urban Population · Vaccination · Vaccination Coverage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The programme evidence is consistent across three designs. A 2010 systematic review of 59 studies found school-located influenza vaccination (SLIV) programmes feasible and effective, with consent-form design, incentives, education, reminders and offering both injected and intranasal vaccine raising consent and coverage. A randomised programme trial in western New York elementary schools raised the proportion of children vaccinated by 11.2 and 12.0 percentage points over control schools in its two years, at about $59.88 per additionally vaccinated child excluding vaccine purchase — falling to about $24 per child once averted parental costs were counted. A city-wide Oakland matched-cohort evaluation (at least 95 schools, 2014–2018) found coverage 7 and 11 percentage points higher in the later seasons, illness-related absences lower by 0.63–0.80 days per 100 school days, and fewer laboratory-confirmed influenza hospitalisations in the wider community in seasons when the vaccine was moderately effective. No individual-patient efficacy claim is made here — this is a delivery question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Cawley 2010: a systematic review of 59 studies found school-located influenza vaccination feasible and effective — consent-form design, reminders and offering both shot and nasal spray raised coverage
cards.summary: Cawley 2010: a systematic review of 59 studies found school-located influenza vaccination feasible and effective — consent-form design, reminders and offering both shot and nasal spray raised coverage
cards.people: Systematic literature review (searches to January 7, 2008, across PubMed, PsychLit and Dissertation Abstracts) of school-located vaccination of children aged 6–12 and adolescents 13–18, undertaken after the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices recommended influenza vaccination for all children 6 months to 18 years: 59 studies met the criteria for review. The record reports no pooled effect size and no single participant total — printed as such.
cards.result: Strategies such as incentives, education, the design of the consent form, and follow-up increased parental consent and the number of returned forms. Minimising out-of-pocket cost, offering both the intramuscular (shot) and intranasal (nasal spray) vaccination, and using reminders increased vaccination coverage among those whose parents consented. Organisation, communication and planning minimised the logistical challenges. The authors conclude school-based vaccination programmes are a promising, feasible and effective option for achieving the expanded recommendation, and call for prospective well-controlled trials of cost-effectiveness — the gap the two later cards on this shelf partly fill.
cards.watchOut: An implementation review, not an effectiveness meta-analysis: it establishes what makes programmes work and that coverage rises, but pools no numbers — the quantitative claims on this shelf rest on the two programme evaluations carded below.
cards.source: Cawley J et al. Strategies for implementing school-located influenza vaccination of children: a systematic literature review. The Journal of School Health. 2010. PMID: 20433642. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Yoo 2015: in a randomised elementary-school programme trial, school-located vaccination raised coverage by about 12 percentage points (40.4% vs roughly 28% in control schools in Year 2)
cards.summary: Yoo 2015: in a randomised elementary-school programme trial, school-located vaccination raised coverage by about 12 percentage points (40.4% vs roughly 28% in control schools in Year 2)
cards.type: Cost-effectiveness analysis of a randomised controlled programme trial (Yoo 2015)
cards.people: Cost-effectiveness analysis of a two-year community-based randomised controlled trial of a school-located influenza vaccination programme in western New York elementary schools: 21 intervention schools (Year 1 n = 9,027; Year 2 n = 9,145 children) offered school-located clinics, versus control schools with standard of care — no school programme (Year 1: 10 schools, n = 4,534; Year 2: 11 schools, n = 4,796). Year 1 (2009–2010) was the unusual H1N1 pandemic season; Year 2 (2010–2011) was a more typical season.
cards.result: The proportion of children vaccinated was 11.2 percentage points higher in intervention than control schools in Year 1 (40.7% in intervention schools) and 12.0 percentage points higher in Year 2 (40.4%). In Year 2 the cost per additionally vaccinated child, excluding vaccine purchase, was $59.88 (2010 US dollars) — school costs $8.25, project coordination $32.33 and vendor costs $16.68 by Monte Carlo simulation — higher than the published $39.54 cost of vaccination in medical practices; but counting indirect costs such as averted parental time and travel, school-located vaccination was less costly ($24.07 in Year 2) than medical-practice vaccination.
cards.watchOut: The trial randomised schools, not children, and the headline product is cost per extra child vaccinated, not illness prevented; the favourable $24 figure depends on valuing averted parental costs, and coordination was the largest cost component — the authors say efficiencies are needed for a sustainable, scalable programme.
cards.source: Yoo BK et al. Cost effectiveness analysis of Year 2 of an elementary school-located influenza vaccination program-Results from a randomized controlled trial. BMC Health Services Research. 2015. PMID: 26573461. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Benjamin-Chung 2020: Oakland's city-wide school programme raised coverage by up to 11 points, cut illness absence, and was followed by fewer flu hospitalisations community-wide in effective-vaccine seasons
cards.summary: Benjamin-Chung 2020: Oakland's city-wide school programme raised coverage by up to 11 points, cut illness absence, and was followed by fewer flu hospitalisations community-wide in effective-vaccine seasons
cards.people: Matched cohort evaluation of a city-wide school-located influenza vaccination intervention in at least 95 preschools and elementary schools in Oakland, California, 2014–2018, against a matched nearby comparison district. Vaccination coverage was surveyed in 22 school pairs (2017 survey N = 6,070; 2018 survey N = 6,507 caregivers); absenteeism was analysed over 42,487,816 student-days (2011–2018), and laboratory-confirmed influenza hospitalisations from surveillance data for 2011–2018. The programme itself vaccinated 7,502 to 10,106 students (22%–28% of eligible students) each year.
cards.result: Coverage among elementary students was 53%–66% in the comparison district; it was similar between districts in 2014–2015 and 2015–2016 and significantly higher in the intervention district in 2016–2017 (by 7 percentage points, 95% CI 4 to 11) and 2017–2018 (by 11 percentage points, 95% CI 7 to 15). In those same seasons, illness-related school absences were lower by 0.63 (95% CI −1.14 to −0.13) and 0.80 (−1.28 to −0.31) absences per 100 school days, and difference-in-differences in laboratory-confirmed influenza hospitalisation incidence favoured the intervention site among non-elementary-school-aged people (−17 and −37 per 100,000) and among adults 65 and over (−73 and −160 per 100,000) — indirect (community) effects seen only in seasons when coverage rose and the vaccine was moderately effective.
cards.watchOut: Observational by design — the authors name unmeasured confounding and caregiver-reported vaccination status (poor recall, low response rates) as limitations — and the absence and hospitalisation benefits appeared only in the two seasons when coverage actually separated and the vaccine worked moderately well; in the first two seasons there was no coverage gap and no effect to find.
cards.source: Benjamin-Chung J et al. Evaluation of a city-wide school-located influenza vaccination program in Oakland, California, with respect to vaccination coverage, school absences, and laboratory-confirmed influenza: A matched cohort study. PLoS Medicine. 2020. PMID: 32810149. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: school-located flu vaccination reliably adds roughly 7–12 percentage points of coverage where it is run well, and the one large city evaluation links that gain to less illness absence and fewer community flu hospitalisations
cards.summary: Synthesis: school-located flu vaccination reliably adds roughly 7–12 percentage points of coverage where it is run well, and the one large city evaluation links that gain to less illness absence and fewer community flu hospitalisations
cards.people: The carded evidence: one systematic implementation review (59 studies), one randomised elementary-school programme trial with cost-effectiveness analysis (about 9,100 intervention and 4,800 control children in Year 2), and one city-wide matched cohort evaluation (at least 95 schools; 42.5 million student-days of absence data). No card tests vaccine efficacy itself — only the delivery route.
cards.result: Coverage rose wherever the programme was delivered: +11.2 and +12.0 percentage points in the randomised New York programme (Yoo 2015), and +7 and +11 percentage points in Oakland's later seasons against an already high 53%–66% comparison-district background (Benjamin-Chung 2020); the 2010 review (Cawley) identifies the levers — consent-form design, reminders, no out-of-pocket cost, choice of shot or nasal spray. Downstream, Oakland saw 0.63–0.80 fewer illness absences per 100 school days and lower community influenza hospitalisation rates in the seasons the coverage gap opened. Costs are real (about $59.88 per extra child vaccinated before counting averted parental costs). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised programme trial plus observational programme evidence.
cards.watchOut: Effects are season-dependent: they require both a real coverage gap and a vaccine that matches and works that year. A district already achieving high coverage through clinics may gain little, and none of these studies was powered on child hospitalisation as its own endpoint.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cawley J et al. The Journal of School Health. 2010 (PMID: 20433642); Yoo BK et al. BMC Health Services Research. 2015 (PMID: 26573461); Benjamin-Chung J et al. PLoS Medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32810149).
